fomalhaut.name: Fomalhaut
fomalhaut.introduction: is the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, about 25 light-years away, and one of the four “royal stars” of ancient Persia. Its brilliant white primary anchors a wide triple system: its companions, the orange dwarf TW Piscis Austrini and the red dwarf LP 876-10, lie about 8 degrees apart in our sky.

sections.title: Belts beyond the star
sections.text: Webb revealed nested belts of dusty debris around Fomalhaut A. Collisions between smaller bodies continually replenish the dust, making this one of the nearest places to study how planetary systems evolve.

source.title: NASA: Webb reveals Fomalhaut’s debris belts

sections.title: A planet that turned out to be dust
sections.text: In 2008, Fomalhaut b became the first planet candidate ever imaged at visible wavelengths, apparently orbiting just inside the outer debris ring. Analyses in 2019 and 2023 concluded that it is not a planet but an expanding cloud of debris from a massive collision.

sections.title: Collisions caught in the act
sections.text: In 2025, astronomers reported a second, newly appearing cloud of collision debris in Hubble images: a rare chance to watch destructive collisions around another star as they happen.

source.title: NASA: Hubble observes new collision debris around Fomalhaut, 2025

cns5-4607.name: Vega
cns5-4607.introduction: is the fifth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in Lyra, about 25 light-years away. Called “arguably the next most important star in the sky after the Sun,” it has long served as a yardstick for stellar brightness.

sections.title: A string of firsts
sections.text: On July 17, 1850, William Bond and John Adams Whipple at Harvard photographed Vega, the first star other than the Sun ever captured on a photographic plate. In 1872, Henry Draper photographed its spectrum, the first stellar spectrum to show absorption lines. Vega was also one of the stars used to define the zero point of the magnitude scale.

sections.title: A pole star of the past and future
sections.text: Earth’s slowly wobbling axis made Vega the northern pole star around 12,000 BCE, and it will be again around the year 13,700. It is the brightest of all the stars that take turns as the northern pole star.

sections.title: A fast spinner seen pole-on
sections.text: Vega spins at about 236 km/s at its equator, but we look almost straight down on one of its poles. Its equator bulges outward and is cooler than its poles, so a simple-looking point of light hides a strongly uneven surface.

sections.title: The first dusty disk
sections.text: In 1983, the IRAS satellite found more infrared light than Vega alone should emit: it was the first star found to have a disk of dust, and similar stars are now called Vega-like. In the 1997 film Contact, the first alien radio message arrives from the Vega system.

sections.title: A remarkably smooth debris disk
sections.text: Hubble and Webb observations published in 2024 showed a broad, unusually smooth disk of dust, with no obvious gaps carved by large planets.

source.title: NASA: Hubble and Webb probe Vega’s smooth disk, 2024

cns5-1912.name: Pollux
cns5-1912.introduction: is an orange giant in Gemini, about 34 light-years away, and the closest giant star to the Sun. Though designated beta, it is brighter than its twin, Castor.

sections.title: The heavenly twins
sections.text: Castor and Pollux are the twins of Greek and Roman myth who give Gemini its name. The two stars are unrelated, though: Pollux is a single evolved giant, while Castor is a family of six stars.

sections.title: A giant with a giant planet
sections.text: Pollux b, announced in 2006, takes about 590 days to orbit and has at least twice Jupiter’s mass. In 2015 it was named Thestias, after the patronym of Leda, the twins’ mother in myth.

sections.title: A standard giant
sections.text: Since 1943, Pollux’s spectrum has served as one of the stable anchor points for classifying other stars. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, it shows what becomes of a star somewhat more massive than the Sun after its main-sequence life.

hip-57632.name: Denebola
hip-57632.introduction: is the lion’s tail in Leo, about 36 light-years away; its name comes from the Arabic for “tail of the lion.” This white star has about 75% more mass than the Sun and 15 times its luminosity.

sections.title: Dust from a debris system
sections.text: Denebola shows a strong infrared excess: cool dust in a circumstellar debris disk, left by collisions among smaller orbiting bodies.

sections.title: A spinning, pulsating star
sections.text: It rotates rapidly and shows small Delta Scuti pulsations. These slight changes in brightness let astronomers investigate a stellar interior that cannot be seen directly.

cns5-3517.name: Arcturus
cns5-3517.introduction: is the fourth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere: an orange giant in Boötes about 37 light-years away. It has about the Sun’s mass but has swollen to 25 times its size.

sections.title: Arc to Arcturus
sections.text: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle to find Arcturus, then “speed on to Spica.” Arcturus also forms one corner of the Spring Triangle.

sections.title: Starlight opens a World’s Fair
sections.text: In 1933, light from Arcturus was used to trigger the opening of the Chicago World’s Fair. The star was chosen because its light was thought to have set out around the time of the previous Chicago fair, in 1893; at 36.7 light-years, it actually left in 1896.

sections.title: A preview of the Sun’s future
sections.text: About 7 billion years old, Arcturus has used up the hydrogen in its core and evolved into a red giant some 170 times as luminous as the Sun: a glimpse of what lies ahead for our own star.

sections.title: A star on the move
sections.text: Arcturus moves about 6 degrees across the sky every 10,000 years, enough to noticeably shift its place in Boötes. It is an old disk star traveling with a group of 52 others, known as the Arcturus stream.

cns5-3442.name: Muphrid
cns5-3442.introduction: is a yellow-white subgiant in Boötes, about 37 light-years away, and Arcturus’s closest stellar neighbor: the two are close together in space as well as in our sky.

sections.title: Arcturus as a beacon
sections.text: From a planet orbiting Muphrid, Arcturus would shine at about magnitude −5.2, roughly twice as bright as Venus appears to us. From Arcturus, Muphrid would look more than twice as bright as Sirius does from Earth.

sections.title: Caught between dwarf and giant
sections.text: Muphrid is a subgiant, expanding as it leaves its long period of core hydrogen burning. Since 1943 its spectrum has served as a standard for classifying other stars, and measurements of its size and oscillations test models of this brief transition.

sections.title: A companion remains uncertain
sections.text: A companion on a roughly 494-day orbit has been reported from the star’s spectrum, but attempts to resolve it have not confirmed it.

capella.name: Capella
capella.introduction: is the sixth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in Auriga, about 43 light-years away. Its name means “little goat” in Latin, after the goat Amalthea who nursed Zeus, and what looks like one golden star is actually four.

sections.title: Two giants in one orbit
sections.text: The two bright stars, each about 2.5 times the Sun’s mass, orbit only 0.74 AU apart every 104 days. Though born together, they are at different stages: the cooler Aa already fuses helium in its core, while the hotter Ab is in a brief subgiant phase, still expanding toward the red giant stage.

sections.title: An X-ray beacon
sections.text: Capella is one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, first detected by rocket flights in 1962 and 1963. In 1974 it produced the strongest stellar X-ray emission measured up to that time, more than 10,000 times the Sun’s X-ray output.

sections.title: Small stars far from the spotlight
sections.text: Capella H and L, a pair of faint red dwarfs, orbit about 10,000 AU from the giants: small, long-lived stars sharing a system with two enormous evolved ones.

sections.title: A goat star in many cultures
sections.text: Persian astronomy called it Soroush, and the Incas, who knew it as Colça, held it in high regard. Because the Greek word for goat sounds like the name of the Aegean Sea, the star was also used in weather lore about seasonal winds.

orb6-17349+1234-a-b.name: Rasalhague
orb6-17349+1234-a-b.introduction: is the brightest star in Ophiuchus, marking the head of the serpent-bearer. A white star spinning fast enough to bulge, it is orbited by a smaller companion every 8.6 years.

sections.title: A star pulled out of round
sections.text: Rasalhague A spins at about 240 km/s, giving it an equatorial bulge about 20% larger than its polar radius. Its poles are hotter and brighter than its equator, an effect called gravity darkening.

sections.title: Weighing a distorted star
sections.text: Adaptive-optics observations in 2011 finally pinned down the companion’s orbit, and a 2021 study refined it: A has about 2.2 times the Sun’s mass and B about 0.82. Such direct masses are rare for fast-spinning stars and test how rotation changes a star’s apparent brightness and temperature.

hip-105199.name: Alderamin
hip-105199.introduction: is the brightest star in Cepheus, about 49 light-years away. Earth’s slowly wobbling axis periodically brings it within 3 degrees of the north celestial pole, so it takes its turn as a pole star.

sections.title: A day shorter than ours
sections.text: Alderamin spins at least 246 km/s, turning once in less than 12 hours. The CHARA interferometer array shows it flattened: 2.74 solar radii across the equator but 2.16 at the poles.

sections.title: Magnetism in a fast spinner
sections.text: It emits about as much X-ray radiation as the Sun, a sign of considerable magnetic activity. Its rapid rotation also seems to keep chemical elements from separating in its atmosphere, as they often do in similar stars.

msc-07346+3153.name: Castor
msc-07346+3153.introduction: is the white member of Gemini’s famous pair of “twins.” Unlike the orange giant Pollux, Castor is a six-star system arranged as three close binaries.

sections.title: Pairs within a family
sections.text: A telescope separates the bright A and B components, but spectroscopy reveals that each has a close companion. The more distant Castor C is another close pair, made of red dwarfs.

sections.title: Eclipses and flares
sections.text: Castor Ca and Cb are the red-dwarf pair YY Geminorum. They eclipse one another every 0.814 days. Spectroscopy combined with the eclipsing inclination gives each a mass close to 0.606 Suns; their measured sizes also help test models of magnetically active small stars.

source.title: Kochukhov & Shulyak 2019: the YY Gem eclipsing pair

sections.title: A binary you can watch move
sections.text: James Pound first recorded Castor as a double star in 1718, and Giovanni Cassini may have split it as early as 1678. The separation between Castor A and B has grown from about 2 arcseconds in 1970 to about 6 in 2026 as their orbit slowly unfolds.

source.title: Torres et al. 2022: Castor orbits and dynamical masses

hip-746.name: Caph
hip-746.introduction: is the star at the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, about 54 light-years away. A line from Caph through Alpheratz runs down to the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator at the equinoxes.

sections.title: Spinning near its limit
sections.text: Caph rotates at about 92% of the speed that would tear it apart, completing more than one rotation per day. This flattens the star and makes its poles hotter than its equator.

sections.title: A pulse every few hours
sections.text: Caph is a Delta Scuti variable, brightening and fading slightly over about 2.5 hours as it pulsates. It is the fourth-brightest star of this type, after Denebola, Vega and Altair.

sections.title: Beside Tycho’s Star
sections.text: In 1572, the supernova now known as Tycho’s Star blazed up about 5 degrees northwest of Caph.

hip-54872.name: Zosma
hip-54872.introduction: is a white star on the lion’s back in Leo, about 58 light-years away. Its name means “girdle” in ancient Greek.

sections.title: A flattened star
sections.text: Zosma spins at about 280 km/s at its equator, enough to give it a pronounced bulge. Interferometry measures its apparent size, but no single radius describes its flattened shape.

sections.title: From white star to giant
sections.text: In about 600 million years, Zosma will swell into an orange or red giant, before ending as a white dwarf made of carbon and oxygen.

orb6-01546+2049-a-b.name: Sheratan
orb6-01546+2049-a-b.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Aries, about 58 light-years away, marking one of the ram’s horns. Its name, from the Arabic for “the two signs,” recalls the time several thousand years ago when it and Gamma Arietis marked the spring equinox.

sections.title: An elongated orbit
sections.text: A white primary and a fainter companion orbit every 107 days on a strongly elongated path, so their separation changes considerably during each circuit.

sections.title: Resolved by interferometry
sections.text: The pair is too close for ordinary telescopes, but the Mark III interferometer at Mount Wilson resolved it. Combined with Doppler measurements of the orbit, this gives the stars’ masses.

hip-68933.name: Menkent
hip-68933.introduction: is an orange giant in Centaurus, about 59 light-years away, whose name blends the Arabic word for “shoulder” with “Centaurus.” It lies farther north than Alpha and Beta Centauri, so many northern observers can see it.

sections.title: Helium in the core
sections.text: Menkent is generally interpreted as a red-clump giant, generating energy by fusing helium in its core. That places it beyond the first expansion that follows the exhaustion of central hydrogen.

sections.title: A visitor from the outer disk
sections.text: It crosses the sky at 0.73 arcseconds a year, a hint that it may have formed in the outer disk of the Milky Way and is just passing through our neighborhood.

cns5-gj-639.1.name: Epsilon Scorpii
cns5-gj-639.1.introduction: is an orange giant in Scorpius, about 64 light-years away and the fifth-brightest star in the constellation. Its proper name, Larawag, comes from the Wardaman people of northern Australia and means “clear sighting.”

sections.title: A giant’s subtle heartbeat
sections.text: Small, Sun-like oscillations have been measured in its light. These are excited by convection and reveal information about the interior of a star whose surface has expanded far beyond the Sun’s.

sections.title: A small companion
sections.text: In 2018, a faint companion was found sharing its motion 14 arcseconds away: a small star with less than 1% of the Sun’s luminosity.

hip-9884.name: Hamal
hip-9884.introduction: is the brightest star in Aries, an orange giant about 66 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “head of the ram.”

sections.title: Where spring once began
sections.text: Between 2000 and 100 BCE, the Sun stood in Aries at the northern spring equinox. Precession has since moved that point into Pisces, but Hamal has remained a landmark of a place that mattered to early sky watchers.

sections.title: Real and fictional planets
sections.text: A planet more massive than Jupiter was reported in 2011, on a roughly 381-day orbit about 1.2 AU from the star. Hamal also has a fictional planet: Lithia, the setting of James Blish’s 1953 novel A Case of Conscience.

cns5-gj-171.1.name: Aldebaran
cns5-gj-171.1.introduction: is the orange eye of Taurus, about 67 light-years away, and typically the fourteenth-brightest star in the night sky. Its Arabic name means “the follower,” because it seems to follow the Pleiades across the sky.

sections.title: Not part of the Hyades
sections.text: Aldebaran appears among the V-shaped Hyades cluster but lies in the foreground and is much older. A red giant about 45 times the Sun’s radius but with roughly the Sun’s mass, it is over six billion years old and takes 520 days to rotate once.

sections.title: A royal star often hidden by the Moon
sections.text: Aldebaran was one of the four “royal stars” of Persia. Lying about 5.5 degrees from the ecliptic, it can be occulted by the Moon; a series of 49 occultations ran from 2015 to 2018.

sections.title: A disputed planet signal
sections.text: Long-period changes in its radial velocity have been interpreted as a planet of at least about 6 Jupiter masses, but stellar activity also shapes the signal, and the planet remains disputed.

sections.title: Pioneer 10’s direction
sections.text: The silent Pioneer 10 spacecraft is drifting in the general direction of Aldebaran. William Herschel found a faint companion beside the star in 1782.

hip-77070.name: Unukalhai
hip-77070.introduction: is the brightest star in Serpens, in the serpent’s head, about 74 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the serpent’s neck”; its Latin name, Cor Serpentis, means “heart of the serpent.”

sections.title: An orange giant with a spectral clue
sections.text: Its spectrum shows unusually strong cyanogen bands, earning it the label of a “strong CN star.” These molecular signatures reveal its atmospheric composition rather than changing its naked-eye color.

sections.title: Beyond central hydrogen burning
sections.text: Unukalhai is an evolved giant, probably burning helium in its core. Its cool outer layers have expanded, allowing it to radiate far more light than the Sun despite a lower surface temperature.

msc-20462+3358.name: Aljanah
msc-20462+3358.introduction: is the orange giant on one wing of Cygnus, about 73 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the wing.”

sections.title: A nine-billion-year-old giant
sections.text: With about 10% more mass than the Sun and an age of about nine billion years, it has passed through the red giant stage and a helium flash, and now fuses helium in its core at 11 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A giant with an unseen partner
sections.text: A companion orbits every 53 years on a highly eccentric path, revealed through the giant’s changing line-of-sight velocity.

sections.title: One name, two stars
sections.text: It was long called Gienah, Arabic for “the wing,” a name also used for Gamma Corvi; it was sometimes written Gienah Cygni to tell them apart. The IAU now uses Aljanah for this star and Gienah for the one in Corvus.

hip-76267.name: Alphecca
hip-76267.introduction: is the brightest star in Corona Borealis, about 75 light-years away. Its Latin name, Gemma, means “jewel,” fitting its place in the arc of the Northern Crown.

sections.title: A crown jewel that dims
sections.text: Its two stars, one of class A and one of class G, orbit every 17.4 days in a plane almost edge-on to us, so they eclipse each other like Algol. The dimming, from magnitude 2.21 to 2.32, is hardly noticeable to the eye.

sections.title: A lively smaller companion
sections.text: The cooler star has a magnetically active, X-ray-emitting corona. Eclipses and orbital velocities together help separate the properties of two stars that otherwise appear as a single point.

sections.title: Dust and family
sections.text: A dusty disk extends to about 60 AU from the system, and Alphecca is thought to belong to the Ursa Major moving group, like most stars of the Big Dipper.

msc-10084+1158.name: Regulus
msc-10084+1158.introduction: is the brightest star in Leo, about 79 light-years away, and the bright star closest to the ecliptic. Its name is Latin for “prince” or “little king,” and Persia counted it among its four royal stars.

sections.title: An almost breakneck spin
sections.text: Regulus spins once every 15.9 hours, its equator moving at about 320 km/s, or 96.5% of the speed at which it would break apart. The result is a strongly flattened star with hotter poles.

sections.title: A stripped companion
sections.text: A very faint, low-mass stellar companion orbits in about 40 days. Spectroscopy supports a stripped, pre-white-dwarf identity: past mass transfer likely helped spin up the bright primary. A much wider pair adds another layer to the system.

source.title: Gies et al. 2020: Spectroscopic detection of Regulus’s pre-white-dwarf companion

sections.title: Often hidden by the Moon
sections.text: Lying less than half a degree from the ecliptic, Regulus is often occulted by the Moon. Planets can cover it too, but rarely: the last was Venus, on July 7, 1959.

msc-13239+5456.name: Mizar
msc-13239+5456.introduction: is the famous double star in the Big Dipper’s handle, about 83 light-years away. Together with Alcor it forms a classic naked-eye pair and eyesight test, and Mizar itself contains four stars.

sections.title: Firsts in double-star history
sections.text: Mizar may have been the first double star seen through a telescope: Benedetto Castelli asked Galileo to observe it in 1617. Mizar A was the first spectroscopic binary ever discovered, with an orbit published in 1890, and Mizar B was found to be one too in 1908.

sections.title: A double that became a quadruple
sections.text: A small telescope resolves Mizar A and B. Spectroscopy then reveals that each visible component has its own close companion: two nested levels of multiplicity in a familiar sky landmark.

sections.title: Horse and rider
sections.text: Arabic tradition called Mizar and Alcor the horse and rider. In the Mi’kmaq story of the great bear and seven hunters, Mizar is Chickadee and Alcor is his cooking pot. Both stars belong to the Ursa Major moving group.

orb6-05595+4457-aa-ab.name: Menkalinan
orb6-05595+4457-aa-ab.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Auriga, a pair of nearly identical white stars about 79 light-years away. It is approaching the Sun and in about a million years will be the brightest star in the night sky.

sections.title: Nearly matching stars, grazing eclipses
sections.text: The pair circles in about 3.96 days and undergoes shallow eclipses. A 2026 analysis combined resolved CHARA observations with spectra and light curves, measuring masses of about 2.36 and 2.29 Suns and radii of about 2.75 and 2.62 Suns.

sections.title: Unusual metal lines
sections.text: Both stars show metallic-line spectra, with some chemical elements unusually prominent. Such abundance patterns form in stellar atmospheres; they do not mean the entire stars have the same exaggerated composition.

sections.title: Tomorrow’s brightest star
sections.text: Menkalinan and the Sun are closing in on each other. In about 1.3 million years it should pass within about 32 light-years of us and outshine every other star in the night sky.

source.title: Jonak et al. 2026: the joint beta Aurigae solution

hip-2081.name: Ankaa
hip-2081.introduction: is the brightest star in Phoenix, an orange giant whose name comes from the Arabic word for the phoenix.

sections.title: A slow spectroscopic orbit
sections.text: Ankaa is a binary with an orbital period of about 10.5 years. The companion is revealed through the motion of the bright star, even though the system looks like one point to the eye.

sections.title: A firebird or a skiff
sections.text: The name Ankaa was attached to the star sometime after 1800. Medieval Arab astronomers saw a boat in this part of the sky, so the star was also known as Nair al Zaurak, “the bright one of the skiff.”

hip-62956.name: Alioth
hip-62956.introduction: is the brightest star in Ursa Major, the handle star nearest the Big Dipper’s bowl. It belongs to the Ursa Major moving group and is one of the 57 classic navigational stars.

sections.title: Chemical patches on a magnetic star
sections.text: Alioth’s magnetic field, about 100 times stronger than Earth’s, sorts elements into patches on its surface. Its magnetic and rotation axes are almost at right angles, so the patches swing in and out of view and change its light every 5.1 days.

sections.title: A wobble with another explanation
sections.text: A 2008 study suggested that the 5.1-day pattern might come from a companion of about 15 Jupiter masses. The rotation of its patchy surface is the accepted explanation.

hip-58001.name: Phecda
hip-58001.introduction: is the lower-left star of the Big Dipper’s bowl, about 83 light-years away. It belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, and only about 8.6 light-years separate it from Mizar and Alcor.

sections.title: A hidden partner in the motion
sections.text: An astrometric wobble reveals a cooler companion on a roughly 20-year orbit. Tracking a star’s changing position can expose a partner even when its light is difficult to isolate.

sections.title: A spectral anchor
sections.text: Since 1943, Phecda’s spectrum has served as one of the stable anchor points for classifying other stars. Its blue-white A-type primary contrasts with its much cooler companion.

hip-53910.name: Merak
hip-53910.introduction: is the lower of the Big Dipper’s two pointer stars: a line from Merak through Dubhe leads to Polaris.

sections.title: A member of a moving family
sections.text: Merak belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, along with several other central Dipper stars. Their similar motions reflect a shared history, although the whole seven-star pattern is not one bound system.

sections.title: Dust beyond the star
sections.text: Infrared observations reveal a debris disk much like those around Vega and Fomalhaut, with dust at about 120 K centered roughly 47 AU from the star.

orb6-19026-2953-a-b.name: Ascella
orb6-19026-2953-a-b.introduction: is a triple star at the bottom of the Teapot’s handle in Sagittarius, about 88 light-years away. Its name comes from a Late Latin word for “armpit.”

sections.title: An orbit measured across decades
sections.text: The two visible stars orbit every 21 years, about 13 AU apart.

sections.title: A closer pair inside the pair
sections.text: A companion reported in 2023 turns one component into a much closer binary, with an estimated orbit of about a month. A nearby star long listed as a distant companion is instead an unrelated background object.

source.title: Waisberg et al. 2023: Discovery of a close companion to Ascella A

orb6-17104-1544-a-b.name: Sabik
orb6-17104-1544-a-b.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Ophiuchus, about 88 light-years away: two similar white stars whose light merges into one. Its Arabic name means “the preceding one.”

sections.title: An extreme orbit
sections.text: The stars take 87.8 years per orbit on an extremely elongated path: about 31 AU apart on average but only about 2 AU at closest approach. The last such approach, in 2024, let the Very Large Telescope pin down the orbit and the stars’ combined mass.

hip-61084.name: Gacrux
hip-61084.introduction: is the reddish star at the top of the Southern Cross, about 89 light-years away, and the nearest M-type red giant to the Sun.

sections.title: A red star in a blue cross
sections.text: Its cool surface gives Gacrux the orange-red color visible beside the Cross’s blue-white stars. It is a semi-regular variable with several periods.

sections.title: A barium mystery
sections.text: Its atmosphere is enriched with barium, usually a sign that a companion once transferred material to it, but no such companion has been found.

sections.title: On five flags
sections.text: As part of the Southern Cross, Gacrux appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa, Papua New Guinea and Brazil. Its name is a navigators’ contraction of Gamma Crucis, coined by the 1940s.

msc-03082+4057.name: Algol
msc-03082+4057.introduction: is the “Demon Star” in Perseus, about 90 light-years away, and one of the first variable stars ever discovered. Every 2.87 days it fades from magnitude 2.1 to 3.4 for about ten hours, as one star of a close pair eclipses the other.

sections.title: An eclipse you can follow
sections.text: About every 2.87 days, the cooler star crosses the hotter star and the system dims noticeably. Comparing Algol with nearby stars over several hours reveals orbital geometry without needing a telescope.

sections.title: A demon’s head
sections.text: Its association with a monster is old: the Gorgon in Greek tradition, a ghoul in Arabic, which gave the English name “Demon Star.” An Egyptian calendar of lucky and unlucky days from some 3,200 years ago may record its cycle, though that claim has been questioned.

sections.title: Solving the puzzle
sections.text: Geminiano Montanari noticed its changing brightness in 1667. In 1783, John Goodricke showed that the fades repeat regularly and suggested that a dark body passes in front of the star.

sections.title: The Algol paradox
sections.text: The less massive member is the more evolved one. It was originally more massive, aged faster, and then transferred gas to its partner, reversing the masses and revealing how binary interaction can rewrite a star’s history.

hip-3419.name: Diphda
hip-3419.introduction: is the brightest star in Cetus, about 96 light-years away, despite its beta designation. Its Arabic name means “frog” — the second frog, after Fomalhaut — and it stands out in an otherwise dark part of the sky.

sections.title: A giant with a hot crown
sections.text: Diphda has passed the red giant stage and now fuses helium in its core. It emits about 2,000 times the Sun’s X-ray luminosity, enough for Chandra to image it, and its flares last far longer than solar flares, which typically end within hours.

msc-00084+2905.name: Alpheratz
msc-00084+2905.introduction: is the brightest star in Andromeda and a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, about 97 light-years away. Ptolemy considered it shared by both constellations, and Bayer gave it two names: Alpha Andromedae and Delta Pegasi.

sections.title: A binary behind the square
sections.text: A hot primary and a fainter companion orbit every 96.9 days. Their blended light makes one bright landmark, while spectroscopy separates their orbital motion.

sections.title: Mercury and manganese in the light
sections.text: The primary is the brightest mercury-manganese star known, with unusually high amounts of mercury, manganese, gallium and xenon in its atmosphere.

hip-109268.name: Alnair
hip-109268.introduction: is the brightest star in Grus, the Crane, about 101 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the bright one,” short for “the bright one from the fish’s tail.”

sections.title: A rapid rotator
sections.text: Its broadened spectral lines show a surface spinning at more than 215 km/s.

sections.title: A southern navigation light
sections.text: Alnair is one of the 58 stars selected for celestial navigation, useful across the southern sky even though observers at high northern latitudes never see it.

hip-6686.name: Ruchbah
hip-6686.introduction: is one of the five stars of Cassiopeia’s W, about 99 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “knee.”

sections.title: An eclipse claim with uncertainty
sections.text: Eclipses have been reported every 759 days, dimming it by 0.07 magnitudes, but modern observations have not consistently confirmed them.

hip-67301.name: Alkaid
hip-67301.introduction: is the star at the end of the Big Dipper’s handle and one of the hottest in the pattern. Unlike most Dipper stars, it does not belong to the Ursa Major moving group.

sections.title: A spectral yardstick
sections.text: Since 1943, Alkaid’s spectrum has served as the standard for hot B3 V stars, a stable reference for classifying less familiar objects.

sections.title: Mourners and a bier
sections.text: In Arabic tradition, the handle stars Alkaid, Mizar and Alioth were mourning maidens following a bier formed by the four stars of the bowl.

orb6-06377+1624-aa-ab.name: Alhena
orb6-06377+1624-aa-ab.introduction: is the third-brightest star in Gemini, about 109 light-years away, marking one of the twins’ feet. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the brand” on a camel’s neck.

sections.title: A long, eccentric orbit
sections.text: The companion completes an orbit in roughly 12.6 years. Its strongly changing separation is traced by combining spectroscopy with measurements that resolve the pair.

sections.title: Unequal stars formed together
sections.text: The bright primary has begun to expand beyond its main-sequence state, while its less massive companion remains a hydrogen-burning star. Their shared origin makes the pair useful for comparing how stars of different masses evolve.

orb6-10468-4925-a-b.name: Mu Velorum
orb6-10468-4925-a-b.introduction: is a binary in Vela, about 117 light-years away: a yellow giant and a fainter, less evolved companion on a 138-year orbit.

sections.title: A giant flare
sections.text: In 1998, the Extreme Ultraviolet Explorer recorded a flare whose X-ray output nearly equaled that of the entire star.

sections.title: Two stages in one system
sections.text: The bright star has expanded into a giant, while its companion remains on the main sequence. Their orbit is extremely elongated, with an eccentricity of 0.94.

hip-45238.name: Miaplacidus
hip-45238.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Carina, about 113 light-years away, and the brightest star of the Diamond Cross. Its name may combine Arabic for “waters” with Latin for “placid.”

sections.title: A giant that still spins quickly
sections.text: Although it has expanded beyond its earlier main-sequence size, Miaplacidus retains rapid rotation. Broad spectral lines reveal the motion of its surface.

sections.title: Part of the old ship
sections.text: Carina represents the keel of the ancient, much larger constellation Argo Navis. Miaplacidus is one of the bright stars that remain as landmarks after the ship was divided into separate modern constellations.

msc-11037+6145.name: Dubhe
msc-11037+6145.introduction: is the outer star of the Big Dipper’s bowl and the northern of the two pointers to Polaris, about 123 light-years away. Despite its alpha designation, it is only the second-brightest star in Ursa Major.

sections.title: A giant with a close companion
sections.text: The bright giant has a companion on a 44.5-year orbit, about 23 AU away. A separate pair 7 arcminutes away, orbiting every 6 days, completes the family.

sections.title: A pointer with a different origin
sections.text: Dubhe is not a member of the Ursa Major moving group shared by five of the Dipper’s central stars. The familiar pattern combines a real stellar association with unrelated foreground or background landmarks.

msc-12415-4858.name: Gamma Centauri
msc-12415-4858.introduction: is a binary in Centaurus whose two similar white stars blend into one naked-eye point. Its proper name, Muhlifain, shares an Arabic root with Muliphein in Canis Major.

sections.title: Two stars on a human timescale
sections.text: Their positions have been measured since 1897, long enough to estimate an orbit of 84.5 years.

sections.title: A possible much wider family
sections.text: Tau Centauri shares its motion about 1.7 light-years away and very likely forms a wide pair with it.

hip-72607.name: Kochab
hip-72607.introduction: is the brightest star in the bowl of the Little Dipper, about 131 light-years away and only slightly fainter than Polaris. With Pherkad it forms the “Guardians of the Pole.”

sections.title: An earlier guide to north
sections.text: Around 1100 BCE, Kochab was within about 7 degrees of the north celestial pole, close enough for some old references to call it the pole star. Polaris will come within half a degree of the pole by 2100.

sections.title: A planet around a giant
sections.text: A planet about 6 times Jupiter’s mass has been announced around this roughly 3-billion-year-old giant, on a 522-day orbit.

sections.title: A guide for telescopes
sections.text: The celestial pole lies very close to the line from Polaris to Kochab, so amateur astronomers use it to align equatorial telescope mounts.

hip-113963.name: Markab
hip-113963.introduction: is a blue-white star at a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. Its name may come from the Arabic for “saddle,” or from a phrase meaning the horse’s “shoulder.”

sections.title: A star changing its fuel supply
sections.text: Its spectrum places it near the end of core hydrogen burning, as its outer layers begin to expand. It also spins fast, at more than 130 km/s.

sections.title: A square drawn in depth
sections.text: The Great Square is an apparent pattern, not a bound group. Markab, Scheat, Algenib and Alpheratz lie at different distances and have quite different physical properties.

hip-25428.name: Elnath
hip-25428.introduction: is the tip of the bull’s northern horn in Taurus, about 134 light-years away; its name means “the butting” in Arabic. Ptolemy considered it shared with Auriga, and it was also called Gamma Aurigae until constellation boundaries were fixed in 1930.

sections.title: Heavy elements in the spectrum
sections.text: Elnath is chemically peculiar, with a high abundance of manganese but little calcium and magnesium in its atmosphere.

sections.title: Toward the galactic anticenter
sections.text: Elnath lies a few degrees from the galactic anticenter, the direction directly away from the Milky Way’s center, in front of star clusters such as M36, M37 and M38.

orb6-01377-5714-a-b.name: Achernar
orb6-01377-5714-a-b.introduction: is the ninth-brightest star in the night sky, at the southern end of Eridanus, about 139 light-years away. It is the hottest and bluest of the ten brightest stars, and one of the most flattened stars known.

sections.title: A star flattened by rotation
sections.text: In 2003, ESO’s Very Large Telescope Interferometer revealed how strongly Achernar bulges at its equator, making it the flattest star seen up to that time.

source.title: ESO: Interferometry reveals Achernar’s flattened shape

sections.title: Gas around a spinning star
sections.text: Later measurements put its equatorial diameter about 35% larger than its polar diameter, comparable to the dwarf planet Haumea. Achernar is a Be star: gas thrown off by its rapid spin forms a disk that changes shape and sometimes seems to disappear. A smaller companion orbits about 7 AU away.

sections.title: Hidden from the ancients
sections.text: Precession carried Achernar much farther south in antiquity: around 3400 BCE it lay just 7.5 degrees from the south celestial pole.

hip-90185.name: Kaus Australis
hip-90185.introduction: is the brightest star in Sagittarius, a lower corner of the Teapot. Its equator spins at about 95% of breakup speed, the highest rate ever measured for a star in the Milky Way.

sections.title: Spinning at the limit
sections.text: Rotating at 95% of the critical velocity at which it would break apart, the star is flattened: its equatorial circumference is 34% larger than its polar circumference.

sections.title: A cooler companion in the glare
sections.text: A faint companion, identified in 1993 with an adaptive-optics coronagraph, may explain spectral oddities that were once attributed to the primary.

sections.title: The southern bow
sections.text: Its name means the southern part of the bow. Together with Kaus Media and Kaus Borealis, it traces the weapon of the celestial archer, an older figure within the modern Teapot pattern.

hip-61359.name: Kraz
hip-61359.introduction: is the yellowish bright giant at one corner of Corvus’s four-star figure. Despite its beta designation, it is slightly fainter than Gienah, the constellation’s gamma star.

sections.title: Youth and old age are relative
sections.text: Kraz has about 3.3 times the Sun’s mass and is roughly 300 million years old, old enough for a star this massive to have used up the hydrogen in its core. Massive stars spend their fuel far faster than the Sun.

sections.title: A crow beside the cup
sections.text: Corvus, neighboring Crater and the long body of Hydra preserve an interconnected sky story. Kraz helps draw the compact crow-shaped figure above Hydra’s back.

hip-59803.name: Gienah
hip-59803.introduction: is the brightest star in Corvus, the Crow, about 154 light-years away: a hot blue-white star with a much fainter companion.

sections.title: An atmosphere rich in heavy elements
sections.text: The primary is a mercury-manganese star. Its unusual spectrum reflects selective accumulation and settling of elements in the atmosphere, producing a chemical pattern very different from the Sun’s.

sections.title: A slow companion
sections.text: Its companion, of about 0.8 solar masses, may orbit some 50 AU away, taking about 158 years.

sections.title: Two wings with similar names
sections.text: Gienah refers to a wing. A similar traditional name was also used for Epsilon Cygni, now officially Aljanah; the two are unrelated stars in different bird constellations.

hip-87833.name: Eltanin
hip-87833.introduction: is the brightest star in Draco, an orange giant marking the dragon’s head, about 154 light-years away.

sections.title: A failed distance measurement, a major discovery
sections.text: While trying to measure Eltanin’s parallax, James Bradley discovered stellar aberration in 1728. Earth’s motion changes the apparent direction of incoming starlight, providing evidence of its orbit around the Sun.

sections.title: The zenith star
sections.text: Eltanin passes almost directly overhead at Greenwich, London, earning it the name “zenith star.” That favorable position made it ideal for precise measurements.

sections.title: A future brightest star
sections.text: Eltanin is approaching us. In about 1.5 million years it will pass within 28 light-years and, for a time, be the brightest star in the night sky, nearly as bright as Sirius is today.

orb6-05597+3713-a-b.name: Mahasim
orb6-05597+3713-a-b.introduction: is a binary in Auriga, about 166 light-years away. Its bright primary is a chemically peculiar star rich in silicon, with a fainter companion visible through a telescope.

sections.title: A magnetic, patchy surface
sections.text: The primary has a magnetic field of about 1 kilogauss and patches of unusual composition on its surface. As it rotates every 3.6 days, these patches change its spectrum and brightness, letting astronomers map a surface they cannot see directly.

hip-112122.name: Beta Gruis
hip-112122.introduction: is a red giant in Grus whose proper name, Tiaki, comes from the Tuamotu islands. Its warm color contrasts with blue-white Alnair nearby; medieval Arab astronomers counted it as part of the Southern Fish.

sections.title: A vast, cool envelope
sections.text: Tiaki is an asymptotic-giant-branch star with about 2.4 times the Sun’s mass and a surface of about 3,500 K, just over half the Sun’s temperature.

sections.title: A changing red light
sections.text: Its variability was announced in 1952. It alternates between regular changes on a 37-day cycle and slow, irregular variations.

hip-100751.name: Peacock
hip-100751.introduction: is the blue-white star at the head of Pavo, the Peacock. The bright point is a spectroscopic binary, probably a member of the young Tucana–Horologium association.

sections.title: A close partner
sections.text: The system’s stars orbit in about 11.8 days. Doppler shifts reveal the pairing, but the faint companion remains much less well characterized than the luminous primary.

sections.title: A modern English star name
sections.text: The name was assigned by His Majesty’s Nautical Almanac Office in the late 1930s for the Royal Air Force’s Air Almanac. Of its 57 navigation stars, two had no classical name: Alpha Pavonis and Epsilon Carinae, now Avior.

hip-46390.name: Alphard
hip-46390.introduction: is the orange giant in Hydra whose Arabic name means “the solitary one.” It stands out in an unusually sparse stretch of bright-star sky.

sections.title: The heart of Hydra
sections.text: Tycho Brahe called it Cor Hydrae, “the heart of Hydra,” and Arab astronomers also called it the backbone of the serpent. Hydra is the longest of the modern constellations.

sections.title: A giant with a complex voice
sections.text: Small changes in its velocity and spectral lines reveal oscillations lasting from hours to days. Its spectrum also shows a mild excess of barium, often a sign that a companion once transferred material to the star.

hip-74785.name: Zubeneschamali
hip-74785.introduction: is the brightest star in Libra, a hot star whose name, “the northern claw,” preserves its older identity as part of the scorpion.

sections.title: The famous “green” star
sections.text: Earlier observers often described it as the only greenish star visible to the naked eye. Modern observers usually see it as white or bluish, and there is no accepted explanation for the green reports.

sections.title: Brighter than Antares?
sections.text: Eratosthenes recorded it as brighter than Antares; Ptolemy, 350 years later, called them equal. Whether Antares brightened or Zubeneschamali varied is not known.

sections.title: Claws became scales
sections.text: The stars now making Libra were associated with Scorpius in older traditions. Their surviving names record the change from the scorpion’s claws to the separate constellation of the Scales.

hip-113881.name: Scheat
hip-113881.introduction: is the red giant at the upper right corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, much cooler than the Square’s blue-white stars.

sections.title: A breathing corner of the square
sections.text: Johann Schmidt discovered in 1847 that Scheat varies: it ranges between magnitudes 2.3 and 2.7 over about 43 days, without the clockwork regularity of an eclipsing binary.

sections.title: Matter leaving the star
sections.text: Scheat is losing mass, creating an expanding shell of gas and dust with a radius of about 16 AU.

hip-5447.name: Mirach
hip-5447.introduction: is a red giant in Andromeda, widely used as a stepping stone to the Andromeda Galaxy.

sections.title: A star beside a “ghost”
sections.text: The small galaxy NGC 404 lies just seven arcminutes from Mirach and is nicknamed Mirach’s Ghost. It is vastly farther away; the pairing is a chance alignment.

sections.title: A late phase of stellar life
sections.text: Mirach’s cool surface belongs to an enormously expanded envelope. It is on the asymptotic giant branch, a late stage during which stars can lose substantial material to their surroundings.

msc-18553-2618.name: Nunki
msc-18553-2618.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Sagittarius, in the handle of the Teapot. Its name is an ancient Assyrian or Babylonian one, recovered by archaeologists.

sections.title: Two stars hidden in the light
sections.text: Interferometry resolves two similarly bright stars in a 134.779-day orbit. Published evolutionary models estimate masses of about 6.5 and 6.3 Suns and radii of about 4.1 and 3.9 Suns. These are individual model estimates; the mass inferred dynamically from the orbit applies to the pair together.

sections.title: An orbit tilted away from us
sections.text: The orbit is inclined by only about 20 degrees to the sky plane, so eclipses are not expected. Both stars rotate rapidly: broad spectral lines can hide a close pair even when it is resolved by interferometry.

sections.title: Covered by Venus
sections.text: Lying 3.45 degrees from the ecliptic, Nunki can be occulted by the Moon and, rarely, by planets: Venus last passed in front of it on November 17, 1981.

source.title: Waisberg & Katz 2026: the resolved orbit of Nunki

hip-3179.name: Schedar
hip-3179.introduction: is the orange giant marking the breast of Cassiopeia; its name comes from the Arabic for “breast.” Its brightness closely matches Caph’s, but measurements by NASA’s WISE telescope confirm Schedar as the brightest star in Cassiopeia.

sections.title: An expanded, cooler surface
sections.text: Schedar’s orange color distinguishes it from the hotter stars nearby in the W. Its great surface area makes it luminous despite a lower temperature than the Sun.

sections.title: A familiar pattern, unrelated stars
sections.text: Cassiopeia’s five principal stars occupy different distances and evolutionary stages. Their W is a useful landmark drawn by perspective, rather than a single cluster traveling through space.

msc-14450+2704.name: Izar
msc-14450+2704.introduction: is a contrasting pair in Boötes: an orange giant and a hotter white main-sequence star about 180 AU apart in projection. A much fainter candidate brown dwarf lies roughly 4,900 AU away.

sections.title: The “loveliest” pair
sections.text: Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve called it Pulcherrima, Latin for “loveliest,” in reference to its color contrast. The perceived bluish or greenish tint of the fainter star is strengthened by the orange primary beside it.

sections.title: Why A, B and D?
sections.text: The catalog retains the Multiple Star Catalog labels A, B and D. D identifies Gaia DR3 1279752168030730496, a candidate brown dwarf found through its similar proper motion and parallax. Its membership and substellar nature remain provisional; the missing letter is not evidence for a missing confirmed star.

sections.title: A shared distance, with limits
sections.text: The map uses an approximate common distance of 62 parsecs (about 203 light-years), based on Hipparcos. Gaia’s bright-primary solution is affected by saturation, and B has no Gaia DR3 parallax. Their uncertain individual parallaxes cannot resolve the true depth within the system. The displayed separations preserve their measured sky directions; they are projected separations, not a measured three-dimensional orbit.

source.title: Hipparcos, HIP 72105; approximate shared system distance

sections.title: Another possible companion
sections.text: Kervella and colleagues also identify 2MASS J14454000+2615167 as a common-proper-motion candidate about 186,000 AU away in projection, nearly three light-years. That much wider candidate is distinct from MSC component D. Its physical association remains uncertain, so it is described here without assigning a new component letter or a bound orbit.

hip-14135.name: Menkar
hip-14135.introduction: is the red giant at the nose of Cetus, about 250 light-years away; its name comes from the Arabic for “nostril.” Despite its alpha designation, it is fainter than Diphda.

sections.title: An atmosphere large enough to measure
sections.text: Interferometry resolves Menkar’s apparent diameter and tests models of its cool atmosphere. Molecular absorption and the brightness change toward the apparent edge help reveal conditions in its outer layers.

sections.title: An enormous, cool star
sections.text: With more than twice the Sun’s mass, Menkar has expanded to about 100 times the Sun’s radius. Its huge surface makes it luminous even though its photosphere is cool enough for molecules to survive.

msc-13252-1110.name: Spica
msc-13252-1110.introduction: is the brightest star in Virgo and one of the 20 brightest in the night sky. Its name means “the virgin’s ear of wheat,” and its blue-white light comes mainly from two hot stars so close that their mutual gravity stretches them into egg shapes.

sections.title: Stars stretched by tides
sections.text: The pair circles in about four days. Their mutual gravity distorts their shapes, producing slight brightness changes as different areas turn toward us, rather than ordinary eclipses.

sections.title: Separating the stars
sections.text: The close pair has published individual masses of about 11.4 and 7.2 Suns. An interferometric study also detected a third source, whose light is included in measurements of the whole system.

source.title: Frost et al.: interferometric B-star multiplicity

sections.title: The star that revealed precession
sections.text: Spica is believed to have given Hipparchus the data that led him to discover the precession of the equinoxes, and Copernicus observed it with a homemade instrument for his own studies of precession. A temple at Thebes built around 3200 BCE was aligned with Spica.

sections.title: A future supernova
sections.text: The primary is massive enough to end its life as a supernova, making Spica one of the nearest stars with that fate.

source.title: Tkachenko et al. 2016: resolved Spica binary parameters

hip-25336.name: Bellatrix
hip-25336.introduction: is the third-brightest star in Orion, on the hunter’s shoulder opposite Betelgeuse. At about 245 light-years, it is the closest of Orion’s major stars, and its name is Latin for “female warrior.”

sections.title: Hotter than its color suggests
sections.text: Bellatrix radiates strongly in the ultraviolet. The light visible to our eyes represents only part of the energy emitted by its hot surface.

sections.title: An unsettled evolutionary label
sections.text: Its spectrum has a giant classification, but models suggest it may still be burning hydrogen in its core. High-resolution observations have also challenged the idea that two similarly bright stars explain its properties.

sections.title: A navigator’s star and a future supernova
sections.text: Bellatrix is one of the four navigational stars in Orion. It is also one of the closest known candidates for a core-collapse supernova.

hip-62434.name: Mimosa
hip-62434.introduction: is the second-brightest star of the Southern Cross and the 20th-brightest in the night sky, a hot blue-white triple system. It appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa, Papua New Guinea and Brazil.

sections.title: Pulsations reveal the interior
sections.text: The primary is a Beta Cephei variable with oscillations lasting a few hours. Combining its brightness changes with polarization measurements allows unusually detailed tests of its internal structure and orientation.

source.title: Cotton et al. 2021: Polarimetric detection of oscillation modes in Beta Crucis

sections.title: More than one companion
sections.text: A spectroscopic companion follows a roughly five-year orbit, and a second companion announced in 2007 may be a young star still contracting toward the main sequence.

hip-26634.name: Phact
hip-26634.introduction: is the brightest star in Columba, the Dove, south of Orion, about 261 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “ring dove.”

sections.title: A disk written into the spectrum
sections.text: Phact is a Be star, spinning at least 176 km/s and surrounded by a hot gas disk that produces emission lines in its spectrum.

sections.title: A dove below the hunter
sections.text: Columba was introduced to European star maps much later than Orion. Its compact figure occupies a patch of southern sky beneath the far more conspicuous hunter and his dogs.

msc-17373-4300.name: Sargas
msc-17373-4300.introduction: is the yellow-white star near the bend of Scorpius’s tail, about 330 light-years away. It is a binary dominated by a luminous, evolved primary.

sections.title: A giant flattened by rotation
sections.text: Interferometry shows its equatorial radius is 33% larger than its polar radius. Such fast rotation is unusual for an evolved star and suggests that it formed when two stars merged.

hip-71352.name: Eta Centauri
hip-71352.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Centaurus, about 306 light-years away, with about 12 times the Sun’s mass, enough to end its life as a supernova. It belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest group of young massive stars.

sections.title: A day shorter than Earth’s
sections.text: Its surface spins at about 330 km/s, completing a turn in less than a day.

sections.title: A variable gas disk
sections.text: Eta Centauri is a Be star, with emission from material around it. Changes in the circumstellar gas contribute to its variability, allowing astronomers to follow exchanges of matter between a hot star and its surroundings.

hip-30438.name: Canopus
hip-30438.introduction: is the second-brightest star in the night sky, outshone only by Sirius: a white giant in Carina about 310 light-years away and more than 10,000 times as luminous as the Sun.

sections.title: A star beyond the red-giant stage
sections.text: Canopus is interpreted as a core-helium-burning star on a blue loop: it has already expanded and cooled, then moved back toward higher surface temperatures. Stellar evolution need not follow a one-way change from blue to red.

sections.title: A guide for spacecraft
sections.text: Its brightness and position well away from the ecliptic make Canopus a reference star for spacecraft navigation, a role far beyond its traditional one for sailors.

sections.title: A star of many cultures
sections.text: Greek legend named it after Canopus, the navigator of Menelaus’s ship. In India it is linked to the sage Agastya, Chinese astronomers called it the Old Man of the South Pole, and Bedouin people knew it as Suhayl and navigated by it and Polaris. The southeastern wall of the Kaaba in Mecca is aligned with its rising point.

sections.title: Brightest star of other epochs
sections.text: Because it is more luminous than any closer star, Canopus has been the brightest star in the night sky during three epochs over the past four million years.

msc-12372-6908.name: Alpha Muscae
msc-12372-6908.introduction: is the brightest star in Musca, the small constellation of the Fly beside the Southern Cross: a hot B-type star with nearly nine times the Sun’s mass, about 18 million years old.

sections.title: A young stellar neighborhood
sections.text: It belongs to the Lower Centaurus–Crux subgroup of the Scorpius–Centaurus association. The group provides a shared age and birthplace context for stars now spread over a large area of sky.

sections.title: A two-hour pulse
sections.text: Alpha Muscae is a Beta Cephei variable, pulsating with a period of about 2.17 hours.

sections.title: A boomerang’s forehead band
sections.text: The Wardaman people of Australia call it Burangalul, the “forehead band” of Buran, a boomerang constellation corresponding to Musca.

msc-12266-6306.name: Acrux
msc-12266-6306.introduction: is the brightest star of the Southern Cross and the 13th-brightest in the night sky, about 350 light-years away. It is the southernmost first-magnitude star, and the single point seen by the eye contains seven stars.

sections.title: The second binary ever recognized
sections.text: A Jesuit priest discovered in 1685 that Acrux is double, making it only the second binary star ever recognized. Both visible stars are hot B-type stars, each itself a close binary, and a more distant companion adds further members.

sections.title: Finding south from the Cross
sections.text: The long axis from Gacrux through Acrux points toward the south celestial pole. The Cross is an orientation guide, though Acrux itself is not a southern pole star.

sections.title: On five flags
sections.text: Acrux appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Samoa and Papua New Guinea; on Brazil’s flag, it represents the state of São Paulo.

hip-68002.name: Leepwal
hip-68002.introduction: is Zeta Centauri, a hot blue-white binary in the body of the Centaur, about 382 light-years away. Its primary has nearly 8 times the Sun’s mass and is about 40 million years old.

sections.title: An eight-day partnership
sections.text: Spectral lines reveal two stars in an eccentric orbit lasting just over eight days. Their separation is far too small for the unaided eye to distinguish.

sections.title: A Marshallese name
sections.text: In Marshallese tradition, Ļeepwal is the third of the ten sons of Lōktañūr, the star Capella. The IAU approved the name in July 2024.

msc-14585-4308.name: Beta Lupi
msc-14585-4308.introduction: is a blue-white giant in Lupus, the Wolf, about 383 light-years away. It belongs to the young Upper Centaurus–Lupus stellar association.

sections.title: A massive star’s pulse
sections.text: Beta Lupi is a Beta Cephei variable with a principal cycle of about 5.6 hours. These small oscillations let astronomers study the interiors of massive stars.

sections.title: Young, yet already changing
sections.text: Only about 25 million years old, it is already nearing the end of core hydrogen burning, on its way to becoming a red supergiant. Its rapid evolution contrasts with the Sun’s much longer main-sequence life.

hip-82273.name: Atria
hip-82273.introduction: is the orange beacon at the brightest corner of Triangulum Australe, the Southern Triangle, about 391 light-years away. Its name contracts its designation, Alpha Trianguli Australis.

sections.title: A giant on a grand scale
sections.text: Atria has about 6.4 times the Sun’s mass and gives off some 4,600 times as much light, from an enormous, cool envelope.

sections.title: On Brazil’s flag
sections.text: Atria appears on the flag of Brazil, representing the state of Rio Grande do Sul.

msc-14038-6022.name: Hadar
msc-14038-6022.introduction: is the eleventh-brightest star in the night sky, a blue-white triple system in Centaurus about 360 light-years away. With Alpha Centauri it forms the southern “Pointers” to the Southern Cross, though it lies more than 80 times farther away.

sections.title: A triple behind the bright point
sections.text: The inner pair, two similar massive stars, orbit every 357 days on a very eccentric path. A third B-type star lies farther out.

sections.title: Asteroseismology in a multiple system
sections.text: The bright components show pulsations that help probe their interiors. Combining these oscillations with orbital measurements provides complementary information about stellar structure and mass.

msc-02039+4220.name: Almach
msc-02039+4220.introduction: is the third-brightest star in Andromeda, about 390 light-years away, and one of the sky’s loveliest double stars: a golden giant beside a blue companion.

sections.title: A double that became a quadruple
sections.text: Johann Tobias Mayer discovered in 1778 that it is double. The blue companion later turned out to be a triple star itself, so the single naked-eye point is a quadruple system.

sections.title: Color shaped by contrast
sections.text: The large temperature difference between the visible components makes the pair especially striking. Their apparent colors are also influenced by comparison with one another through the eyepiece.

msc-16054-1948.name: Beta Scorpii
msc-16054-1948.introduction: is a multiple star near the head of Scorpius, also called Acrab. A small telescope splits it in two, but the full family has six members.

sections.title: Pairs within pairs
sections.text: β¹ and β² Scorpii, 13.5 arcseconds apart, top a hierarchy of six stars. The brighter, β¹, alone contains a pair that takes 610 years per orbit.

sections.title: A shared young origin
sections.text: The system belongs to Upper Scorpius, a nearby association of young stars. Its hot components have evolved together over only millions of years, providing a useful comparison with much older nearby Sun-like systems.

sections.title: Covered by planets
sections.text: Lying about 1 degree from the ecliptic, Beta Scorpii can be occulted by the Moon and occasionally by planets: Venus covered it in 1906 and Jupiter in 1971.

adhara.name: Adhara
adhara.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Canis Major, about 405–430 light-years away. Some 4.5 million years ago, when it was only about 30 light-years from the Sun, it was the brightest star in the night sky, shining at about magnitude −4.

sections.title: Brilliance beyond visible light
sections.text: Adhara is the brightest source of extreme-ultraviolet light in the night sky, far more prominent at those wavelengths than its visible-light ranking suggests.

sections.title: A difficult visual companion
sections.text: Its companion lies 7.5 arcseconds away but is about 250 times fainter, so separating the two requires a large telescope.

hip-89931.name: Kaus Media
hip-89931.introduction: is the orange giant in the middle of Sagittarius’s bow, also part of the Teapot figure. Its name combines Arabic for “bow” and Latin for “middle.”

sections.title: An archer inside a teapot
sections.text: Kaus Australis, Kaus Media and Kaus Borealis mark successive parts of the archer’s bow. The Teapot is a newer observing pattern made from some of the same stars.

sections.title: A cooler surface, a larger star
sections.text: Kaus Media has evolved beyond the main sequence into a K-type giant, and it is listed as having a white dwarf companion. Its warm color contrasts with the hotter blue-white stars nearby.

hip-66657.name: Epsilon Centauri
hip-66657.introduction: is a hot blue-white giant in Centaurus, about 430 light-years away, with 8.2 times the Sun’s mass. In Chinese astronomy, it and Alpha Centauri form the Southern Gate.

sections.title: Multiple pulses in the light
sections.text: It is a Beta Cephei variable, pulsating mainly with a period of 4 hours and 4 minutes, plus additional oscillations that test models of massive stellar interiors.

sections.title: A young star with a fast life
sections.text: Only about 16 million years old, it already has an evolved spectrum. Massive stars race through stages that a Sun-like star takes billions of years to reach.

msc-02318+8916.name: Polaris
msc-02318+8916.introduction: is the North Star, less than 1 degree from the north celestial pole, about 430–450 light-years away in Ursa Minor. Its yellow supergiant is the nearest Cepheid variable and belongs to a triple system.

sections.title: A fixed point in the sky
sections.text: Because it barely moves, Polaris has long guided navigators, and its height above the horizon gives the observer’s latitude. It will come closest to the pole, about 0.45 degrees, soon after 2100. Shakespeare’s Caesar called himself “as constant as the northern star,” although in Caesar’s time there was no such star.

sections.title: A distance-scale heartbeat
sections.text: Polaris is a Cepheid, pulsating over about four days. Cepheid pulsation periods are linked to luminosity, making this nearest example a foundation of the cosmic distance ladder. It was also the first classical Cepheid to have its mass determined from an orbit.

sections.title: Spots on the North Star
sections.text: CHARA observations published in 2024 resolved bright and dark spots on the North Star and followed the close companion’s orbit, a direct check on the mass of the pulsating primary.

source.title: CHARA: Polaris’s orbit, mass and spotted surface, 2024

sections.title: A family of three
sections.text: William Herschel discovered the outer companion, Polaris B, in August 1779. The close companion, Ab, was confirmed only in the early 20th century.

hip-81377.name: Zeta Ophiuchi
hip-81377.introduction: is the nearest O-type star to the Solar System, about 440 light-years away in Ophiuchus. It is a runaway star, ploughing through dust clouds near the Rho Ophiuchi complex.

sections.title: A bow wave in space
sections.text: Its stellar wind collides with gas and dust ahead of its path, forming an arcing bow shock visible in infrared images. The surrounding structure makes the star’s motion tangible.

source.title: Green et al. 2022: Three-dimensional models of Zeta Ophiuchi’s bow shock

sections.title: An uncertain ejection story
sections.text: Runaway stars can be thrown out by encounters among several stars, but Zeta Ophiuchi may instead be the survivor of a binary whose more massive partner exploded as a supernova.

sections.title: Spinning near breakup
sections.text: It may rotate about once a day, close to breakup speed, so its poles reach about 39,000 K while its equator is nearer 31,000 K. Within a few million years it should swell into a red supergiant wider than Jupiter’s orbit and then explode.

hip-23015.name: Hassaleh
hip-23015.introduction: is the orange giant Iota Aurigae, marking part of the Charioteer’s figure, about 450 light-years away. Interstellar dust dims and reddens its light on the way to Earth.

sections.title: A cool star with hot plasma
sections.text: Although its visible surface is cool, X-rays reveal much hotter gas in the outer atmosphere. Magnetic structures can heat a small amount of material far above the photospheric temperature.

sections.title: From Chaucer to a modern atlas
sections.text: As Alkab, “the ankle of the rein-holder,” it was a marker on the astrolabe described by Geoffrey Chaucer in 1391. The name Hassaleh first appeared in Antonín Bečvář’s 1951 star atlas, and its origin is uncertain.

hip-71860.name: Alpha Lupi
hip-71860.introduction: is the brightest star in Lupus, the Wolf, about 460 light-years away: a hot blue-white giant in the young Upper Centaurus–Lupus association and one of the nearest supernova candidates.

sections.title: A short stellar heartbeat
sections.text: In 1956, Bernard Pagel and colleagues identified Alpha Lupi as a Beta Cephei variable, whose small brightness changes over a few hours probe a massive star’s interior.

sections.title: Part of a dispersed nursery
sections.text: Its association is a loose family rather than a compact cluster. Shared motion and youth connect stars that now occupy a large region around Centaurus and Lupus.

hip-86670.name: Kappa Scorpii
hip-86670.introduction: is a close binary in the curved tail of Scorpius, about 480 light-years away. The bright component is a hot, massive star whose light changes subtly.

sections.title: An orbit and a pulse
sections.text: The stars orbit in about 195 days, while the primary pulsates on a much shorter timescale of about 4.8 hours. Spectroscopy separates the two kinds of motion.

sections.title: A view inside a massive star
sections.text: Its Beta Cephei oscillations let astronomers test how material mixes and energy moves within hot stars. The companion supplies additional orbital information that a truly isolated pulsator would not offer.

orb6-16003-2237-a-b.name: Dschubba
orb6-16003-2237-a-b.introduction: is a blue-white binary marking the forehead of Scorpius. Since 2000, its primary has been throwing off gas into a disk and changing the familiar look of the constellation.

sections.title: A star that grew visibly brighter
sections.text: In June 2000, Sebastian Otero noticed Dschubba 0.1 magnitudes brighter than normal. It has since reached at least magnitude 1.6 as it sheds luminous gas from its equator, effectively turning into a Be star before our eyes.

sections.title: Close approaches in an elongated orbit
sections.text: The companion returns on a highly eccentric orbit of about 10.5 years. Monitoring the pair near closest approach helps investigate the relationship between binary interaction and the primary’s disk.

hip-30324.name: Mirzam
hip-30324.introduction: is the hot blue-white star west of Sirius in Canis Major, about 500 light-years away. Its name means “the herald,” fitting its rising just before the Dog Star.

sections.title: A star with several rhythms
sections.text: Mirzam is a Beta Cephei variable with multiple pulsations near six hours. Their overlapping rhythms create a more complex signal than a single regular brightening and fading.

sections.title: Once the brightest star
sections.text: About four million years ago, Mirzam was the brightest star in the night sky, at magnitude −3.65, more than seven times as bright as Sirius is today.

hip-27989.name: Betelgeuse
hip-27989.introduction: is the red supergiant on Orion’s shoulder, usually the tenth-brightest star in the night sky. Placed at the Sun’s position, its surface would extend beyond the asteroid belt, and it is expected to explode as a supernova within about the next 100,000 years.

sections.title: The first star measured
sections.text: In 1920, Albert Michelson and Francis Pease used an interferometer on the Mount Wilson telescope to make Betelgeuse the first star beyond the Sun whose angular size was measured. Only R Doradus and the Sun appear larger from Earth.

sections.title: The Great Dimming
sections.text: Between late 2019 and early 2020, Betelgeuse faded dramatically. Observations linked the event to surface cooling and newly formed dust hiding part of the star; it was not a sign that a supernova had begun.

source.title: ESO: The dust responsible for Betelgeuse’s Great Dimming

sections.title: A likely hidden companion
sections.text: VLT images reported in July 2026 strengthened the case for a faint stellar companion, Betelgeuse B. Its possible influence on the supergiant’s evolution is being investigated; the star’s eventual supernova date remains uncertain.

source.title: ESO: Strongest evidence yet for Betelgeuse’s companion, July 2026

sections.title: Her bracelet
sections.text: The companion has been named Siwarha, Arabic for “her bracelet,” complementing the supergiant’s own name, which comes from the Arabic for “the hand of al-Jawzā’.” A medieval misreading of a single Arabic letter turned Yad into the European Betelgeuse.

sections.title: A brilliant end
sections.text: When Betelgeuse explodes, it should shine as brightly as the half Moon for more than three months, without harming life on Earth.

hip-15863.name: Mirfak
hip-15863.introduction: is the yellow-white supergiant at the center of the Alpha Persei Cluster, about 510 light-years away. It is the brightest star in Perseus, outshining the more famous Algol.

sections.title: A cluster for binoculars
sections.text: Mirfak sits within the Alpha Persei Cluster, or Melotte 20, which is easy to see in binoculars and includes many of the fainter stars of Perseus. Unlike most constellation patterns, it is a real stellar family.

sections.title: The most conspicuous elder
sections.text: With 6 to 7 times the Sun’s mass, Mirfak has already expanded to about 54 times the Sun’s size, while many of its cluster siblings are still on the main sequence.

hip-44816.name: Suhail
hip-44816.introduction: is the orange supergiant Lambda Velorum in Vela, about 545 light-years away. Its large, cool envelope gives it a very different appearance from nearby blue-white stars.

sections.title: A slowly changing giant
sections.text: Suhail is a slow irregular variable, ranging between magnitudes 2.14 and 2.30.

sections.title: A name shared across southern skies
sections.text: Its traditional name, Suhail al-Wazn, was shortened to Suhail for navigation. The name Suhail was also used for at least three other stars: Canopus, Gamma Velorum and Zeta Puppis.

msc-00567+6043.name: Gamma Cassiopeiae
msc-00567+6043.introduction: is the star at the center of Cassiopeia’s W, about 550 light-years away. In 1866, Angelo Secchi saw emission lines in its spectrum, the first star ever observed with them, and it is now the prototype of a class of variable Be stars. Together with a nearby companion system, it may contain eight stars.

sections.title: A star feeding a disk
sections.text: Rapid rotation and episodes of mass ejection produce a disk of gas around the primary. In the late 1930s, during one such episode, its brightness rose above magnitude 2.0 and then dropped rapidly to 3.4.

sections.title: An X-ray puzzle
sections.text: It is the prototype of a small group of X-ray sources at least ten times stronger than other Be stars. A magnetic field interacting with its disk is one proposed explanation.

sections.title: Navi
sections.text: Apollo astronauts used it as a navigation reference and called it Navi, “Ivan” spelled backwards, in honor of Apollo 1 astronaut Virgil Ivan “Gus” Grissom. The name was coined in 1967 by the Apollo 9 crew and Clarence Cleminshaw, not by Grissom himself.

spectroscopic-bright-antares.name: Antares
spectroscopic-bright-antares.introduction: is the red supergiant at the heart of Scorpius, about 550 light-years away. Its name means “rival to Ares” for its Mars-like color, and placed at the Sun’s position, it would reach into the asteroid belt.

sections.title: A moving atmosphere mapped directly
sections.text: Interferometry has resolved the supergiant’s surface and mapped gas motions above it. Unexpected turbulence in the extended atmosphere helps frame the puzzle of how red supergiants lose so much material.

source.title: ESO: Resolving Antares’s surface and atmospheric motions

sections.title: A striking unequal pair
sections.text: A much hotter companion was first reported in 1819, when Johann Tobias Bürg saw it during a lunar occultation. Through a telescope it can look greenish beside the red primary, an effect of contrast rather than of green light.

sections.title: A royal star on the Moon’s path
sections.text: Antares was one of Persia’s four royal stars. It is one of four first-magnitude stars close enough to the ecliptic to be occulted by the Moon; the others are Spica, Regulus and Aldebaran. It also lights up the nearby Rho Ophiuchi clouds.

msc-17336-3706.name: Shaula
msc-17336-3706.introduction: is the brighter of the two stars marking Scorpius’s sting. What looks like one blue-white star is a triple system.

sections.title: A close pair and a third star
sections.text: The inner companion circles in about six days, while another hot star orbits the pair in roughly three years. The short-period companion is interpreted as a young star still approaching the main sequence.

sections.title: Two kinds of changing light
sections.text: The system includes eclipses and small pulsations of the luminous primary. Distinguishing the orbital effects from the star’s own oscillations helps recover the properties of the individual members.

sections.title: An ancient pair
sections.text: Together with Lesath, Shaula appears in the Babylonian compendium MUL.APIN as Sharur and Shargaz.

hip-45941.name: Markeb
hip-45941.introduction: is the blue-white binary Kappa Velorum, one of the four stars of the False Cross, about 572 light-years away. That asterism is sometimes mistaken for the Southern Cross, causing navigation errors.

sections.title: A close binary in the sails
sections.text: Spectroscopy reveals two stars orbiting every 116.8 days, about 1.3 AU apart.

sections.title: A probe of intervening clouds
sections.text: Narrow absorption lines reveal interstellar gas between Markeb and Earth. Changes in those lines over time expose small-scale cloud structure as the line of sight moves across the material.

bright-lesath.name: Lesath
bright-lesath.introduction: is the hot blue-white star beside Shaula at the tip of Scorpius’s tail, about 580 light-years away. The two draw the scorpion’s sting and are sometimes called the Cat’s Eyes.

sections.title: A pair in the drawing
sections.text: Lesath and Shaula form a conspicuous optical pair, but Lesath is not part of Shaula’s triple system.

sections.title: Most of the energy is unseen
sections.text: Lesath’s high surface temperature shifts much of its radiation into the ultraviolet. Its visible brightness therefore understates its total energy output compared with a cooler star of the same visual magnitude.

spectroscopic-bright-avior.name: Avior
spectroscopic-bright-avior.introduction: is a southern binary whose light combines an orange giant and a hot blue star. It marks a corner of the False Cross.

sections.title: Very different stars, one point
sections.text: The cooler giant and hotter companion contribute different parts of the blended spectrum. The companion, at magnitude 3.85, would be visible to the naked eye on its own, and it may form an eclipsing pair with a further star.

sections.title: A name made for navigation
sections.text: Avior was coined in the late 1930s for the Royal Air Force’s Air Almanac, because Epsilon Carinae and Alpha Pavonis were the only two of its 57 navigation stars without classical names. The superintendent who named it never explained the word’s origin.

msc-12084-5043.name: Delta Centauri
msc-12084-5043.introduction: is a hot Be star in Centaurus, about 410 light-years away, associated with the young Lower Centaurus–Crux population. Its bright primary is part of a wider multiple system.
