sections.title: The Stars of the Flock
sections.text: The 15th-century astronomer Ulugh Beg grouped it with Alderamin and Alfirk as Al Kawākib al Firḳ, “the Stars of the Flock”. In Chinese astronomy it belongs to the Celestial Hook.

gj-34.name: Achird
gj-34.introduction: is Eta Cassiopeiae, a pair of nearby stars in Cassiopeia only 19 light-years away. The primary, Eta Cassiopeiae A, is a near twin of the Sun, with 3% more mass and 13% more light, so it shows how the Sun would look from a nearby star.

sections.title: An orbit wider than Neptune’s
sections.text: William Herschel found the orange dwarf companion, Eta Cassiopeiae B, in August 1779. The two stars circle each other every 472 years on a stretched orbit that brings them as close as 35 AU and as far apart as about 105 AU; Neptune orbits the Sun at 30 AU. Both stars contain only about half the Sun’s share of heavy elements.

sections.title: A planet still in doubt
sections.text: Achird’s velocity shows a repeating signal of about 868 days that could come from a planet at least 22 times as massive as Earth. A 2025 study found a similar 841-day period but warned that it may be a false signal, and ruled out any giant planet around the primary.

cns5-2903.name: Zavijava
cns5-2903.introduction: is Beta Virginis, a yellow-white star in Virgo about 36 light-years away, a little larger and more massive than the Sun. Despite its “beta” label, it is only the fifth-brightest star in Virgo.

sections.title: In the Moon’s path
sections.text: Zavijava lies just 0.69 degrees from the ecliptic, so the Moon regularly passes in front of it, and planets occasionally do. The next planetary occultation will be by Venus on 9 November 2210.

sections.title: A planet hinted by a wobble
sections.text: Planet claims from 1988 and 1998 were never confirmed. In 2025, a comparison of Hipparcos and Gaia measurements showed that the star’s motion across the sky is changing, an acceleration that suggests an unseen giant planet.

sections.title: The corner of the barking dog
sections.text: Its name comes from the Arabic zāwiyat al-ʿawwāʾ, “corner of the barking dog”. About 3 billion years old, the star appears to be nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life, and Sun-like oscillations let astronomers probe its interior.

orb6-21148+3803-a-b.name: Tau Cygni
orb6-21148+3803-a-b.introduction: is a binary star in Cygnus, about 66 light-years away: a yellow-white subgiant and a Sun-like companion that circle each other every 49.6 years. In July 2026, the primary received the name Enduri Senggu.

sections.title: A hedgehog goddess
sections.text: Enduri Senggu is a Manchu constellation that represents a hedgehog goddess, and Tau Cygni A is one of its stars. The IAU Working Group on Star Names adopted the name on 16 July 2026.

sections.title: A pulsing primary
sections.text: Tau Cygni A, several times as bright as the Sun, is a Delta Scuti variable whose pulsations make the pair’s combined light vary between magnitude 3.65 and 3.75. Its sixth-magnitude companion, B, is similar to the Sun in size, temperature and brightness.

msc-11182+3132.name: Alula Australis
msc-11182+3132.introduction: is Xi Ursae Majoris, a system of five objects in Ursa Major about 28 light-years away, marking the Great Bear’s left hind paw. It is the second-nearest known quintuple system, after V1054 Ophiuchi.

sections.title: The first orbit ever calculated
sections.text: William Herschel saw it as a double star in 1780 and reported orbital motion in 1804. In 1828, Félix Savary made it the first visual double star with a computed orbit. The two Sun-like stars, A and B, circle each other every 59.84 years and will appear widest apart, 3 arcseconds, in 2035.

sections.title: Pairs within a pair
sections.text: A and B each have an unseen partner revealed by their wobbling spectra: Aa and Ab orbit every 669 days, Ba and Bb every 3.98 days. Both partners are probably red dwarfs, but Ba is rich in barium, suggesting that Bb may instead be a white dwarf that once shed material onto it.

sections.title: A cold brown dwarf far out
sections.text: In 2012, data from the WISE space telescope revealed a fifth member: a cold T-type brown dwarf about 8.5 arcminutes away, roughly 4,000 AU from the bright pair.

hip-78527.name: Theta Draconis
hip-78527.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Draco, about 70 light-years away, with a close companion that whips around it every 3.07 days.

sections.title: Swelling in a tight embrace
sections.text: About 2 billion years old and 20% more massive than the Sun, the primary is nearly three times the Sun’s width and may be starting to become a subgiant. Because its partner orbits so closely, it could already fill up to 60% of the space it can hold before gas spills over.

sections.title: A century-old binary
sections.text: W. W. Campbell discovered the companion from the star’s shifting spectrum in 1899, and H. D. Curtis published its first orbit in 1907. Later velocity changes hint at a third member.

hip-91792.name: Zeta Pavonis
hip-91792.introduction: is an orange giant in Pavo, the Peacock, about 215 light-years away.

sections.title: Drifting with the Hyades stream
sections.text: Its motion through space marks it as a member of the Hyades Supercluster, a group of stars sharing the motion of the Hyades cluster. Having used up the hydrogen in its core, it has grown to 19 times the Sun’s radius and shines 133 times as brightly.

cns5-gj-455.3.name: Alchiba
cns5-gj-455.3.introduction: is Alpha Corvi, a yellow-white star in Corvus about 49 light-years away with a faint red dwarf companion. Despite its “alpha” label, it is only the fifth-brightest star in the Crow.

sections.title: A pair that may be coming apart
sections.text: Alchiba and its red dwarf companion, B, are 3.1 arcseconds apart and were confirmed as a physical pair in 2021. Their motions differ more than an orbit should allow, which may mean the pair is drifting apart. Alchiba itself changes its spectrum every three days, probably because it pulsates.

sections.title: Tent and beak
sections.text: Its name comes from the Arabic al-xibā, “tent”. Another old name, Minkar al Ghurab, was translated into Latin as Rostrum Corvi, “the beak of the crow”. In Chinese astronomy it is the “right linchpin” of the Chariot mansion, and the US Navy ship USS Alchiba was named after it.

cns5-2551.name: I Carinae
cns5-2551.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Carina, about 53 light-years away and younger than the Sun, at about 1.3 billion years. In about 2.7 million years it will pass within 24 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: Near the future south pole
sections.text: As Earth’s axis slowly wobbles, the south celestial pole will pass close to I Carinae and Omega Carinae within the next 7,500 years.

sections.title: A hidden giant planet?
sections.text: Hipparcos and Gaia measured slightly different motions for the star, an acceleration that suggests a giant planet on a close orbit.

hip-43409.name: Gamma Pyxidis
hip-43409.introduction: is an orange giant in Pyxis, the Compass, about 210 light-years away.

sections.title: Helium at its heart
sections.text: About four billion years old, it now fuses helium in its core. With 1.64 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to nearly 22 times the Sun’s radius and shines 178 times as brightly.

sections.title: A wide path around the Galaxy
sections.text: It moves at 54 km/s relative to the Sun, and its orbit carries it between 21,300 and 30,700 light-years from the center of the Milky Way.

cns5-gj-426.1.name: Iota Leonis
cns5-gj-426.1.introduction: is a quadruple star system in Leo, about 77 light-years away. Its two brightest stars, A and B, circle each other every 190 years and have been drawing apart since their closest approach in 1948.

sections.title: Two pairs, far apart
sections.text: Iota Leonis A is a yellow-white subgiant, and B is a main-sequence star 18% more massive than the Sun. More than 5 arcminutes away lies Iota Leonis C, a faint orange pair that shares their motion through space.

sections.title: The Second Western General
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it is part of the Right Wall of the Supreme Palace Enclosure, together with Beta Virginis and three other stars of Leo, and represents the Second Western General.

msc-01084-5515.name: Wurren
msc-01084-5515.introduction: is Zeta Phoenicis, a multiple star system in Phoenix about 290 light-years away. Its two brightest stars, both hot and blue-white, eclipse each other every 1.67 days, dimming the system from magnitude 3.9 to 4.4.

sections.title: The little fish
sections.text: Wurren means “child” in the language of the Wardaman people of northern Australia. Here it refers to a little fish that brings water to a porcupine or echidna, represented by nearby Achernar.

sections.title: More stars around the eclipses
sections.text: Beyond the eclipsing pair, a white star, B, circles every 210 years or so, and a yellow-white star, C, takes more than 5,000 years.

hip-43103.name: Iota Cancri
hip-43103.introduction: is a double star in Cancer, about 346 light-years away: a yellow giant and a fast-spinning white companion 30 arcseconds apart. In February 2026, the giant received the name Yuyu.

sections.title: A crab from Java
sections.text: Yuyu is the Balinese name of the constellation Cancer, from a Javanese word for the freshwater crabs of Indonesia’s rice fields. The constellation is attested for at least 1,300 years.

sections.title: Barium from a vanished partner
sections.text: The giant, Iota Cancri A, is a mild barium star. Such stars usually received material from a companion late in its life, so an unseen white dwarf is assumed to orbit it.

sections.title: A spinning shell star
sections.text: Iota Cancri B spins at least 170 km/s and is surrounded by a shell of gas thrown off by its rapid rotation. The two stars are at least 3,236 AU apart.

hip-80000.name: Gamma² Normae
hip-80000.introduction: is the brightest star in Norma, an orange giant about 138 light-years away that now fuses helium in its core.

sections.title: A companion that wasn’t
sections.text: A 10th-magnitude star 45 arcseconds away was long listed as its binary companion, but Gaia showed it to be much farther away. Instead, a white dwarf 24 arcseconds away shares Gamma² Normae’s distance and motion.

hip-93244.name: Epsilon Aquilae
hip-93244.introduction: is an orange giant in Aquila, about 180 light-years away, with an unseen companion that circles it every 3.5 years. In June 2026, it received the Marshallese name Arin-majlep, “replica of the Big Eye,” the Big Eye being Altair.

sections.title: The eagle’s tail
sections.text: It shared the old Arabic name Deneb el Okab, “the tail of the eagle,” with Zeta Aquilae. In Chinese astronomy, it represents the ancient states of Wu and Yue.

sections.title: Sixty years to confirm
sections.text: Friedrich Küstner reported the hidden companion in 1914, but it was not confirmed until 1974. The giant has been called a barium star, rich in heavy elements, but a 1990 analysis found normal abundances.

hip-118268.name: Omega Piscium
hip-118268.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Pisces, about 107 light-years away, where the tail of the western fish begins east of the Circlet. In September 2026, it received the name Pili, from the Chinese for “thunderbolt”.

sections.title: Last in line, then first
sections.text: In the year 2000, it was the named star with the highest right ascension, the sky’s equivalent of longitude. The slow wobble of Earth’s axis carried it just past 0 hours in 2013.

sections.title: A binary that wasn’t
sections.text: Changes in its spectrum were once read as a 2.16-day orbit, but that claim was later shown to be false. As a single star, it is 20 times as bright as the Sun.

hip-101421.name: Aldulfin
hip-101421.introduction: is Epsilon Delphini, a blue-white star at the tail of Delphinus, the Dolphin, about 365 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the dolphin’s tail”.

sections.title: A hot star moving on
sections.text: At 13,600 K, it shines 676 times as brightly as the Sun and has used up the hydrogen in its core. It may be slightly variable, occasionally brightening to magnitude 3.95. In Chinese astronomy, it is the first star of the Rotten Gourd.

hip-111497.name: Eta Aquarii
hip-111497.introduction: is a blue-white star in Aquarius, about 178 light-years away, near the radiant of the Eta Aquariid meteor shower, which is named after it. In September 2026, it received the name Fenmu, from the Chinese for “tomb”.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: Only about 65 million years old, it spins at least 271 km/s. The rotation flattens the star so that it is 24% wider at the equator than from pole to pole.

sections.title: Tent and tomb
sections.text: Arabic astronomers counted it among al Aḣbiyah, “the Tent”, with three other stars of Aquarius. The same four stars form the Chinese asterism Fén Mù, “the Tomb”.

hip-57380.name: Nu Virginis
hip-57380.introduction: is a red giant at the western tip of Virgo, about 330 light-years away, nearly due south of Denebola. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon.

sections.title: Four rhythms at once
sections.text: Data from the Hipparcos satellite revealed that it flickers by about a hundredth of a magnitude, with periods of 11.1, 12.3, 16.8 and 23.7 days. With slightly less mass than the Sun, it has swollen to 54 times the Sun’s radius and shines 520 times as brightly.

hip-40702.name: Alpha Chamaeleontis
hip-40702.introduction: is a yellow-white star in the far-southern constellation Chamaeleon, about 64 light-years away. It is approaching the Sun and will come within about 47 light-years in some 666,000 years.

sections.title: Short on iron
sections.text: Its spectrum shows unusually little iron. About 1.8 billion years old, it has 1.4 times the Sun’s mass and shines 7.5 times as brightly.

cns5-gj-549.name: Theta Boötis
cns5-gj-549.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Boötes, about 47 light-years away, marking a corner of the Herdsman’s raised left hand. Its traditional name, Asellus Primus, is Latin for “first donkey colt”.

sections.title: A Sun-like star near middle age
sections.text: Theta Boötis A has 23% more mass than the Sun and shines 4.2 times as brightly. At 3–4 billion years old, it may be nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life. An 11th-magnitude red dwarf, B, lies about 70 arcseconds away, at least 1,000 AU from A, and shares its motion through space.

sections.title: Whelps and a spear
sections.text: Arabic astronomers counted it with Iota, Kappa and Lambda Boötis among “the Whelps of the Hyenas”. In Chinese astronomy it is the third star of the Celestial Spear.

hip-71536.name: Rho Lupi
hip-71536.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Lupus, about 347 light-years away, and a member of the Scorpius–Centaurus association, the nearest region of recent massive-star formation.

sections.title: Young and spinning
sections.text: Only about 44 million years old, it has 4.7 times the Sun’s mass and shines 365 times as brightly. It spins at least 166 km/s, bulging 6% at the equator, and flickers by less than a hundredth of a magnitude every 10.7 hours.

hip-74824.name: Beta Circini
hip-74824.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Circinus, a white star about 96 light-years away, roughly twice the Sun’s mass and 19 times as bright.

sections.title: A brown dwarf far out
sections.text: In 2015, astronomers found a brown dwarf, Beta Circini b, sharing the star’s motion about 6,656 AU away. With about 59 Jupiter masses and a temperature near 2,100 K, it is far too small to burn hydrogen like a star.

hip-18614.name: Menkib
hip-18614.introduction: is Xi Persei, a blue giant in Perseus about 1,400 light-years away and one of the hottest stars visible to the naked eye. Its name comes from the Arabic for “shoulder” of the Pleiades.

sections.title: The star that lights the California Nebula
sections.text: At about 35,000 K and some 30 times the Sun’s mass, Menkib gives off more than 260,000 times the Sun’s energy, mostly as ultraviolet light. This radiation makes the nearby California Nebula glow.

sections.title: A runaway?
sections.text: Menkib belongs to the Perseus OB2 association of young stars moving together, but it now lies about 650 light-years from the group’s center and has an unusually high velocity. It may have been flung out as a runaway star.

hip-55705.name: Gamma Crateris
hip-55705.introduction: is a double star at the center of Crater, about 86 light-years away, that a small telescope can split. Its motion suggests it may belong to the Castor Moving Group.

sections.title: A fast spinner with a faint partner
sections.text: The white primary spins at least 144 km/s and pulses by a thousandth of a magnitude every 52.5 minutes, a variation found by students mining survey data. Its 9.6-magnitude companion, B, lies 5 arcseconds away, at least 126 AU from the primary.

hip-36962.name: Upsilon Geminorum
hip-36962.introduction: is a red giant in Gemini, about 252 light-years away. With 1.5 times the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to 40 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: Remnant of a lost cluster
sections.text: It belongs to the Wolf 630 moving group, a set of stars about 2.7 billion years old that travel through space in parallel and may be the scattered remains of a dissolved cluster.

hip-12387.name: Delta Ceti
hip-12387.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Cetus, about 630 light-years away, just north of the celestial equator. It lies less than a degree from the galaxy M77, which needs a telescope to be seen.

sections.title: A one-beat pulsator
sections.text: Delta Ceti is a Beta Cephei variable that brightens and fades every 3.9 hours. Unlike most stars of its kind, it pulsates with just one period. With 7.9 times the Sun’s mass and 5,100 times its light, it is nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life.

sections.title: A 169-year companion
sections.text: Old observations and velocity measurements from 2014–2018 reveal an unseen companion with at least 1.1 times the Sun’s mass, orbiting every 169 years.

hip-67459.name: Upsilon Boötis
hip-67459.introduction: is an orange giant in Boötes, about 242 light-years away and roughly 10 billion years old, more than twice the age of the Sun.

sections.title: Weighed by its vibrations
sections.text: Its oscillations show that it has only 1.1 times the Sun’s mass, while interferometers measure it at about 38 times the Sun’s radius. It shines 332 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-53740.name: Alkes
hip-53740.introduction: is Alpha Crateris, an orange giant at the base of Crater, the Cup, about 160 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the cup”.

sections.title: First star of the Cup
sections.text: An Arabic star catalog called it “first [star] of the Cup”, and in Chinese astronomy it is the first star of the Wings mansion. The US Navy cargo ship USS Alkes was named after it.

sections.title: Helium burner or not?
sections.text: Alkes is probably a red clump giant fusing helium in its core, about 1.8 times the Sun’s mass and two billion years old. It could instead still be burning hydrogen around an inert core, which would make it older and slightly lighter.

hip-104139.name: Theta Capricorni
hip-104139.introduction: is a white star in Capricornus, about 149 light-years away, with a small companion that circles it every 140 days. In February 2026, the primary received the name Udang.

sections.title: The Shrimp of Bali
sections.text: Udang, “the Shrimp”, is the Balinese constellation identified with Capricornus, part of a calendar tradition attested for about 1,300 years.

sections.title: A companion found at last
sections.text: Velocity changes long hinted at a partner, but infrared searches found nothing until an interferometer resolved it in 2023. The companion has about half the Sun’s mass and orbits just 0.78 AU from the primary, closer than Earth is to the Sun.

sections.title: Behind the Sun in February
sections.text: Lying just 0.58 degrees from the ecliptic, it passes almost behind the Sun around 3 February and can be hidden by the Moon.

hip-69701.name: Syrma
hip-69701.introduction: is Iota Virginis, a yellow-white star in Virgo about 72 light-years away with an unseen companion. Its name comes from the Greek for “train” of a garment.

sections.title: Pulled by an invisible partner
sections.text: Syrma wobbles around a companion that has never been seen directly. With about 0.6 times the Sun’s mass, the partner may be a small star or a white dwarf, and a preliminary orbit takes about 55 years.

sections.title: A distant pair in tow
sections.text: In 2011, astronomers noticed that the faint orange star HD 125354, itself a close double, shares Syrma’s motion. It lies about 1.2 light-years away from Syrma.

hip-33160.name: Theta Canis Majoris
hip-33160.introduction: is an orange giant forming the nose of the Great Dog, about 270 light-years away.

sections.title: Twice the Sun’s age
sections.text: About ten billion years old, it has slightly less mass than the Sun but has grown to 33 times its width. It is moving away from us at 96 km/s.

hip-94114.name: Meridiana
hip-94114.introduction: is Alpha Coronae Australis, the brightest star in the Southern Crown, about 120 light-years away. It is the only star in the constellation with a traditional name.

sections.title: The southern Alphecca
sections.text: Its full traditional name, Alphekka Meridiana, means “southern Alphekka” in Latin, after Alphecca, the brightest star in the Northern Crown.

sections.title: Spinning near the limit
sections.text: Like Vega, it gives off excess infrared light that hints at a disk of dust. It spins at almost 200 km/s at the equator, turning once in about 14 hours, close to the speed at which it would start to fly apart.

hip-11001.name: Delta Hydri
hip-11001.introduction: is a white star in Hydrus, the southern Water Snake, about 140 light-years away.

sections.title: A young, flattened star
sections.text: About 209 million years old, it has 2.25 times the Sun’s mass and spins at least 162 km/s, which makes it bulge 7% at the equator. It shines about 40 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-14146.name: Tau³ Eridani
hip-14146.introduction: is a white star in Eridanus, about 88 light-years away.

sections.title: A dusty candidate
sections.text: In 2001, it was reported as a possible Vega-like star with an infrared glow from a surrounding disk, but this has not been confirmed. About 476 million years old, it spins at least 133 km/s and shines 14 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-77450.name: Gudja
hip-77450.introduction: is Kappa Serpentis, a red giant in the head of the Serpent, about 381 light-years away. Its name means “water goanna” in the language of the Wardaman people of northern Australia.

sections.title: Near the top of the giant branch
sections.text: Gudja has expanded to about 71 times the Sun’s radius and shines nearly 1,000 times as brightly. Detailed study places it near the most luminous stage of a red giant’s first ascent, just before helium begins to burn in its core.

hip-94160.name: Beta Coronae Australis
hip-94160.introduction: is an orange bright giant in Corona Australis, about 550 light-years away. In August 2026, it received the name Alqubba, from the traditional Arabic name of the constellation, “the dome” or domed tent.

sections.title: Rich in carbon and nitrogen
sections.text: Its spectrum shows an unusually strong signature of cyanogen, making it a CN star. With 5.2 times the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to 39 times the Sun’s width and shines 614 times as brightly. Interstellar dust dims it by about 0.3 magnitudes.

hip-12394.name: Epsilon Hydri
hip-12394.introduction: is a blue-white star in Hydrus, about 153 light-years away, and a member of the Tucana–Horologium moving group, a family of young stars that travel together.

sections.title: A youthful spinner
sections.text: Only about 133 million years old, it has 2.6 times the Sun’s mass, spins at least 96 km/s and shines 60 times as brightly as the Sun.

gj-61.name: Titawin
gj-61.introduction: is Upsilon Andromedae, a yellow-white star in Andromeda about 44 light-years away, about 10 degrees east of the Andromeda Galaxy. It was the first Sun-like star found to have more than one planet, and the first multiple-planet system known in a binary star system.

sections.title: Three giant planets
sections.text: Geoffrey Marcy and Paul Butler found the first planet, b, in 1996. In 1999, two teams independently concluded that three planets were needed to explain the star’s wobble. All three are probably gas giants: b orbits only about 0.05 AU from the star, while d circles within the system’s habitable zone.

sections.title: Tilted, stretched orbits
sections.text: The planets do not orbit in one plane. Planet c is strongly tilted relative to the others, and both c and d follow more stretched orbits than any planet in the Solar System. A close encounter with a lost fourth planet may have shaped them. A fourth-planet signal reported in 2010 is more likely an instrumental artifact.

sections.title: Names from Morocco and Muslim Spain
sections.text: In the 2015 NameExoWorlds vote, a Moroccan astronomy club named the star after Tiṭṭawin, the Berber name of the cities of Tétouan and Tataouine. Planets b, c and d became Saffar, Samh and Majriti, honoring astronomers of 10th- and 11th-century Muslim Spain.

sections.title: A red dwarf far out
sections.text: In 2002, a faint red dwarf, Upsilon Andromedae B, was found sharing the system’s motion at least 750 AU from Titawin. Its pull may have swept away any outer dust belt like the Solar System’s Kuiper belt.

gj-107.name: Theta Persei
gj-107.introduction: is a nearby double star in Perseus, about 36 light-years away and one of the closest stars visible to the naked eye. Its primary is a yellowish star somewhat larger and brighter than the Sun.

sections.title: A red dwarf and an impostor
sections.text: A red dwarf, Theta Persei B, orbits about 250 AU from the primary. An 11th-magnitude star listed as component C is a distant background object moving quickly away from the pair in our sky. A possible brown dwarf reported near B in 2010 remains unconfirmed.

hip-48356.name: Zhang
hip-48356.introduction: is Upsilon¹ Hydrae, a yellow giant in Hydra about 248 light-years away with a brown dwarf companion. Its name comes from Zhāng, the Chinese “Extended Net” mansion, of which it is the first star.

sections.title: A brown dwarf on a stretched orbit
sections.text: In 2005, the Okayama Planet Search team announced a companion with at least 49 times Jupiter’s mass that circles Zhang every 4.1 years on a highly elongated orbit. The giant itself has 3.3 times the Sun’s mass and is only about 270 million years old.

hip-90568.name: Zeta Telescopii
hip-90568.introduction: is the second-brightest star in Telescopium, an orange giant about 122 light-years away.

sections.title: Helium in the core
sections.text: A red clump giant, it fuses helium in its core. Only 40% more massive than the Sun, it has grown to eight times the Sun’s radius and shines about 30 times as brightly.

hip-113638.name: Zeta Gruis
hip-113638.introduction: is an orange giant in Grus, the Crane, about 163 light-years away.

sections.title: Poor in iron
sections.text: Its spectrum shows less iron and cyanogen than usual. Having used up the hydrogen in its core, it has expanded to nine times the Sun’s girth and shines 39 times as brightly.

hip-12486.name: Iota Eridani
hip-12486.introduction: is an orange giant in Eridanus, about 146 light-years away.

sections.title: A measured giant
sections.text: Interferometers have measured its disk at 2.25 thousandths of an arcsecond. About 3.6 billion years old and only 29% more massive than the Sun, it is eleven times as large and now fuses helium in its core.

hip-51839.name: Gamma Chamaeleontis
hip-51839.introduction: is an orange giant in Chamaeleon, about 445 light-years away, faintly visible from dark southern skies.

sections.title: A cool, swollen giant
sections.text: At 3,870 K, it has expanded to 78 times the Sun’s radius and shines 864 times as brightly. It may vary slightly, by about a hundredth of a magnitude.

msc-07038-1538.name: Muliphein
msc-07038-1538.introduction: is Gamma Canis Majoris, a blue-white bright giant in Canis Major about 430 light-years away. Why such a faint star received the “gamma” label is uncertain; it may be because it lies in the same part of the constellation as Sirius and Mirzam.

sections.title: On the flag of Brazil
sections.text: Muliphein appears on the flag of Brazil, where it represents the state of Rondônia. The US Navy cargo ship USS Muliphen was also named after it.

sections.title: A mercury star
sections.text: Muliphein is a chemically peculiar mercury-manganese star with unusual spectral lines. It turns once every 6.2 days, has 4.2 times the Sun’s mass and shines 537 times as brightly. It belongs to the open cluster Collinder 121 and may have a close companion.

hip-116771.name: Iota Piscium
hip-116771.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Pisces, about 45 light-years away, slightly larger and brighter than the Sun. In September 2026, it received the name Puwuh Atarung, “battling quails”, from a Balinese constellation in Pisces.

sections.title: Companions that weren’t
sections.text: It was once thought to have one or two companion stars, but both turned out to be chance alignments. A faint candidate 8.5 arcseconds away may still share its motion. Excess far-infrared light suggests a cold disk of debris around the star.

hip-102978.name: Omega Capricorni
hip-102978.introduction: is an orange giant in Capricornus, about 560 light-years away, near the border with Microscopium. With 7.6 times the Sun’s mass, it is only about 48 million years old yet has already swollen to 93 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: A possible runaway
sections.text: It moves about 26 km/s faster than the stars around it, making it a possible runaway star. It is also a barium star, enriched in heavy elements that probably came from a companion now a white dwarf.

msc-06024+0939.name: Mu Orionis
msc-06024+0939.introduction: is a system of four stars in Orion, about 155 light-years away, arranged in two close pairs like Mizar or Epsilon Lyrae.

sections.title: Two tight pairs
sections.text: Mu Orionis Aa, a white metallic-line star with twice the Sun’s mass, has a yellow dwarf partner, Ab, only 0.077 AU away, a fifth of Mercury’s distance from the Sun. The B pair, two yellow-white stars, is just as tight. The two pairs are only a few tenths of an arcsecond apart in our sky.

hip-102485.name: Psi Capricorni
hip-102485.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Capricornus, about 48 light-years away. It passed within 20 light-years of the Sun about 467,000 years ago.

sections.title: A dusty spinner
sections.text: About 2.3 billion years old, it spins at about 41 km/s, twenty times as fast as the Sun, and like the Sun its equator rotates faster than its poles. Infrared light reveals a cold debris disk about 39 AU from the star, roughly the distance of Pluto from the Sun.

hip-112405.name: Beta Octantis
hip-112405.introduction: is a white star in Octans, near the south celestial pole, about 149 light-years away. Its wobbling motion hints at an unseen companion.

sections.title: Leaving the main sequence
sections.text: About 500 million years old, it has 2.3 times the Sun’s mass and is starting to evolve away from the hydrogen-burning stage, with a spectrum between a dwarf and a subgiant. It shines 42 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-78159.name: Epsilon Coronae Borealis
hip-78159.introduction: is an orange giant in the Northern Crown, about 241 light-years away, with a giant planet and a distant companion star. It lies one degree north of the variable star T Coronae Borealis and serves as a guide to find it.

sections.title: A planet around a giant
sections.text: Seven years of velocity measurements, from 2005 to 2012, revealed a 418-day wobble caused by a planet at least 6.7 times as massive as Jupiter, orbiting at 1.3 AU.

sections.title: A quarter of Mercury’s orbit
sections.text: The giant is nearly 24 times the Sun’s size, about a quarter the diameter of Mercury’s orbit. An orange dwarf companion, B, circles it at about 135 AU every 900 years.

orb6-15329+3122-a-b.name: Theta Coronae Borealis
orb6-15329+3122-a-b.introduction: is a double star in the Northern Crown, about 375 light-years away. In May 2026, its primary received the name Guansuo, from the Chinese constellation of the “Coiled Thong”.

sections.title: A star spinning off a disk
sections.text: Theta Coronae Borealis A spins at about 393 km/s, so fast that it has shed a disk of gas, making it a Be shell star. In 1970, it faded by 0.7 magnitude, perhaps because ejected dust blocked its light.

sections.title: A young pair
sections.text: The white companion, B, orbits at about 86 AU, taking roughly 300 years. The system is only about 85 million years old, and the primary will run out of core hydrogen within another 75 million years.

hip-98032.name: Iota Sagittarii
hip-98032.introduction: is an orange giant in Sagittarius, about 201 light-years away, with a faint red dwarf companion.

sections.title: Seen at last
sections.text: Hipparcos measurements showed the giant wobbling, and in 2014 the SPHERE instrument on the Very Large Telescope imaged the cause: a red dwarf only 0.24 arcseconds away and more than 4,000 times fainter.

hip-42313.name: Delta Hydrae
hip-42313.introduction: is a triple star at the head of Hydra, about 177 light-years away. An old Arabic catalog called it Lisan al Shudja, “the snake’s tongue”.

sections.title: A spinning star and a red dwarf
sections.text: The bright white primary spins at least 285 km/s, bulging 20% at the equator. A red dwarf circles it every 200 days at 0.9 AU, and may one day share an envelope with it when the primary swells into a giant. A faint third star lies about 147 AU away.

sections.title: Willow and crab
sections.text: It is the first star of the Chinese Willow mansion. The people of Groote Eylandt in northern Australia saw it and nearby stars of Hydra as Unwala, “the Crab”.

msc-21446+2539.name: Kappa Pegasi
msc-21446+2539.introduction: is a triple star in Pegasus, about 112 light-years away, made of two close components that circle each other every 11.6 years.

sections.title: A pair hiding a pair
sections.text: Sherburne W. Burnham discovered in 1880 that it is double. The fainter component, B, is itself a spectroscopic binary whose two stars orbit each other every six days.

cns5-2970.name: Eta Crucis
cns5-2970.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Crux, the Southern Cross, about 64 light-years away, surrounded by two belts of dust.

sections.title: An asteroid belt and a Kuiper belt
sections.text: A warm dust belt lies about 13 AU from the star, fed by colliding planetesimals and perhaps by comets. A narrow cold ring circles at about 134 AU. The cold ring was imaged by ALMA and SMA and presented in 2025.

sections.title: A past visitor
sections.text: Eta Crucis made its closest approach about 1.6 million years ago, passing roughly 26 light-years from the Sun.

msc-06290+2013.name: Nu Geminorum
msc-06290+2013.introduction: is a multiple star in Gemini, about 730 light-years away, with an outer Be star circling a close inner pair. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon.

sections.title: Orbits within orbits
sections.text: The inner pair orbits every 54 days. A classical Be star, spinning fast enough to shed gas, circles them every 19.1 years. The two orbits run in the same direction and nearly in the same plane.

sections.title: Venus in front, 2028
sections.text: On 15 August 2028, Venus will pass in front of Nu Geminorum as seen from southern Africa and Madagascar. With Alhena, Propus, Tejat and Alzirr, it formed the Arabic asterism Al Nuḥātai, the Camel’s Hump.

msc-06041+2316.name: 1 Geminorum
msc-06041+2316.introduction: is a triple star at the western edge of Gemini, about 155 light-years away, the first star in Flamsteed’s list for the constellation.

sections.title: Found while focusing on Uranus
sections.text: In 1948, astronomers found that it is a close double while using it to focus a telescope for observing Uranus. A giant, A, is circled every 13.4 years by a tight pair, Ba and Bb, whose stars are only 0.12 AU apart.

hip-34769.name: Delta Monocerotis
hip-34769.introduction: is a white star in Monoceros, about 414 light-years away, just south of the celestial equator. It came within 88 light-years of the Sun about 7.3 million years ago.

sections.title: A fast spinner
sections.text: With 2.4 times the Sun’s mass and an age of about 405 million years, it spins at least 175 km/s and shines 350 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-109937.name: 1 Lacertae
hip-109937.introduction: is an orange giant in Lacerta, about 674 light-years away, between a giant and a bright giant in brightness.

sections.title: Old before its time
sections.text: Only about 170 million years old, it has four times the Sun’s mass and has already swollen to 69 times the Sun’s radius, shining about 1,450 times as brightly. It was once suspected of varying, but this was later withdrawn.

hip-110003.name: Ancha
hip-110003.introduction: is Theta Aquarii, a yellow giant in Aquarius about 190 light-years away. Its name is Medieval Latin for “the haunch”.

sections.title: A star of weeping
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it is the second star of Qì, “Weeping”, a two-star asterism with Rho Aquarii. Lying near the ecliptic, it can be hidden by the Moon and, very rarely, by a planet.

sections.title: Between subgiant and giant
sections.text: About 437 million years old and roughly 2.4–2.8 times the Sun’s mass, it is partway through its expansion into a giant and has already reached about 12 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-77853.name: Theta Librae
hip-77853.introduction: is an orange giant in Libra, about 167 light-years away near the border with Scorpius. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon.

sections.title: Which kind of giant?
sections.text: With about 1.5 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 12 times the Sun’s girth. It is most likely still burning hydrogen in a shell around an inert core, but there is a 41% chance that it already burns helium.

hip-17874.name: g Eridani
hip-17874.introduction: is HD 24160, a yellow giant in Eridanus about 218 light-years away.

sections.title: A far-flung moving group member
sections.text: It is an outlying member of the Ursa Major Moving Group, stars that share a common motion through space. About 1.8 billion years old, it has 2.3 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to about 11 times its radius.

msc-17237+3709.name: Rho Herculis
msc-17237+3709.introduction: is a double star in Hercules, about 393 light-years away, whose two white components lie four arcseconds apart.

sections.title: Three stars in two points
sections.text: Rho Herculis A, a giant, is itself a close pair resolved by speckle interferometry, 0.25 arcseconds apart. B is a slightly hotter star still burning hydrogen. A was once considered chemically peculiar, but this is now doubted.

msc-22407-2703.name: Epsilon Piscis Austrini
msc-22407-2703.introduction: is a blue-white star in Piscis Austrinus, about 550 light-years away, that spins so fast it has thrown off a disk of gas.

sections.title: Near its breaking point
sections.text: It spins at least 216 km/s, compared with the 301 km/s at which it would start to come apart. With 6 times the Sun’s mass, it shines 661 times as brightly.

sections.title: Partners near and far
sections.text: A faint red dwarf shares its motion about 11,700 AU away. The star’s changing motion between Hipparcos and Gaia also hints at a closer companion, perhaps as massive as the Sun, between 6 and 30 AU.

cns5-gj-274.name: Rho Geminorum
cns5-gj-274.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Gemini, about 59 light-years away and about 5 degrees west of Castor, with a distant orange companion.

sections.title: The companion nobody can find
sections.text: Observers measured a 12.5-magnitude companion, Rho Geminorum B, five times between 1910 and 1935. Nobody has seen it since, and later attempts to resolve it have failed, although the old measurements do not fit a background star.

sections.title: A restless partner
sections.text: About 18,600 AU away, the orange dwarf V376 Geminorum shares the system’s motion. Starspots make it vary every 11.6 days, and it is surprisingly active for a system about 2.1 billion years old.

hip-17608.name: Merope
hip-17608.introduction: is one of the bright stars of the Pleiades cluster in Taurus, about 440 light-years away. It is named after one of the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione in Greek mythology.

sections.title: The Merope Nebula
sections.text: Merope is surrounded by the Merope Nebula, NGC 1435, which appears brightest close to the star.

sections.title: A gentle pulsator
sections.text: In 1985, Bernard McNamara announced that Merope varies. It is a Beta Cephei variable that pulsates every 0.49 days by up to a hundredth of a magnitude, and shines about 930 times as brightly as the Sun.

sections.title: A cluster’s disputed distance
sections.text: Hipparcos measurements placed the Pleiades closer than other methods did. Gaia, the Hubble Space Telescope and other techniques showed that Hipparcos suffered a systematic error and that the cluster is most likely about 440 light-years away.

cns5-4658.name: 110 Herculis
cns5-4658.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Hercules, about 63 light-years away, roughly halfway between Rasalhague and Albireo.

sections.title: A disk around a bigger Sun
sections.text: With 1.4–1.7 times the Sun’s mass and about twice its width, it gives off excess infrared light that reveals a surrounding disk of material.

orb6-16341+4226-a-b.name: Sigma Herculis
orb6-16341+4226-a-b.introduction: is a binary star in Hercules, about 301 light-years away, whose two white stars circle each other every 7.4 years at about 7 AU.

sections.title: Dust that keeps coming back
sections.text: The primary is surrounded by a cold debris disk at about 157 AU and perhaps a warmer belt between 7 and 30 AU. Dust in the inner belt should vanish within about 46,000 years, so collisions between larger bodies must keep replenishing it.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: Sigma Herculis A spins at least 280 km/s, which makes it bulge 18% at the equator. It has 2.6 times the Sun’s mass and shines 230 times as brightly.

msc-22467+1210.name: Xi Pegasi
msc-22467+1210.introduction: is a yellow-white star in the neck of Pegasus, about 53 light-years away, with a faint red dwarf companion. In August 2026, it received the name Tugongli, from the Chinese asterism of the Clerks of the Earth Official.

sections.title: A red dwarf companion
sections.text: The 12th-magnitude red dwarf NLTT 54820 shares its motion 11.4 arcseconds away, at least 192 AU from the primary. The main star is 87% larger than the Sun and shines 4.6 times as brightly.

hip-17651.name: Tau⁶ Eridani
hip-17651.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Eridanus, about 58 light-years away near the border with Fornax.

sections.title: Between dwarf and subgiant
sections.text: With 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, it shines 5.3 times as brightly, and its spectrum shows traits of both a hydrogen-burning dwarf and a subgiant. Unlike the Sun, it shows no surface magnetic activity.

hip-19893.name: Gamma Doradus
hip-19893.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Dorado, about 67 light-years away, and the prototype of the Gamma Doradus variables, a whole class of pulsating stars named after it.

sections.title: The first of its kind
sections.text: Instead of simply swelling and shrinking, Gamma Doradus pulsates in waves driven by gravity, which change its brightness by less than a tenth of a magnitude. Four rhythms have been found, with periods between 12.8 and 18.2 hours.

sections.title: Two dust belts
sections.text: Excess infrared light at several wavelengths shows that the star is circled by a pair of debris disks. Its motion links it to the IC 2391 supercluster of stars.

hip-20635.name: Kappa¹ Tauri
hip-20635.introduction: is a white star in the Hyades cluster in Taurus, about 156 light-years away. With its fainter neighbor Kappa² Tauri, about six light-years from it, it forms the wide double Kappa Tauri.

sections.title: Proof for Einstein
sections.text: Kappa Tauri was among the stars photographed during the solar eclipse of 29 May 1919 by Arthur Eddington’s expedition to Príncipe and a second team in Sobral, Brazil. Their positions confirmed Einstein’s prediction that the Sun’s gravity bends starlight.

sections.title: A disk and a crowd
sections.text: Kappa¹ Tauri gives off excess infrared light from a disk about 67 AU from the star. Several fainter stars nearby are much more distant background objects.

hip-92609.name: Lambda Pavonis
hip-92609.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Pavo, about 1,100 light-years away, that spins fast enough to have built a disk of gas around itself.

sections.title: An unsettled shell star
sections.text: With 12.5 times the Sun’s mass and 8,450 times its light, it spins at least 190 km/s and occasionally brightens to magnitude 4.0. Varying signals have kept astronomers debating whether it is single, double or pulsating.

hip-113246.name: Delta Piscis Austrini
hip-113246.introduction: is a yellow giant in Piscis Austrinus, about 170 light-years away, with a faint companion 5.2 arcseconds away that shares its motion.

sections.title: Tent ropes
sections.text: Its Chinese name means “materials for making tents”, a one-star asterism of the Encampment mansion. The giant is about 3.7 billion years old and now fuses helium in its core.

spectroscopic-hip-93825.name: Gamma Coronae Australis
spectroscopic-hip-93825.introduction: is a pair of nearly identical yellow-white stars in Corona Australis, about 56 light-years away, that circle each other every 122 years.

sections.title: Stellar twins
sections.text: Each star has about 1.15 times the Sun’s mass and 1.4–1.5 times its radius, and both have surface temperatures near 6,100 K. They appear about 1.9 arcseconds apart.

hip-69427.name: Kang
hip-69427.introduction: is Kappa Virginis, an orange giant in Virgo about 281 light-years away. Its name comes from Kàng, the Chinese “Neck” mansion, of which it is the first star.

sections.title: Twice the Sun’s age
sections.text: About 9.7 billion years old, Kang has 1.5 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to more than 25 times the Sun’s radius, shining about 230 times as brightly.

msc-10279+3642.name: Beta Leonis Minoris
msc-10279+3642.introduction: is a binary star in Leo Minor, about 154 light-years away. It is the only star in the constellation with a Bayer letter, yet only the second brightest, after 46 Leonis Minoris.

sections.title: A 39-year orbit
sections.text: A yellow giant that fuses helium in its core and a yellow-white subgiant circle each other every 39 years on a stretched orbit. Their apparent separation changes from 0.1 to 0.6 arcseconds, so they can be resolved only for part of each orbit.

hip-82080.name: Epsilon Ursae Minoris
hip-82080.introduction: is an eclipsing binary in the Little Dipper, about 330 light-years away. A yellow giant and a smaller white star orbit each other every 39.5 days, edge-on to Earth.

sections.title: Discovered in three steps
sections.text: W. W. Campbell found that it is double in 1899, John Plaskett calculated the first orbit in 1910, and Paul Guthnick discovered the eclipses in 1946–1947. The tidal pull of the companion keeps the giant spinning at about 26 km/s.

hip-105858.name: Gamma Pavonis
hip-105858.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Pavo, only 30 light-years away, slightly smaller in mass than the Sun but almost one and a half times as bright. It is poor in heavy elements and, at about 5.9 billion years, older than the Sun.

sections.title: A target for finding another Earth
sections.text: Gamma Pavonis ranked 14th among the top 100 targets of NASA’s planned Terrestrial Planet Finder coronagraph, which was to search for rocky planets in habitable zones. Here, that zone lies about 1.2 AU from the star, a little beyond Earth’s distance from the Sun.

hip-92175.name: Beta Scuti
hip-92175.introduction: is a yellow bright giant in Scutum, about 690 light-years away, with a hot companion that circles it every 2.3 years. It was once known as 6 Aquilae.

sections.title: A companion pinned down
sections.text: Hubble observations hinted at the companion but were not conclusive. The Navy Precision Optical Interferometer then detected it directly, just 17 thousandths of an arcsecond from the giant. The same instrument measured the giant at about 49 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-13254.name: 16 Persei
hip-13254.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Perseus, about 126 light-years away, that is evolving away from its hydrogen-burning stage.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: About 1.4 billion years old, it spins at least 149 km/s, so fast that its equator bulges an estimated 24% beyond its polar radius. It may pulsate slightly, but a 1998 study found no variation.

hip-16228.name: CS Camelopardalis
hip-16228.introduction: is HD 21291, a blue-white supergiant in Camelopardalis about 3,100 light-years away, embedded in the reflection nebula vdB 14. It is visible to the naked eye under good conditions.

sections.title: A supergiant pair
sections.text: Hipparcos data revealed that it varies slightly, between magnitude 4.19 and 4.23, as an Alpha Cygni variable. A blue giant companion lies 2.4 arcseconds away, and a near-identical supergiant, CE Camelopardalis, lies half a degree to the south in the same group of young stars.

hip-86565.name: Omicron Serpentis
hip-86565.introduction: is a white star in the tail of the Serpent, about 159 light-years away.

sections.title: A 76-minute pulse
sections.text: It is a Delta Scuti variable whose brightness changes very slightly every 76 minutes. In 1909, the nova RT Serpentis appeared nearby, but it reached only 10th magnitude.

hip-60000.name: Beta Chamaeleontis
hip-60000.introduction: is a blue-white star in Chamaeleon, about 304 light-years away and only about 23 million years old.

sections.title: Spinning and pulsing
sections.text: With five times the Sun’s mass, it spins at least 255 km/s, which makes it bulge 12% at the equator. Measurements by the TESS space telescope show that it pulsates slowly, as many young B-type stars do.

hip-1599.name: Zeta Tucanae
hip-1599.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Tucana, about 28 light-years away, with nearly the Sun’s mass, size and temperature. It was one of the least variable stars measured by the Hipparcos satellite.

sections.title: A slightly older Sun
sections.text: About 5.3 billion years old, it turns once every 15.65 days and has a magnetic activity cycle of about 950 days. Excess infrared light shows a warm debris disk at least 2.3 AU from the star. Its Sun-like nature makes it a target in the search for life-bearing planets.

cns5-3401.name: i Centauri
cns5-3401.introduction: is 1 Centauri, a yellow-white star in Centaurus about 63 light-years away with an unseen companion.

sections.title: A ten-day orbit
sections.text: Spectra taken at the Cape Observatory between 1921 and 1923 showed its velocity changing, revealing a companion that orbits every 9.94 days. Astronomers have classified the primary in many ways, from a main-sequence star to a giant.

hip-12770.name: Pi Ceti
hip-12770.introduction: is a blue-white star in Cetus, about 388 light-years away near the border with Eridanus, with an unseen companion that circles it every 7.45 years.

sections.title: A suspiciously round orbit
sections.text: Such a long orbit is rarely so nearly circular. This suggests that the companion is a white dwarf whose orbit was rounded off when it transferred mass to the primary.

hip-68520.name: Tau Virginis
hip-68520.introduction: is a white star in Virgo, about 226 light-years away and some 700 million years old.

sections.title: Fast and bright
sections.text: With nearly twice the Sun’s mass, it spins at least 186 km/s and shines 70 times as brightly as the Sun. Its spectrum shows traits of both a hydrogen-burning dwarf and a subgiant.

hip-81852.name: Beta Apodis
hip-81852.introduction: is an orange giant in Apus, the Bird of Paradise, about 156 light-years away near the south celestial pole.

sections.title: An exotic bird
sections.text: Interferometers have measured its disk, showing that it is about 11 times as wide as the Sun. In Chinese astronomy it is the third star of the Exotic Bird.

msc-08585+1151.name: Acubens
msc-08585+1151.introduction: is Alpha Cancri, a white star in Cancer about 178 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the claws” of the crab.

sections.title: Two claws, two names
sections.text: Acubens and a second name, Sertan, from the Arabic for “the crab”, were traditionally shared with Iota Cancri, which marks the crab’s other claw. The US Navy ship USS Acubens was named after the star.

sections.title: A double tested by the Moon
sections.text: Acubens is a chemically peculiar Am star with an 11th-magnitude companion. It may also have a close partner 0.1 arcseconds away, but when the Moon passed in front of it in 2014, the light curve showed no sign of one.

hip-64394.name: Beta Comae Berenices
hip-64394.introduction: is a Sun-like yellow star in Coma Berenices, about 30 light-years away and about 2 billion years old. Despite its “beta” label, it is slightly brighter than Alpha Comae Berenices.

sections.title: A longer solar cycle
sections.text: Its surface activity follows a 16.6-year cycle, compared with the Sun’s 11 years, and there may be a second cycle of 9.6 years. It turns once every 11–13 days, with different latitudes rotating at different speeds, as on the Sun.

sections.title: A bronze vessel
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it is the first star of Zhōudǐng, a three-legged bronze food vessel formed with 37 and 41 Comae Berenices. A spectroscopic companion once suspected was ruled out by more precise measurements.

hip-61317.name: Chara
hip-61317.introduction: is Beta Canum Venaticorum, a nearby near-twin of the Sun in Canes Venatici, about 28 light-years away. With brighter Cor Caroli, it forms the “southern dog” of the Hunting Dogs.

sections.title: A top target in the search for life
sections.text: In 2006, astronomer Margaret Turnbull named Chara the top candidate star in the search for extraterrestrial life. It has about 3% less mass than the Sun, a radius 3% larger and 25% more light, and astrobiologists count it among the most interesting stars within 33 light-years.

sections.title: A standard for other stars
sections.text: Since 1943, its spectrum has served as one of the fixed reference points for classifying other stars. Its very weak calcium emission makes it a useful standard for measuring the activity of similar stars.

sections.title: Joy or beloved
sections.text: Chara means “joy” in Greek, but “dear” or “beloved” in Latin. The name first belonged to the whole southern dog before it was attached to this star. It is also listed in the New General Catalogue as NGC 4530.

msc-23159-0905.name: Psi¹ Aquarii
msc-23159-0905.introduction: is 91 Aquarii, an orange giant in Aquarius about 148 light-years away with a planet and a pair of companion stars.

sections.title: A planet confirmed after ten years
sections.text: A planet around the giant, 91 Aquarii A, was announced in 2003, but its confirmation was not published until 2013. The giant has expanded to more than ten times the Sun’s size.

sections.title: A pair in tow
sections.text: Two 10th-magnitude stars, B and C, share the giant’s motion 52 arcseconds away. They form their own tight binary, only 0.3 arcseconds apart.

hip-51172.name: Alpha Antliae
hip-51172.introduction: is the brightest star in Antlia, the Air Pump, an orange giant about 365 light-years away. It is one of the brightest stars without a proper name.

sections.title: A late-stage giant
sections.text: It is suspected to be on the asymptotic giant branch, with an inert carbon core. With 2.2 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 41 times the Sun’s radius. Benjamin Gould reported in 1879 that it varies in brightness, but modern observations have not confirmed this.

hip-16611.name: Tau⁵ Eridani
hip-16611.introduction: is a pair of blue-white stars in Eridanus, about 318 light-years away, that orbit each other every 6.2 days.

sections.title: A neighbor of galaxies
sections.text: The two stars are on average only 0.18 AU apart, less than half Mercury’s distance from the Sun. In the sky, the galaxy IC 1953 lies less than 10 arcminutes away, one of the brighter members of the Eridanus Group of galaxies scattered around the stars of Tau Eridani.

orb6-20467+1607-a-b.name: Gamma² Delphini
orb6-20467+1607-a-b.introduction: is the brighter star of Gamma Delphini, a wide double in Delphinus about 116 light-years away that marks a corner of the asterism “Job’s Coffin”. Seen in a modest telescope, the orange subgiant and its yellow-white companion, Gamma¹ Delphini, are often called one of the prettiest pairs in the sky.

sections.title: A 3,000-year orbit
sections.text: Christian Mayer found the double, and William Herschel observed it on 27 September 1779. The two stars have closed from 12 to 8.9 arcseconds apart since then. A preliminary orbit takes about 3,249 years and swings them between roughly 40 and 600 AU apart.

sections.title: Dhanishta
sections.text: In July 2026, Gamma¹ Delphini was named Dhanishta, after the Indian nakshatra, or lunar mansion, that corresponds to Delphinus.

sections.title: A planet in doubt
sections.text: Gamma² Delphini, a subgiant with twice the Sun’s mass, shows a velocity change every 1.44 years. A planet of at least 0.7 Jupiter masses orbiting at nearly 1.5 AU was proposed in 1999 as one explanation, but it remains unconfirmed.

hip-41075.name: Alsciaukat
hip-41075.introduction: is 31 Lyncis, the fourth-brightest star in Lynx, an orange giant about 368 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for “the thorn”.

sections.title: A restless giant
sections.text: With almost twice the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to 53 times the Sun’s radius. It is a semiregular variable, BN Lyncis, that changes between magnitude 4.21 and 4.27. Another old name, Mabsuthat, means “the outstretched paw”.

hip-11407.name: Kappa Eridani
hip-11407.introduction: is a blue-white star in Eridanus, about 526 light-years away and roughly 93 million years old.

sections.title: Measured across
sections.text: Interferometers have measured its tiny disk at 0.35 thousandths of an arcsecond, which makes it about six times the Sun’s radius. With five times the Sun’s mass, it shines about 1,200 times as brightly.

msc-04422+2257.name: Tau Tauri
msc-04422+2257.introduction: is a quadruple star system in Taurus, about 398 light-years away, near the ecliptic where the Moon can hide it. In February 2026, its primary received the name Gaja, from the Balinese elephant constellation that corresponds to Taurus.

sections.title: In the elephant’s tusk
sections.text: Gaja means “elephant” in Sanskrit, and Tau Tauri Aa marks the elephant’s tusk in a Balinese constellation attested in the Palelintangan calendar.

sections.title: Four stars, three orbits
sections.text: In 1903, Edwin Frost and Walter Adams found that the blue-white primary has a close partner that orbits every 2.96 days. A white star circles that pair every 58 years, and a fourth star lies 63 arcseconds away. The system belongs to a group of young stars between Orion and Taurus.

hip-8198.name: Torcular
hip-8198.introduction: is Omicron Piscium, a yellow giant in Pisces about 260 light-years away with a probable unseen companion. Its name goes back to a mistranslation in a 1515 edition of Ptolemy’s Almagest.

sections.title: Venus in front, 2027
sections.text: Torcular lies near the ecliptic, so the Moon and, very rarely, planets pass in front of it. On 13 May 2027, Venus will occult it as seen from Newfoundland and the Atlantic Ocean.

sections.title: A young giant
sections.text: Only about 390 million years old, it has three times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to more than 14 times the Sun’s radius. It most likely fuses helium in its core.

msc-02449+1007.name: Mu Ceti
msc-02449+1007.introduction: is a binary star in Cetus, about 87 light-years away, whose white primary and orange dwarf companion circle each other every 34 years. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon.

sections.title: Companions that vanished
sections.text: Three more companions were reported during lunar occultations, and an orbit of 1,202 days was even derived for one of them, but later studies found no trace of any. The TESS satellite showed that the primary is a Gamma Doradus pulsating star, about to become a subgiant.

hip-15510.name: e Eridani
hip-15510.introduction: is 82 G. Eridani, or HD 20794, a Sun-like star in Eridanus only 20 light-years away. As of 2026, it is the nearest Sun-like star with confirmed planets, including one that passes through its habitable zone.

sections.title: A planet in the habitable zone
sections.text: In October 2024, Oxford researchers analyzing 20 years of data confirmed HD 20794 d, a planet about six times Earth’s mass that orbits at a distance where liquid water could exist. Its orbit is so elliptical that it spends part of each year outside the habitable zone. It could be rocky or a mini-Neptune.

sections.title: Planets that came and went
sections.text: In 2011, European astronomers announced three super-Earths on orbits of 90 days or less. One, a 40-day signal, now appears to come from the star’s rotation instead. Further candidates proposed in 2017 remain unconfirmed, while 2023 studies confirmed the two remaining inner planets.

sections.title: An old, fast traveler
sections.text: About nine billion years old and nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life, it moves at 101 km/s relative to the Sun. It plows through the thin interstellar gas at more than three times the local speed of sound. The number 82 comes from Benjamin Gould’s 19th-century southern catalog, Uranometria Argentina.

hip-109139.name: Iota Aquarii
hip-109139.introduction: is a blue-white star in Aquarius, about 211 light-years away, first cataloged in Bayer’s Uranometria in 1603 but found to be double only in 2009.

sections.title: A hidden yellow partner
sections.text: A HARPS velocity survey revealed the companion in 2009, and its spectrum was detected directly in 2016. The yellow-white star, 1.2 times the Sun’s mass, orbits only 0.38 AU from the primary, roughly every 40 days. Hipparcos and Gaia data hint at a third member with an orbit of about a year.

hip-23972.name: Lambda Eridani
hip-23972.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Eridanus, about 900 light-years away, that gives its name to a type of variable star, the LERI type.

sections.title: A star near its breaking point
sections.text: It spins at least 327 km/s, close to the 440 km/s at which it would fly apart, and probably turns once every 1.4 days. Its fast rotation has spun off a disk of gas that we see edge-on. It was one of the first stars found to vary on a timescale of hours.

sections.title: An X-ray flare
sections.text: In 1993, Lambda Eridani produced a giant X-ray flare, becoming six times as bright in X-rays over 39 hours. It has about nine times the Sun’s mass and shines 14,700 times as brightly.

hip-21589.name: c Tauri
hip-21589.introduction: is 90 Tauri, a white star in the Hyades cluster in Taurus about 148 light-years away.

sections.title: A companion and a disk
sections.text: In 2014, astronomers announced an orange dwarf companion that orbits every 84 days or longer. The star, about twice the Sun’s mass, is also circled by a debris disk.

msc-03486-3737.name: f Eridani
msc-03486-3737.introduction: is a double star in Eridanus, about 165 light-years away, whose two white components lie 8.4 arcseconds apart and appear as one star to the naked eye.

sections.title: A young family
sections.text: Both stars belong to the Tucana–Horologium moving group, about 45 million years old. The brighter one spins at least 225 km/s. The fainter may itself be a close binary, with a Sun-like companion that would explain its X-rays.

hip-105515.name: Iota Capricorni
hip-105515.introduction: is a yellow giant in Capricornus, about 201 light-years away, with two giant planets discovered in 2022.

sections.title: Two super-Jupiters
sections.text: A combination of velocity and position measurements revealed two planets, both more massive than Jupiter. The inner one follows a highly elongated orbit.

sections.title: A spotted giant
sections.text: Iota Capricorni is magnetically active, and starspots make it vary as it turns once every 68 days. On 31 January 2034, Venus will pass in front of it, as seen from parts of Siberia, Mongolia and China.

hip-4577.name: Alpha Sculptoris
hip-4577.introduction: is the brightest star in the faint constellation Sculptor, a blue-white giant about 700 light-years away.

sections.title: A chemically spotted star
sections.text: Alpha Sculptoris is an SX Arietis variable, a hot star whose brightness changes by less than a tenth of a magnitude. With five times the Sun’s mass, it shines about 1,500 times as brightly.

hip-95294.name: Arkab Posterior
hip-95294.introduction: is Beta² Sagittarii, a yellow-white star in Sagittarius about 139 light-years away, probably with an unseen companion.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: It spins at least 155 km/s, so fast that its equator bulges 22% beyond its polar radius. In Chinese astronomy, it is the first star of the Celestial Spring, together with Beta¹ and Alpha Sagittarii.

hip-77055.name: Zeta Ursae Minoris
hip-77055.introduction: is a white star at the northernmost corner of the Little Dipper’s bowl, about 359 light-years away.

sections.title: Pulses, eclipses and dust
sections.text: It pulsates every 15.8 hours and also undergoes eclipses. Spinning at least 210 km/s, it may be about to become a giant, and a dust disk circles it at about 42 AU.

sections.title: The dimmer calf
sections.text: Some Arabic star charts call it “the dimmer of the two calves”, paired with Eta Ursae Minoris. The names may originally have described a pair of ibexes and belonged to the bowl’s two brightest stars, Beta and Gamma Ursae Minoris.

hip-4906.name: Epsilon Piscium
hip-4906.introduction: is a yellow-orange giant in Pisces, about 183 light-years away, cooler than the Sun but larger and brighter.

sections.title: Soaring Forever Star
sections.text: In Japanese it is called Haruto-boshi, “Soaring Forever Star”. A gas giant planet candidate was detected by its wobble in 2021, and lunar occultations hint that it may be a close double of two equal stars.

hip-57936.name: Beta Hydrae
hip-57936.introduction: is a double star in Hydra, about 310 light-years away, first reported as double by John Herschel in 1834. It was once known as 28 Crateris, until the constellation boundaries were fixed in 1930.

sections.title: A magnetic, spotted star
sections.text: The brighter star is a magnetic, chemically peculiar star with an unusual abundance of silicon, chromium and strontium. Its brightness changes every 2.34 days as it rotates. The Kalapalo people of Mato Grosso, Brazil, called it and Psi Hydrae Kafanifani.

hip-20711.name: Upsilon Tauri
hip-20711.introduction: is a white star in the Hyades cluster in Taurus, about 150 light-years away.

sections.title: Ten-hour days
sections.text: It rotates once every 0.415 days, about ten hours, which makes it bulge 9% at the equator. It also pulsates as a Delta Scuti variable every 3.56 hours. With Phi, Kappa and Chi Tauri, it formed the Arabic asterism Al Kalbain, the Two Dogs.

msc-00315-6257.name: Beta¹ Tucanae
msc-00315-6257.introduction: is the brightest member of Beta Tucanae, a loose family of six stars in Tucana about 143 light-years away. Three of them are bright enough to carry their own Bayer letters, Beta¹, Beta² and Beta³ Tucanae.

sections.title: Six stars, three groups
sections.text: Blue-white Beta¹ Tucanae has a faint companion at least 100 AU away. Beta², 27 arcseconds away, is a triple of white stars, two of them only 0.6 AU apart. Beta³, 9 arcminutes away, shares the group’s motion and is surrounded by a debris disk.

hip-111188.name: Beta Piscis Austrini
hip-111188.introduction: is a white star in Piscis Austrinus, about 147 light-years away. In September 2026, it received the name Tiangang, from the Chinese “Celestial Rope” used to pitch tents.

sections.title: A fast spinner seen from the pole
sections.text: It seems to rotate slowly, but we see it nearly pole-on, and its equator actually spins at about 314 km/s. This stretches its equator by about 26% and makes it 20% cooler than the poles.

sections.title: Dust and a Sun-like partner
sections.text: A debris disk circles it at about 12 AU. A Sun-like companion, CD−32°17127, shares its motion about 1,376 AU away.

hip-24845.name: Lambda Leporis
hip-24845.introduction: is a massive blue-white star in Lepus, about 970 light-years away, and a high-velocity runaway from the Orion OB1 association.

sections.title: Young and hot
sections.text: Only about eight million years old, it has around 15 times the Sun’s mass and a surface temperature of 30,400 K, shining about 15,500 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-22783.name: Alpha Camelopardalis
hip-22783.introduction: is a blue supergiant in Camelopardalis, roughly 5,600 light-years away. With about 38 times the Sun’s mass, it shines some 676,000 times as brightly.

sections.title: A runaway with a bow shock
sections.text: In 1961, astronomers suggested it is a runaway star ejected from the cluster NGC 1502. Its fast wind, pushed against the interstellar gas, piles up into a bow shock of dust that NASA’s WISE infrared telescope has imaged.

sections.title: A Sun’s mass every 160,000 years
sections.text: Its clumpy stellar wind carries away about one Sun’s worth of mass every 160,000 years. Spectral changes once taken as signs of a companion are now thought to come from its restless atmosphere and wind.

hip-61174.name: Eta Corvi
hip-61174.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Corvus, about 60 light-years away, with two belts of dust. Its inner belt glows brighter than its own collisions can explain, suggesting that comets are raining in from the outer belt.

sections.title: Comets falling inward
sections.text: The warm inner dust resembles cometary material, with primitive silicates, carbon compounds and water, and silica that points to collisions at 5–10 km/s. Planetesimals from the outer belt may be scattered inward, perhaps by planets, and destroyed near the star.

sections.title: A cold ring at 150 AU
sections.text: The outer belt, first imaged directly in 2005, lies about 150 AU from the star with a largely empty cavity inside. Webb observed the system on 20 May 2025. About 30% of the Sun’s age, the star spins more than 30 times faster than the Sun.

hip-20648.name: Delta³ Tauri
hip-20648.introduction: is a double star in the Hyades cluster in Taurus, about 154 light-years away and 0.72 degrees from Delta¹ Tauri. Some astronomy books call it Cleeia, after one of the Hyades sisters of Greek mythology.

sections.title: A possible blue straggler
sections.text: The white primary rotates slowly and shows the unusual metal lines of an Am star. It is a candidate blue straggler, a star that looks younger than the cluster around it. An 8th-magnitude companion lies 1.8 arcseconds away.

hip-115830.name: Theta Piscium
hip-115830.introduction: is an orange giant in Pisces, about 169 light-years away, the third star of the Chinese asterism Thunderbolt.

sections.title: Helium burning at 2.5 billion years
sections.text: About 2.5 billion years old and 1.6 times the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to about 11 times the Sun’s girth and now fuses helium in its core, shining 51 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-17531.name: Taygeta
hip-17531.introduction: is 19 Tauri, one of the bright stars of the Pleiades cluster in Taurus, about 343 light-years away. It is named after Taygete, one of the Pleiades sisters of Greek mythology.

sections.title: An early bloomer
sections.text: Taygeta is a blue-white subgiant, one of only a handful of stars in the young Pleiades that have begun to evolve away from the main sequence. It has served as a standard star for its spectral type.

sections.title: A tight pair
sections.text: It is a spectroscopic binary whose two stars, only 0.012 arcseconds apart, orbit every 1,313 days. An 8th-magnitude companion 69 arcseconds away is probably a yellow star farther away than the cluster.

sections.title: Taygetans
sections.text: Some modern UFO and contact literature claims that human-like beings called Taygetans come from here. These stories are not astronomical observations and have nothing to do with the real star.

hip-92791.name: Delta² Lyrae
hip-92791.introduction: is a red bright giant in Lyra, about 776 light-years away, and the brightest member of the scattered cluster Stephenson 1. In June 2026, it received the name Jiantai, from the Chinese “Clepsydra Terrace”, which represents timekeeping with water clocks.

sections.title: From blue to red
sections.text: It began life as a hot blue star of about five solar masses. Now near the end of its life, it has a carbon-oxygen core, has swollen to 290 times the Sun’s size and shines 10,200 times as brightly. It is a standard star for its spectral type and varies irregularly by about 0.2 magnitudes.

sections.title: Not a double after all
sections.text: Delta² Lyrae was once thought to form a binary with Delta¹ Lyrae, but they only line up from Earth. A pair of 10th-magnitude stars 87 arcseconds away may truly be bound to it, perhaps 24,000 AU away.

hip-42799.name: Eta Hydrae
hip-42799.introduction: is a blue-white star in Hydra, about 512 light-years away, and the faintest of the five stars forming the Water Snake’s head.

sections.title: Young and hot
sections.text: Only about 32 million years old, it has seven times the Sun’s mass and shines about 2,700 times as brightly. With other stars of the head, it belongs to the Chinese Willow mansion and to Unwala, “the Crab”, of the people of Groote Eylandt.

cns5-0923.name: 10 Tauri
cns5-0923.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Taurus, about 45 light-years away, and once the brightest star of the obsolete constellation Psalterium Georgii, “George’s Harp”.

sections.title: An older Sun
sections.text: About 5.7 billion years old, it has 1.14 times the Sun’s mass and has used up the hydrogen in its core, becoming a subgiant almost three times as bright as the Sun. Infrared light reveals a debris disk around it.

hip-11484.name: Xi² Ceti
hip-11484.introduction: is a blue-white star in Cetus, about 197 light-years away, used as a standard for measuring the brightness and colors of other stars.

sections.title: A past approach
sections.text: Only about 127 million years old, it has already started to evolve into a giant. It made its closest approach to the Sun about 2.7 million years ago, at about 128 light-years.

hip-70638.name: Delta Octantis
hip-70638.introduction: is an orange giant in Octans, about 299 light-years away. It is the southern pole star of Saturn.

sections.title: As old as the Sun
sections.text: About 4.3 billion years old, similar to the Sun, it has 1.2 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to about 25 times the Sun’s radius. In Chinese astronomy it is the fifth star of the Exotic Bird.

hip-42568.name: d Carinae
hip-42568.introduction: is V343 Carinae, a blue giant in Carina about 1,800 light-years away, with 12.5 times the Sun’s mass and about 6,300 times its light.

sections.title: A variable that settled down
sections.text: It was once thought to be a pulsating Beta Cephei star and a possible eclipsing binary, which earned it a variable-star name. It now appears nearly constant. Whether it has a close companion is still debated.

spectroscopic-hip-64241.name: Diadem
spectroscopic-hip-64241.introduction: is Alpha Comae Berenices, a pair of nearly equal yellow-white stars in Coma Berenices about 58 light-years away. It represents the crown of Queen Berenice, though it is slightly fainter than Beta Comae Berenices.

sections.title: Seen edge-on
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 25.87 years at an average distance of about 10 AU, roughly Saturn’s distance from the Sun. We see the orbit almost exactly edge-on, so they seem to move back and forth in a straight line, never more than 0.7 arcseconds apart.

sections.title: Eclipses still awaited
sections.text: Such an alignment should produce eclipses, but none has been seen because the predicted times were wrong. If they happen, the next primary eclipse is expected around 27 September 2040.

sections.title: A triangle with two clusters
sections.text: Diadem forms a triangle just over a degree across with the globular clusters Messier 53 and NGC 5053.

hip-84880.name: Nu Serpentis
hip-84880.introduction: is a white star in the tail of the Serpent, about 204 light-years away.

sections.title: A fast young spinner
sections.text: About 350 million years old, it has 2.6 times the Sun’s mass, spins at least 123 km/s and shines 76 times as brightly as the Sun. A 9th-magnitude star 46 arcseconds away is unrelated.

hip-88866.name: Pi Pavonis
hip-88866.introduction: is a white star in Pavo, about 134 light-years away, with an orange dwarf companion that circles it roughly every 150 years.

sections.title: A strontium-rich star
sections.text: The primary is chemically peculiar, with an excess of strontium. Its companion, about three-quarters of the Sun’s mass, orbits at about 39 AU. Hipparcos and Gaia data hint at a third, closer star.

hip-39863.name: Zeta Monocerotis
hip-39863.introduction: is a yellow supergiant in Monoceros, about 1,000 light-years away, with 6.2 times the Sun’s mass and about 2,200 times its light.

sections.title: Three faint neighbors
sections.text: Its surface, at about 5,300 K, is slightly cooler than the Sun’s. Three faint visual companions lie between 33 and 65 arcseconds away.

hip-76552.name: Omega Lupi
hip-76552.introduction: is a reddish giant in Lupus, just south of Gamma Lupi, about 213 light-years away, with a faint 11th-magnitude companion 11.4 arcseconds away.

sections.title: Measured across
sections.text: Interferometers have measured its disk, showing that the giant is about 40 times as wide as the Sun. Its faint companion is most likely bound to it in a wide orbit.

msc-23069-4331.name: Theta Gruis
msc-23069-4331.introduction: is a triple star system in Grus, about 132 light-years away.

sections.title: A magnetic star and two partners
sections.text: The primary is a magnetic, chemically peculiar yellow-white star with a close, fainter companion. A Sun-like star circles farther out.

hip-85822.name: Yildun
hip-85822.introduction: is Delta Ursae Minoris, a white star in Ursa Minor about 182 light-years away, the second star in the Little Bear’s tail. Its name comes from the Turkish yıldız, “star”.

sections.title: A small partner
sections.text: Adaptive optics revealed a 12th-magnitude companion with about 0.16 times the Sun’s mass, at least 237 AU away. Yildun itself spins at least 180 km/s, bulging 7% at the equator.

hip-43234.name: Rho Hydrae
