hip-43234.introduction: is a white star in the head of Hydra, about 312 light-years away, with an 11.9-magnitude companion 12 arcseconds away.

sections.title: Part of the snake’s head
sections.text: With Epsilon, Delta, Zeta and Eta Hydrae, it forms the compact head of the Water Snake. The primary has 3.2 times the Sun’s mass and is beginning to evolve away from the main sequence.

hip-60742.name: Gamma Comae Berenices
hip-60742.introduction: is an orange giant in Coma Berenices, about 164 light-years away. It appears to belong to the Coma Star Cluster but is probably not a member.

sections.title: Named for a cluster
sections.text: R. H. Allen gave it the name Al Ḍafīrah, from an Arabic name for the Coma Star Cluster. The giant is about 2.7 billion years old, rich in iron and most likely fusing helium in its core.

orb6-14262-4523-a-b.name: Tau² Lupi
orb6-14262-4523-a-b.introduction: is a binary star in Lupus, about 319 light-years away, whose yellow-white subgiant and white companion orbit each other every 26.2 years.

sections.title: An extreme orbit
sections.text: With an eccentricity of 0.94, their orbit is extremely stretched: the two stars spend most of their time far apart and swing close together only briefly.

hip-10324.name: Xi¹ Ceti
hip-10324.introduction: is a yellow giant in Cetus, about 314 light-years away, with a white dwarf companion. In October 2026, it received the name Bawy, an ancient Egyptian decan.

sections.title: The two souls
sections.text: Bawy, the dual form of Ba, “the soul”, is an Egyptian decan that probably corresponded to a pair of stars in Cetus, perhaps Xi¹ and Xi² Ceti.

sections.title: A giant and a white dwarf
sections.text: William Wallace Campbell found the companion in 1901 with the Lick Observatory’s Mills spectrograph. It orbits every 4.5 years at 3.8 AU, and in 1985 its ultraviolet light revealed it to be a white dwarf. The giant is classed as a mild barium star, although its excess of heavy elements is disputed.

hip-22509.name: Pi² Orionis
hip-22509.introduction: is a white star in Orion, about 218 light-years away, that spins fast enough to flatten itself noticeably.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: It spins at least 261 km/s, which makes its equator bulge 13% beyond its polar radius, and shines 70 times as brightly as the Sun. The Bright Star Catalogue lists it as a spectroscopic binary, but this does not appear to be the case.

msc-06573+5825.name: 15 Lyncis
msc-06573+5825.introduction: is a binary star in Lynx, about 178 light-years away, whose two yellowish stars appear only 0.9 arcseconds apart in a telescope.

sections.title: A 262-year orbit
sections.text: A yellow giant eight times the Sun’s radius and a yellow-white dwarf orbit each other every 262 years on a strongly stretched path.

hip-27100.name: Delta Doradus
hip-27100.introduction: is a white star in Dorado, about 149 light-years away. It is the south pole star of the Moon and of Jupiter.

sections.title: The Moon’s pole star
sections.text: The Moon’s axis wobbles in an 18.6-year cycle, and Delta Doradus is its south pole star once in each cycle, as it is now. At those times it lies closer to the Moon’s pole than Polaris does to Earth’s, though it is much fainter.

sections.title: X-rays from an unseen partner?
sections.text: Stars like Delta Doradus are not expected to produce X-rays, so the X-rays detected here may come from an unseen companion. Excess infrared light suggests a debris disk.

msc-18448+3736.name: Zeta¹ Lyrae
msc-18448+3736.introduction: is a white star in Lyra, about 158 light-years away, with an unseen companion that circles it every 4.3 days. In June 2026, it received the name Kautoki, “the adze handle”, from an asterism of the island of Kapingamarangi.

sections.title: The adze handle
sections.text: On Kapingamarangi, Vega and the stars Delta, Epsilon and Zeta Lyrae form Kautoki, the handle of an adze, a traditional woodworking tool.

sections.title: Found on photographic plates
sections.text: W. W. Campbell and H. D. Curtis discovered the companion in 1905 from Lick Observatory plates taken in 1902–1904, and Frank Jordan calculated an orbit in 1910 that still agrees well with modern results.

hip-28199.name: Gamma Columbae
hip-28199.introduction: is a blue-white subgiant in Columba, about 1,060 light-years away, that appears to be caught in a rare, brief stage of its life.

sections.title: The stripped core of a bigger star
sections.text: About 24 million years old, it is thought to be what remains of a once more massive star that has just finished burning hydrogen in its core and is readjusting its structure. This phase lasts only about ten thousand years. A faint yellow star shares its motion about 8,800 AU away.

msc-18232-6130.name: Xi Pavonis
msc-18232-6130.introduction: is a triple star system in Pavo, about 900 light-years away, with an orange giant at its center.

sections.title: An amateur’s double
sections.text: Australian amateur astronomer Walter Gale discovered its 8.6-magnitude companion 3.3 arcseconds away in 1894. The giant also has a hidden partner, revealed by its shifting spectrum, that orbits every 6.06 years.

hip-29807.name: Kappa Columbae
hip-29807.introduction: is an orange giant in Columba, about 188 light-years away, and a candidate runaway star moving about 20 km/s faster than the stars around it.

sections.title: Grandson
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it is the first star of Sūn, “Grandson”, together with Theta Columbae. About 622 million years old, it has 2.5 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to almost 11 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-116231.name: Beta Sculptoris
hip-116231.introduction: is a blue-white star in Sculptor, about 183 light-years away.

sections.title: Mercury and manganese
sections.text: Its spectrum shows strong overabundances of mercury, manganese and silicon, making it a chemically peculiar mercury-manganese star. It may vary slightly as it rotates, between magnitudes 4.35 and 4.39.

spectroscopic-hip-111022.name: 5 Lacertae
spectroscopic-hip-111022.introduction: is a binary star in Lacerta, about 2,200 light-years away, in which a cool orange or red supergiant is paired with a much hotter blue-white star.

sections.title: A 42-year orbit
sections.text: Early spectra already showed both a hot and a cool star. Their shifting spectral lines reveal an unusually long orbit of almost 42 years, with the stars about 15 AU apart. The pair also varies irregularly in brightness and carries the variable-star name V412 Lacertae.

hip-98412.name: Theta¹ Sagittarii
hip-98412.introduction: is a blue-white star in Sagittarius, about 680 light-years away, with an unseen companion that circles it every 2.1 days.

sections.title: A heavy, young subgiant
sections.text: About 33 million years old, the primary has 6.6 times the Sun’s mass, a peculiar spectrum and about 2,300 times the Sun’s light. Interstellar dust dims it by about a quarter of a magnitude.

hip-96757.name: Sham
hip-96757.introduction: is Alpha Sagittae, a yellow bright giant in Sagitta about 426 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic sahm, “arrow”, once used for the whole constellation; despite its “alpha” label, Gamma Sagittae is brighter.

sections.title: A puzzling stage of life
sections.text: Its temperature and brightness place it where stars evolve so quickly that few are found, yet its surface shows elements dredged up only after a star becomes a red giant. It belongs to a small group of carbon-deficient giants that may have exchanged mass with a partner. A 2025 study concluded that it is burning helium in its core.

hip-96837.name: Beta Sagittae
hip-96837.introduction: is a yellow giant in Sagitta, about 440 light-years away. In June 2026, it received the name Shakh, from the ancient Sumerian constellation of the Pig.

sections.title: The pig’s nose
sections.text: In the Sumerian constellation ŠAḪ, the Pig, Alpha and Beta Sagittae may have represented the animal’s nose. Only about 129 million years old, the giant has 3.8 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to nearly 26 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-33347.name: Iota Canis Majoris
hip-33347.introduction: is a blue-white supergiant in Canis Major, about 3,700 light-years away, with 14 times the Sun’s mass and about 52,000 times its light.

sections.title: A misaligned bow shock
sections.text: Iota Canis Majoris pushes against the interstellar gas and has created a bow shock, but the arc is not aligned with the star’s motion through the Galaxy. It varies slightly, between magnitudes 4.36 and 4.40.

cns5-gj-670.name: Xi Ophiuchi
cns5-gj-670.introduction: is a yellow-white double star in Ophiuchus, about 57 light-years away, whose 8.9-magnitude companion lies 4.1 arcseconds from the primary.

sections.title: The magician
sections.text: R. H. Allen recorded that, with Theta Ophiuchi, it formed the Sogdian “Magician” and the Khorasmian “Serpent-bitten”. The name Aggia, “the Magician”, appears in NASA lists, including a 2023 list of targets for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, but not in the IAU Catalog of Star Names.

hip-29038.name: Nu Orionis
hip-29038.introduction: is a blue-white star in northeastern Orion, about 604 light-years away, with an unseen companion. It should not be confused with the variable star NU Orionis.

sections.title: An eccentric partner
sections.text: The companion circles every 131 days on a stretched orbit. The primary has 6.7 times the Sun’s mass and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly.

msc-08079-6837.name: Epsilon Volantis
msc-08079-6837.introduction: is a quadruple star system at the center of Volans, the Flying Fish, about 651 light-years away, where it connects the fish’s wings.

sections.title: Two close pairs
sections.text: The bright blue-white primary is a pair of hot stars orbiting every 14.17 days. Six arcseconds away, the 8th-magnitude B component is a second pair of white stars that orbit every few days.

msc-06238+0436.name: Epsilon Monocerotis
msc-06238+0436.introduction: is a double star in Monoceros, about 135 light-years away, and a guide for finding the Rosette Nebula.

sections.title: A yellow-white companion
sections.text: The white primary has a 6.7-magnitude yellow-white companion about 12 arcseconds away. The primary may itself have a close companion with an orbit of about 331 days.

hip-22701.name: Omega Eridani
hip-22701.introduction: is a white subgiant in Eridanus, about 218 light-years away.

sections.title: A companion that disappeared
sections.text: Omega Eridani was long thought to have a companion with an 8.4-year orbit, but newer, more precise measurements show no sign of it. The star spins at least 186 km/s, which makes its equator 13% wider than its polar radius.

hip-93015.name: Kappa Pavonis
hip-93015.introduction: is a pulsating star in Pavo, about 620 light-years away, and the brightest W Virginis variable in the sky. Every 9.1 days, it brightens to magnitude 3.9 and fades to 4.8.

sections.title: Mistaken for an eclipsing binary
sections.text: When its variability was reported in 1901, its changing velocity was taken as the sign of a companion and the dimming as eclipses. It was soon recognized as a Cepheid and, in 1937, helped calibrate the Cepheid distance scale before astronomers realized that there are two distinct types of Cepheids.

sections.title: A swelling disk
sections.text: As it pulsates, its radius grows and shrinks by about three times the Sun’s radius, and its changing disk has been observed directly. Its period sometimes jumps by up to 16 minutes from its average of about 9 days and 2 hours.

hip-115102.name: Gamma Sculptoris
hip-115102.introduction: is an orange giant in Sculptor, about 189 light-years away.

sections.title: Helium in its core
sections.text: Four to six billion years old, it has 1.2–1.3 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to almost 12 times the Sun’s radius. It now fuses helium in its core, shining 53 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-85693.name: Maasym
hip-85693.introduction: is Lambda Herculis, an orange giant in Hercules about 393 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic miʽṣam, “wrist”.

sections.title: Where the Sun is heading
sections.text: In 1783, William Herschel used the motions of stars to work out the solar apex, the point in the sky toward which the Solar System is moving, and placed it close to Maasym. The modern position lies only about 10 degrees away, southwest of Vega.

sections.title: A standard giant
sections.text: Maasym is a standard star for its spectral type, with a surface temperature of about 4,000 K and more than 400 times the Sun’s total output. It may be about four or seven billion years old, depending on whether it still burns hydrogen in a shell or already burns helium in its core.

hip-8837.name: Psi Phoenicis
hip-8837.introduction: is a red giant in Phoenix, about 335 light-years away, in the last stage of its life before it becomes a white dwarf.

sections.title: A reference giant
sections.text: In 2001, the VLT Interferometer measured its disk and found it to be about 86 times the Sun’s radius. With its distance, size and luminosity known directly, it became one of 34 reference stars for testing models. Measurements suggest it has only about 5% of the Sun’s iron, though with large uncertainty.

sections.title: A slow flicker
sections.text: Olin Eggen discovered in 1973 that it varies between magnitudes 4.3 and 4.5. A long-suspected spectroscopic companion was ruled out when newer measurements showed a constant velocity.

orb6-20435+1504-a-b.name: Delta Delphini
orb6-20435+1504-a-b.introduction: is a pair of nearly identical stars in Delphinus, about 220 light-years away, and the prototype of a class of pulsating, metal-rich stars named after it.

sections.title: Twin pulsators
sections.text: The two stars orbit each other every 40.58 days. Both are chemically peculiar, with strong lines of strontium, europium and chromium, and both pulsate as Delta Scuti variables, with a dominant period of about 3.8 hours.

msc-07111+3015.name: Tau Geminorum
msc-07111+3015.introduction: is an orange giant in Gemini, about 393 light-years away, with a brown dwarf companion.

sections.title: A brown dwarf in a 305-day orbit
sections.text: In 2004, astronomers discovered Tau Geminorum b, at least 20.6 times Jupiter’s mass, circling the giant every 305 days. An 11th-magnitude orange dwarf about 187 AU away may also be bound to the system. The giant itself has twice the Sun’s mass and 30 times its radius.

cns5-3881.name: Lambda Serpentis
cns5-3881.introduction: is a Sun-like star in the head of the Serpent, about 39 light-years away and approaching at 66 km/s. In about 166,000 years it will pass only about 7.4 light-years from the Sun.

sections.title: A hot Neptune
sections.text: A planet candidate with at least 13.6 Earth masses and a 15-day orbit was detected in 2020 and confirmed in 2021. It is most likely a hot Neptune. The star is 9% more massive than the Sun and shines nearly twice as brightly.

hip-42402.name: Minchir
hip-42402.introduction: is Sigma Hydrae, an orange giant in the head of Hydra about 372 light-years away. Its name comes from the Arabic for the “nostril” of the Water Snake.

sections.title: The snake’s nostril
sections.text: Johann Bode’s Uranographia labeled it Minchir es-schudscha, and the Yale Bright Star Catalogue misspelled it as Al Minliar al Shuja. With the other stars of Hydra’s head, it forms the Chinese Willow mansion and the Crab of the people of Groote Eylandt.

sections.title: Young but swollen
sections.text: Only about 440 million years old, it has 2.8 times the Sun’s mass and has expanded to 28 times the Sun’s radius. It most likely fuses helium in its core.

hip-30060.name: 2 Lyncis
hip-30060.introduction: is a white star in Lynx, about 160 light-years away, with a companion on a 3.6-year orbit.

sections.title: A probable eclipse
sections.text: The pair is probably an eclipsing binary, known as UZ Lyncis, that dims by 0.3 magnitudes when one star passes in front of the other. The companion may produce the system’s X-rays, which stars like the primary rarely give off.

cns5-gj-167.3.name: Epsilon Reticuli
cns5-gj-167.3.introduction: is an orange subgiant in Reticulum, about 60 light-years away, with a giant planet and a white dwarf companion.

sections.title: A planet on a near-circular orbit
sections.text: On 11 December 2000, astronomers announced Epsilon Reticuli b, a planet at least 1.17 times Jupiter’s mass that circles the star every 418 days at 1.16 AU on an almost circular orbit. Like many giant-planet hosts, the star is rich in heavy elements.

sections.title: A white dwarf partner
sections.text: A 12.5-magnitude companion known since 1930 was confirmed in 2006 to share the star’s motion and in 2007 to be a white dwarf. It lies at least 240 AU away and takes more than 2,700 years per orbit. Once a white star of about 1.9 solar masses, it has been cooling for about 200 million years.

hip-7884.name: Nu Piscium
hip-7884.introduction: is an orange giant in Pisces, about 363 light-years away. Before the constellation boundaries were fixed in 1930, it was 51 Ceti.

sections.title: Barium from a white dwarf
sections.text: Nu Piscium is a weak barium star: its atmosphere was enriched with heavy elements from a companion that is now a white dwarf. In 2026, an Italian amateur group, GrAG, found that the giant oscillates.

hip-24327.name: Kappa Leporis
hip-24327.introduction: is a double star in Lepus, about 465 light-years away, whose blue-white primary and 7th-magnitude companion appear 2.2 arcseconds apart.

sections.title: A dusty candidate
sections.text: The primary has nearly five times the Sun’s mass and shines about 1,350 times as brightly. Excess infrared light makes it a candidate host of a debris disk.

hip-3786.name: Delta Piscium
hip-3786.introduction: is an orange giant in Pisces, about 300 light-years away. In September 2026, it received the name Waiping, from the Chinese asterism Wài Píng, the Outer Fence, of which it is the first star.

sections.title: A three-billion-year-old giant
sections.text: About three billion years old and 1.65 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 38 times the Sun’s radius. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon.

hip-110538.name: Beta Lacertae
hip-110538.introduction: is the fourth-brightest star in Lacerta, a yellow giant about 169 light-years away. In August 2026, it received the name Alsamaka, “the fish”.

sections.title: The smaller fish
sections.text: Its name recalls the Arabic asterism Al-Samaka al-Ṣuġrā, “the smaller fish”, in Lacerta and Andromeda. The giant fuses helium in its core and may have a companion 0.2 arcseconds away.

hip-54682.name: Beta Crateris
hip-54682.introduction: is a white star in Crater, about 315 light-years away, with a hot white dwarf companion that circles it every 6 years.

sections.title: A lightweight white dwarf
sections.text: The white dwarf, at about 36,900 K, has been cooling for only about four million years. It has just 43% of the Sun’s mass, which suggests that it gave away matter to its partner before becoming a white dwarf. The primary’s barium-enriched spectrum supports this.

sections.title: The ribs of Hydra
sections.text: The 16th-century astronomer Al Tizini included it in Al Sharāsīf, “the Ribs” of Hydra, a chain of stars running west to Kappa Hydrae.

hip-94648.name: Tau Draconis
hip-94648.introduction: is an orange giant in Draco, about 150 light-years away, with an unseen companion revealed by its wobble.

sections.title: An old, metal-rich giant
sections.text: About 6.5 billion years old, it has 1.25 times the Sun’s mass and shines 48 times as brightly. It is rich in metals but poor in carbon and oxygen.

hip-95771.name: Anser
hip-95771.introduction: is Alpha Vulpeculae, the brightest star in Vulpecula, a red giant about 290 light-years away. Its name, Latin for “goose”, comes from the constellation’s old name, Vulpecula cum Ansere, “the little fox with the goose”.

sections.title: From a swallowed galaxy?
sections.text: Anser has been studied as a member of the Arcturus stream, a group of fast-moving, metal-poor stars thought to be the remains of a small galaxy absorbed by the Milky Way. About 11 billion years old, it has swollen to 41 times the Sun’s radius. It forms a wide optical pair with 8 Vulpeculae.

msc-04406-4152.name: Alpha Caeli
msc-04406-4152.introduction: is the brightest star in Caelum, a yellow-white star about 66 light-years away with a red dwarf companion.

sections.title: A flaring companion
sections.text: The 12.5-magnitude red dwarf, Alpha Caeli B, is a flare star. It lies about 133 AU from the primary and takes about 1,110 years per orbit. A cold debris disk extends up to 46 AU from Alpha Caeli A.

sections.title: A close neighbor
sections.text: The nearest star to Alpha Caeli is LHS 1678, only 3.4 light-years away, closer than Proxima Centauri is to us. Alpha Caeli is probably a member of the Ursa Major moving group.

msc-05123-1152.name: Iota Leporis
msc-05123-1152.introduction: is a triple star system in Lepus, about 231 light-years away, led by a fast-spinning blue-white star.

sections.title: A spotted outer companion
sections.text: The primary, about 94 million years old, spins at least 185 km/s and has a close X-ray-emitting companion. The third member, AM Leporis, 12.7 arcseconds away, is a yellow star whose starspots make it vary.

hip-109111.name: Lambda Gruis
hip-109111.introduction: is an orange giant in Grus, about 249 light-years away. It came within about 183 light-years of the Sun some 805,000 years ago.

sections.title: A cooled, swollen star
sections.text: With 2.4 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 22 times the Sun’s radius and shines 155 times as brightly.

hip-23123.name: Pi⁶ Orionis
hip-23123.introduction: is an orange giant in eastern Orion, about 772 light-years away, with more than four times the Sun’s mass and about 88 times its radius.

sections.title: Dimmed by dust
sections.text: It shines about 2,200 times as brightly as the Sun, but interstellar dust dims it by about half a magnitude. It fuses helium in its core.

hip-13147.name: Beta Fornacis
hip-13147.introduction: is a yellow giant in Fornax, about 177 light-years away, about three degrees northeast of the globular cluster NGC 1049.

sections.title: After the helium flash
sections.text: About 3.3 billion years old, it has gone through a helium flash and now fuses helium in its core. It has 1.3 times the Sun’s mass and 10.5 times its radius.

hip-12843.name: Tau¹ Eridani
hip-12843.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Eridanus, about 47 light-years away, with a companion that circles it every 958 days. It passed within about 30 light-years of the Sun some 305,000 years ago.

sections.title: A disk that wasn’t confirmed
sections.text: Infrared excess measured by IRAS and published in 1993 was taken as a debris disk about 500 AU across. Spitzer observations published in 2004 found no substantial excess. The star was once known as 90 Ceti.

cns5-3615.name: Sigma Boötis
cns5-3615.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Boötes, about 51 light-years away, that appears next to Rho Boötis only by chance. In April 2026, it received the name Genghe, from the Chinese asterism of the Celestial Lance.

sections.title: Dust near the habitable zone
sections.text: Spitzer and Herschel found no infrared excess, but the HOSTS survey with the Large Binocular Telescope detected warm exozodiacal dust near the star’s habitable zone. The star, two to three billion years old, may be nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life and has a simple magnetic field.

cns5-gj-765.name: Theta Cygni
cns5-gj-765.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Cygnus, about 60 light-years away, with a faint red dwarf companion and a possible giant planet.

sections.title: A planet still unconfirmed
sections.text: In 2009, the ELODIE team proposed that velocity changes come from a planet about twice Jupiter’s mass orbiting every 150 days. Lick Observatory data show hints at the same period, but the signal has not reached statistical significance.

sections.title: A crowd of faint companions
sections.text: Theta Cygni B, a 13th-magnitude red dwarf 3 arcseconds away, orbits about 46 AU from the primary and may itself be a pair of red dwarfs. Several other faint stars nearby are either unrelated or possible distant companions.

msc-15234-5919.name: Gamma Circini
msc-15234-5919.introduction: is a double star in Circinus, about 449 light-years away, first noted as double by John Herschel in 1835.

sections.title: A stretched 258-year orbit
sections.text: A blue-white Be star, possibly itself a pair, and a yellow-white companion 0.8 arcseconds away orbit each other every 258 years on an extremely elongated orbit.

hip-29426.name: Xi Orionis
hip-29426.introduction: is a blue-white star in northeastern Orion, about 707 light-years away, well above Betelgeuse and next to Nu Orionis.

sections.title: A young pair
sections.text: Only about 32 million years old, the primary has 6.7 times the Sun’s mass and shines about 1,400 times as brightly. An unseen companion circles it every 45 days.

msc-21199-5327.name: Theta Indi
msc-21199-5327.introduction: is a double star in Indus, about 99 light-years away, with a white primary and a yellow companion 6.7 arcseconds away.

sections.title: Pairs within the pair
sections.text: The companion, Theta Indi B, is itself a binary whose two stars orbit every 30 years. Interferometry suggests that the primary is also a close pair, though its motion does not show the expected wobble.

spectroscopic-hip-107310.name: Mu Cygni
spectroscopic-hip-107310.introduction: is a binary star in Cygnus, about 72 light-years away, whose yellow-white primary and Sun-like companion orbit each other roughly every 800 years.

sections.title: Real and false companions
sections.text: Two more stars listed as companions are only chance alignments. One of them, the 7th-magnitude HD 206874, is itself a more distant pair of yellow-white subgiants.

hip-49641.name: Alpha Sextantis
hip-49641.introduction: is the brightest star in Sextans, a white giant about 430 light-years away that lies less than a quarter of a degree from the celestial equator.

sections.title: A star that crossed the equator
sections.text: In 1900, Alpha Sextantis was 7 arcminutes north of the celestial equator. The slow wobble of Earth’s axis carried it into the southern sky in December 1923.

sections.title: A 9-hour pulse
sections.text: Aven Magded Hamadamen discovered that it pulsates every 9.1 hours. About 385 million years old, it is nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life.

cns5-1793.name: I Puppis
cns5-1793.introduction: is QW Puppis, a yellow-white star in Puppis about 70 light-years away.

sections.title: Halfway through its life
sections.text: It is a Gamma Doradus variable whose brightness changes slightly every 0.96 days. With 1.5 times the Sun’s mass and an age of 1.6 billion years, it is about halfway through its hydrogen-burning life.

hip-49593.name: 21 Leonis Minoris
hip-49593.introduction: is a white star in Leo Minor, about 90 light-years away, and a member of the Sirius supercluster of stars moving together.

sections.title: A fast-spinning standard
sections.text: Spinning at least 155 km/s, it serves as the fast-rotating standard star for its spectral type. It pulsates as a Delta Scuti variable, and a debris disk circles it at about 62 AU.

spectroscopic-hip-104858.name: Delta Equulei
spectroscopic-hip-104858.introduction: is a pair of Sun-like stars in Equuleus, about 60 light-years away, and the constellation’s second-brightest star. In July 2026, it received the name Tepennekhet, “head of the Giant”, from an ancient Egyptian constellation.

sections.title: The Giant’s head
sections.text: The Egyptian constellation Nekhet, the Giant, appears on the Ramesside star clocks, and its head lay in Equuleus.

sections.title: A double hiding in a double
sections.text: William Herschel listed it as a wide pair, but Friedrich von Struve showed that the wide companion was unrelated. In 1852, his son Otto noticed that Delta Equulei itself looked elongated: it is a much tighter binary of two yellow-white and yellow stars.

orb6-13473+1727-a-b.name: Tau Boötis
orb6-13473+1727-a-b.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Boötes, about 51 light-years away, with a massive hot Jupiter and a faint red dwarf companion. In April 2026, its primary received the name Tepiamenit.

sections.title: A heavy, close planet
sections.text: In 1996, a team led by Paul Butler discovered Tau Boötis b, a planet six times Jupiter’s mass that orbits every 3.3 days. The star and planet appear to be tidally locked to each other, and in 2014 water vapor was found in the planet’s atmosphere.

sections.title: A flipping magnetic field
sections.text: Tau Boötis A was the first star other than the Sun seen to reverse the polarity of its magnetic field. Its magnetic cycle lasts only 122 days, and it rotates once every three days.

sections.title: A name rejected, then a new one
sections.text: In the 2015 NameExoWorlds vote, the IAU annulled the winning names because they did not conform to its rules. In 2026, the star became Tepiamenit, “predecessor of the mooring post”, from ancient Egyptian star clocks in which Menit marked the celestial pole.

sections.title: A red dwarf on a stretched orbit
sections.text: An 11th-magnitude red dwarf, Tau Boötis B, orbits the primary at a typical distance of about 220 AU, swinging in to about 28 AU. One orbit takes roughly 2,400 years.

hip-27530.name: Gamma Pictoris
hip-27530.introduction: is an orange giant in Pictor, about 186 light-years away.

sections.title: Measured across
sections.text: Interferometers show that it is about 11 times as wide as the Sun. With 1.5 times the Sun’s mass, it shines 53 times as brightly.

hip-31416.name: Xi² Canis Majoris
hip-31416.introduction: is a white star in Canis Major, about 408 light-years away, with an unseen companion revealed by its changing motion across the sky.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: About 339 million years old, it spins at least 145 km/s, which makes its equator bulge 12%. It has four times the Sun’s mass and shines about 250 times as brightly.

hip-116928.name: Lambda Piscium
hip-116928.introduction: is a white star in Pisces, about 104 light-years away, at the southeast corner of the Circlet asterism.

sections.title: Part of the Ursa Major Stream
sections.text: It lies among the outer members of the Ursa Major Stream, a group of stars that share a common heading through space. In Chinese astronomy, it is the fourth star of Cloud and Rain.

hip-111104.name: 6 Lacertae
hip-111104.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Lacerta, about 1,150 light-years away, with 12.5 times the Sun’s mass and about 35,000 times its light.

sections.title: A young massive binary
sections.text: Only about 16 million years old, it has an unseen companion that orbits every 880 days. It probably belongs to the Lacerta OB1 association of young massive stars.

msc-16272-4733.name: Epsilon Normae
msc-16272-4733.introduction: is a triple star system in Norma, about 623 light-years away. In June 2026, its primary received the name Yaqana, after the Inca dark constellation of the llama.

sections.title: The llama in the Milky Way
sections.text: Yaqana is an Inca dark constellation in the area between Centaurus and Scorpius, including Norma. Nearby lies a smaller dark shape, Uñallamacha, the baby llama.

sections.title: Twin hot stars
sections.text: The inner pair consists of two similar blue-white stars that orbit each other every 3.26 days. A smaller blue-white star, HD 147970, lies 22.8 arcseconds away.

hip-3881.name: Nu Andromedae
hip-3881.introduction: is a close binary in Andromeda, about 565 light-years away and just over a degree east of the Andromeda Galaxy.

sections.title: An escapee from a cluster
sections.text: A blue-white star and a yellow-white companion orbit every 4.28 days. The pair moves about 22 km/s relative to its neighbors, and its path suggests that it left the cluster NGC 6405 some 25 million years ago.

hip-44700.name: HD 77912
hip-44700.introduction: is a yellow bright giant in Lynx, about 700 light-years away, with 4.6 times the Sun’s mass and about 1,170 times its light.

sections.title: A possible runaway
sections.text: It moves about 23 km/s relative to its surroundings, which may mark it as a runaway star. Its spectrum shows a mild excess of barium.

hip-87072.name: X Sagittarii
hip-87072.introduction: is a Cepheid variable in Sagittarius, about 1,150 light-years away, that brightens and fades between magnitudes 4.2 and 4.9 every 7.01 days.

sections.title: Discovered in 1866
sections.text: Julius Schmidt discovered its variability on 4 August 1866. With each pulsation the star’s radius changes by about 9%, and two shock waves run through its atmosphere. A thin shell of material, perhaps carbon dust, surrounds it.

sections.title: A companion at the limit
sections.text: A companion with a 507-day orbit was suggested in 1990. The VLTI reported a faint detection in 2013, at the limit of the instrument, but a 2014 search failed to confirm it.

hip-52468.name: w Carinae
hip-52468.introduction: is V520 Carinae, an orange giant or supergiant in Carina about 1,500 light-years away. Only about 33 million years old, it has 7.9 times the Sun’s mass and has swollen to 217 times the Sun’s radius.

sections.title: An irregular glow
sections.text: Hipparcos data showed that it varies irregularly between magnitudes 4.50 and 4.59, earning it a variable-star name in 1999. It shines about 12,000 times as brightly as the Sun and may belong to the IC 2391 moving group.

orb6-09320-0111-a-b.name: Tau² Hydrae
orb6-09320-0111-a-b.introduction: is a white star in Hydra, about 586 light-years away, probably with an unseen companion.

sections.title: Part of the knot
sections.text: With Tau¹, Iota and 33 Hydrae, it was traditionally known as Ukdah, Arabic for “knot”; the name now belongs officially to Iota Hydrae. The primary shines about 285 times as brightly as the Sun.

cns5-gj-694.1.name: Psi¹ Draconis
cns5-gj-694.1.introduction: is a triple star system in Draco, about 74 light-years away, with a giant planet. Its primary, Psi¹ Draconis A, is named Dziban, from the Arabic for “the two wolves” or “the two jackals”.

sections.title: A Jupiter around the second star
sections.text: In 2015, astronomers found a planet, Psi¹ Draconis Bb, with at least 1.53 times Jupiter’s mass. It circles the yellow-white star B every 8.5 years on a fairly elongated orbit.

sections.title: A hidden third star
sections.text: Also in 2015, Dziban was found to be a close pair itself: its companion, C, orbits it roughly every 20 years. The A–C pair and B are about 31 arcseconds apart, and their preliminary orbit of 10,000 years is highly uncertain.

orb6-09521+5404-a-b.name: Phi Ursae Majoris
orb6-09521+5404-a-b.introduction: is a pair of nearly identical white subgiants in Ursa Major, about 509 light-years away, that orbit each other every 105 years. In about 4.7 million years it will pass within about 370 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: Throne and pond
sections.text: With nearby stars of the Great Bear, it formed the Arabic asterisms “the Throne of the daughters of Na’sh” and “the Pond”. In Chinese astronomy, it is the third star of the Administrative Center.

hip-92946.name: Theta¹ Serpentis
hip-92946.introduction: is the brighter star of Theta Serpentis, a wide pair of white stars in the Serpent’s tail, about 134 light-years away. It is named Alya, from the Arabic for “fat tail” of a sheep.

sections.title: A 10,000-year pair
sections.text: Theta¹ and Theta² Serpentis are 22 arcseconds apart, a separation that has barely changed since the first observations in 1755. At least 900 AU apart, they probably take on the order of 10,000 years per orbit. A 6.7-magnitude star nearby is a much closer, unrelated Sun-like star.

sections.title: The serpent’s tail
sections.text: An Arabic star catalog called it Dzaneb al Haiyet, “the serpent’s tail”. In Chinese astronomy, it represents the state of Xu in the Left Wall of the Heavenly Market Enclosure.

hip-18597.name: Delta Reticuli
hip-18597.introduction: is a red giant in Reticulum, about 541 light-years away, near the end of its life.

sections.title: A late-stage giant
sections.text: On the asymptotic giant branch, it has expanded to about 56 times the Sun’s radius and shines 1,100 times as brightly. Its orbit around the Galaxy ranges between 22,700 and 30,400 light-years from the center.

hip-94005.name: Delta Coronae Australis
hip-94005.introduction: is an orange giant in Corona Australis, about 185 light-years away. In August 2026, it received the name Qedty, from the ancient Egyptian constellation of the Two Nets used in star clocks.

sections.title: Burning helium
sections.text: About 2.8 billion years old and 1.5 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 11 times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium in its core.

hip-98688.name: c Sagittarii
hip-98688.introduction: is 62 Sagittarii, a red giant in Sagittarius about 452 light-years away and, at its brightest, the brightest of the four stars of the Terebellum asterism. In August 2026, it received the name Gouguo, from the Chinese name of that asterism.

sections.title: Land of dogs
sections.text: Gǒu Guó means “land of dogs”. It may represent an area for dogs around a farm, a legendary nation shown on Matteo Ricci’s world map, or the peoples of northern China. The name Terebellum went to Omega Sagittarii.

sections.title: Noted in 1879
sections.text: Benjamin Gould listed it as variable in his Uranometria Argentina in 1879. It changes irregularly between magnitudes 4.45 and 4.64, with several pulsation periods, and has swollen to about 72 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-110609.name: 4 Lacertae
hip-110609.introduction: is a blue-white supergiant in Lacerta, about 2,500 light-years away, with ten times the Sun’s mass and 36 times its radius.

sections.title: Back from red
sections.text: About 25 million years old, it is thought to have already passed through a red supergiant phase and to have heated up again. Its surface shows material processed by fusion in the core.

msc-09291-0246.name: Tau¹ Hydrae
msc-09291-0246.introduction: is a triple star system in Hydra, about 59 light-years away, led by a yellow-white star.

sections.title: Two companions
sections.text: An unseen companion circles the primary every 2,807 days, about 7.7 years. An orange star, B, lies 67.5 arcseconds away, about 1,120 AU from the primary. The primary shows long-term changes that may come from a magnetic cycle like the Sun’s.

hip-46952.name: 10 Leonis Minoris
hip-46952.introduction: is a yellow giant in Leo Minor, about 191 light-years away, also known as the variable star SU Leonis Minoris.

sections.title: An active giant
sections.text: It shows a high level of surface activity and varies by about 0.02 magnitudes. With 2.1 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 8.7 times the Sun’s radius.

hip-8833.name: Xi Piscium
hip-8833.introduction: is an orange giant in Pisces, about 196 light-years away, with a companion that circles it every 4.6 years.

sections.title: The South Cord
sections.text: In 1690, Johannes Hevelius divided Pisces into four parts and placed Xi Piscium in Linum Austrinum, the South Cord. William Wallace Campbell discovered its companion in 1901 with the Lick Observatory’s Mills spectrograph.

hip-17959.name: Gamma Camelopardalis
hip-17959.introduction: is a white subgiant in Camelopardalis, about 385 light-years away. In December 2025, it received the name Shaowei, the Chinese “Second Imperial Guard”.

sections.title: Which star is the guard?
sections.text: Shào Wèi is the sixth star in the right wall of the Purple Forbidden Enclosure. Yuan dynasty sources identified it with Gamma Camelopardalis, while later sources chose Alpha Camelopardalis.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: It spins at least 205 km/s, bulging 17% at the equator, and shines 185 times as brightly as the Sun. A 9th-magnitude star 106 arcseconds away may be a wide companion.

hip-56480.name: A Centauri
hip-56480.introduction: is HD 100673, a blue-white star in Centaurus about 401 light-years away.

sections.title: A disk from spinning
sections.text: A Centauri is a rapidly rotating Be star. Its spectrum shows emission lines from a disk of material it has thrown off, on top of the star’s normal absorption lines.

hip-36145.name: 21 Lyncis
hip-36145.introduction: is a white star in Lynx, about 274 light-years away.

sections.title: A slow spinner
sections.text: Its spectrum shows sharp lines, a sign of slow rotation. About 272 million years old, it has 2.2 times the Sun’s mass and shines about 100 times as brightly.

cns5-4459.name: Zeta Serpentis
cns5-4459.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Serpens, about 75 light-years away and approaching at about 51 km/s. In about 400,000 years it will pass within about 26 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: A bigger, faster Sun
sections.text: About 2.4 billion years old, it has 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, nearly twice its radius and 6.3 times its light, and spins at least 69 km/s.

hip-77760.name: Chi Herculis
hip-77760.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Hercules, about 52 light-years away, that appears to be passing through the solar neighborhood from another part of the Galaxy.

sections.title: A visitor in a quiet phase
sections.text: About 7.4 billion years old, it is poor in metals and moves at about 80 km/s, signs that it comes from elsewhere in the Galaxy. Its magnetic activity is unusually low, making it a good candidate for a quiet phase like the Sun’s Maunder minimum.

hip-77512.name: Delta Coronae Borealis
hip-77512.introduction: is a yellow giant in the Northern Crown, about 167 light-years away. In May 2026, it received the name Matrichakra, from the Indian name for Corona Borealis, “the circle”.

sections.title: A spotted, turning giant
sections.text: In 1989, astronomers noticed that its brightness changes slightly, between magnitudes 4.57 and 4.69. The cycle is now known to be its 59-day rotation, as differently spotted parts of its surface turn into view. It is a strong X-ray source because of its hot corona.

sections.title: Once a blue-white star
sections.text: For most of its life it was a hot blue-white star. It has just crossed the short-lived stage between the main sequence and the red giants, though it may already be burning helium in its core.

cns5-3864.name: g Lupi
cns5-3864.introduction: is HD 139664, a yellow-white star in Lupus about 57 light-years away, with a debris disk imaged by Hubble.

sections.title: A disk with a sharp edge
sections.text: Hubble’s coronagraph showed dust peaking about 83 AU from the star and ending sharply at 109 AU. These features may be shaped by planets. The star belongs to the Hercules–Lyra association, a group of stars about 257 million years old.

hip-78639.name: Eta Normae
hip-78639.introduction: is a yellow giant in Norma, about 234 light-years away, near the radiant of the Gamma Normid meteor shower.

sections.title: Helium in the core
sections.text: With 2.8 times the Sun’s mass, it has swollen to 11 times the Sun’s diameter and now fuses helium in its core, shining 72 times as brightly.

hip-22845.name: Pi¹ Orionis
hip-22845.introduction: is a young white star in Orion, about 121 light-years away and only about 100 million years old.

sections.title: Poor in metals, rich in dust
sections.text: It is a Lambda Boötis star, with less of the heavier elements than expected. A debris disk at about 49 AU contains dust totaling about 2% of Earth’s mass.

hip-84606.name: e Herculis
hip-84606.introduction: is 69 Herculis, a white star in Hercules about 175 light-years away, with a close 8.7-magnitude companion 0.84 arcseconds away.

sections.title: X-rays from the partner
sections.text: The primary, about 155 million years old, spins at least 155 km/s. Stars like it are not expected to give off X-rays, so the X-rays detected from the system most likely come from the companion.

hip-98543.name: 15 Vulpeculae
hip-98543.introduction: is a white star in Vulpecula, about 242 light-years away, also known as the variable star NT Vulpeculae.

sections.title: Losing its peculiarity
sections.text: It was a typical metallic-line Am star while burning hydrogen, but has lost most of those peculiarities as it evolves. In 1974, L. P. Metik found that it varies slightly over a 14-day period.

hip-42806.name: Asellus Borealis
hip-42806.introduction: is Gamma Cancri, a white star in Cancer about 175 light-years away. Its name is Latin for “northern donkey”: with Delta Cancri, it forms the Aselli, the two donkeys flanking the Praesepe cluster.

sections.title: A ghostly mansion
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it is the third star of the Ghost mansion. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon. A companion reported in 1910 is no longer accepted, and the star’s motion links it to the Hyades Stream.

hip-103738.name: Gamma Microscopii
hip-103738.introduction: is the brightest star in Microscopium, a yellow giant about 254 light-years away. About 3.8 million years ago, it was only about 6 light-years from the Sun and shone brighter than Sirius does today.

sections.title: A brilliant past
sections.text: At its closest it would have reached magnitude −3. Hipparcos data suggested an even closer pass about 3.9 million years ago, within 1–3.5 light-years, close enough to disturb the Oort cloud, but Gaia data did not confirm this.

sections.title: Borrowed from the Southern Fish
sections.text: Before Lacaille created Microscopium in 1756, it was 1 Piscis Austrini; its Greek letter was not assigned by Bayer. It is a helium-burning giant and a likely member of the Ursa Major Moving Group.

msc-01137+2435.name: Phi Piscium
msc-01137+2435.introduction: is a quadruple star system in Pisces, about 397 light-years away, led by an orange giant.

sections.title: A stretched 20-year orbit
sections.text: The giant, A, and the B pair, a visible star with an unseen red dwarf, orbit each other about every 20.5 years on a highly elongated path.

hip-27890.name: 36 Doradus
hip-27890.introduction: is 36 G. Doradus (HD 40409), an orange giant in Dorado about 89 light-years away, possibly with an unseen companion.

sections.title: An old, small giant
sections.text: About eight billion years old, it has 28% more mass than the Sun and has expanded to almost five times the Sun’s radius. It crosses the sky relatively quickly, about 0.57 arcseconds per year.

hip-28910.name: Theta Leporis
hip-28910.introduction: is a white star in Lepus, about 167 light-years away. It passed within about 29 light-years of the Sun some 1.6 million years ago.

sections.title: A fast young spinner
sections.text: About 207 million years old, it spins at least 207 km/s, bulging 10% at the equator, and shines 41 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-56633.name: Theta Crateris
hip-56633.introduction: is a blue-white star in Crater, about 300 light-years away, used as a standard for measuring the brightness of other stars.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: About 117 million years old, it spins at least 212 km/s, bulging 7% at the equator, and shines about 107 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-90595.name: Gamma Scuti
hip-90595.introduction: is a white star in Scutum, about 315 light-years away and approaching at 41 km/s. In about 2.35 million years it will pass only about 20 light-years from the Sun and may then be the brightest star in the night sky.

sections.title: A future brightest star
sections.text: At its closest it should reach magnitude −2.1. Today it spins at least 222 km/s, so fast that its equator bulges 21% beyond its polar radius, and it shines 150 times as brightly as the Sun.

xi-bootis.name: Xi Boötis
xi-bootis.introduction: is a pair of young Sun-like stars in Boötes, only 22 light-years away, and the nearest naked-eye star in the constellation. A small telescope shows a yellow primary and an orange companion 5 arcseconds apart.

sections.title: Two young neighbors
sections.text: At about 200 million years old, they are among the closest young Sun-like stars. They orbit each other every 152.5 years on a stretched path. Starspots make Xi Boötis A vary by about 0.15 magnitudes over 10 days.

sections.title: A possible Kuiper belt
sections.text: Infrared observations suggest that A is circled by a Kuiper-like belt of debris with at least 2.4 times the mass of the Moon.

hip-104521.name: Gamma Equulei
hip-104521.introduction: is a chemically peculiar star in Equuleus, about 115 light-years away, that pulses every 12 minutes and may take nearly a century to turn once.

sections.title: Fast pulses, slow spin
sections.text: It is a rapidly oscillating Ap star, with pulsations near 11.7, 11.9, 12.2 and 12.4 minutes. Its magnetic field changes slowly, and 67 years of measurements suggest a rotation period of about 97 years.

sections.title: Layered metals
sections.text: Its spectrum shows unusual amounts of strontium, chromium and europium, probably because the elements have settled into layers in its very slowly rotating atmosphere. An 8.7-magnitude companion lies 1.3 arcseconds away.

cns5-gj-9061.name: Chi Ceti
cns5-gj-9061.introduction: is a triple star in Cetus, about 77 light-years away, made of a yellow-white primary and a pair of smaller stars that share its motion.

sections.title: A spotted companion
sections.text: The 6.75-magnitude companion, EZ Ceti, is a Sun-like yellow star whose starspots make it vary every 8.9 days. A much fainter star accompanies it 6.7 arcseconds away. The primary may host a debris disk.

cns5-4846.name: Alsafi
cns5-4846.introduction: is Sigma Draconis, an orange dwarf in Draco only 19 light-years away. Since the MKK spectral atlas of 1943, it has been one of the fixed reference stars of the Morgan–Keenan classification system.

sections.title: Tripods of a desert kitchen
sections.text: Its name comes from the Arabic word for the tripods of the Bedouins’ open-air kitchens, once used for this star together with Tau and Upsilon Draconis. In Chinese astronomy, it is the second star of the Celestial Kitchen.

sections.title: A steady little star
sections.text: Interferometers measure it at 78% of the Sun’s radius, and it gives off 42% of the Sun’s light. It was among the least variable stars measured by Hipparcos, with a gentle cycle of 5–7 years like the sunspot cycle.

sections.title: A planet still unproven
sections.text: Keck and Lick velocity data from 2004–2013 hint at a Uranus-mass planet on a 308-day orbit, but the team has not ruled out other explanations. Later studies attributed longer signals to the star’s magnetic cycle.

hip-13954.name: Lambda Ceti
hip-13954.introduction: is a blue giant in Cetus, about 441 light-years away. It once bore the name Menkar, which today belongs to Alpha Ceti.

sections.title: Part of a hand
sections.text: With Alpha, Gamma, Delta, Mu and the two Xi stars of Cetus, it formed the Arabic Al Kaff al Jidhmah, “the Part of a Hand”. The star itself is about 100–125 million years old and has five times the Sun’s mass.

cns5-gj-9118.name: Kappa Reticuli
cns5-gj-9118.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Reticulum, about 71 light-years away, with an orange companion 54 arcseconds away.

sections.title: Moving with the Hyades
sections.text: Its motion through space places it in the Hyades supercluster. The primary gives off excess infrared light that suggests a debris disk.

hip-57283.name: Zeta Crateris
hip-57283.introduction: is a double star in Crater, about 341 light-years away, halfway between Epsilon Corvi and Delta Crateris.

sections.title: A giant in the Sirius supercluster
sections.text: Its primary is a yellow giant with 3.4 times the Sun’s mass, fusing helium in its core; a 7.8-magnitude companion lies only 0.2 arcseconds away. The system is a confirmed member of the Sirius supercluster and a candidate member of the Ursa Major Moving Group.

gj-189.name: Zeta Doradus
gj-189.introduction: is a young yellow-white star in Dorado, about 38 light-years away, with a distant orange dwarf companion. It is only about 580 million years old, an eighth of the Sun’s age.

sections.title: A wide pair
sections.text: Hipparcos data showed that the faint star Zeta Doradus B shares the primary’s motion about 3,700 AU away. Both stars are magnetically active, as young stars often are, and the primary has a debris disk several AU from it.

sections.title: A hint of a giant planet
sections.text: HARPS measurements ruled out massive planets close to the star. In 2025, a difference between Hipparcos and Gaia measurements of its motion suggested a giant planet farther out.

hip-105140.name: Epsilon Microscopii
hip-105140.introduction: is a white star in Microscopium, about 169 light-years away. In July 2026, it received the name Aerostaticus, as the brightest star of the obsolete constellation Globus Aerostaticus, the hot-air balloon.

sections.title: A balloon in the sky
sections.text: Johann Elert Bode labeled it “a” in his balloon constellation, and before Lacaille created Microscopium it was 4 Piscis Austrini. The star, about half a billion years old, has an excess of silicon in its atmosphere.

cns5-1332.name: Lambda Aurigae
cns5-1332.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Auriga, about 41 light-years away, receding quickly after passing within about 24 light-years of the Sun some 117,000 years ago.

sections.title: Capella in its sky
sections.text: Capella lies only about 4.5 light-years from Lambda Aurigae. Seen from there, it would shine at about magnitude −5.5, some 40 times as bright as Sirius appears from Earth.

sections.title: A quiet Sun
sections.text: With 8% more mass than the Sun and 78% more light, it shows little magnetic activity and is a candidate for a quiet phase like the Sun’s Maunder minimum. It may once have been called Al Hurr, “the fawn”.

hip-93542.name: Zeta Coronae Australis
hip-93542.introduction: is a young blue-white star in Corona Australis, about 179 light-years away and only about 76 million years old.

sections.title: Fast spin and cold dust
sections.text: It spins at least 308 km/s and shines 51 times as brightly as the Sun. Excess infrared light points to a ring of cold dust about 34 AU from the star.

cns5-3273.name: 61 Virginis
cns5-3273.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Virgo, about 28 light-years away, close to Spica in the sky. It has three known planets that all orbit closer to their star than Venus does to the Sun.

sections.title: Three close planets
sections.text: On 14 December 2009, astronomers using the Keck and Anglo-Australian telescopes announced three planets with minimum masses of 5–25 Earths. The outer two probably resemble Uranus and Neptune, while the innermost may be a mini-Neptune or a rocky super-Earth. The outermost, d, was once dismissed as a false positive but was confirmed in 2023.

sections.title: A comet-rich disk
sections.text: Spitzer revealed a cold debris disk, now placed between about 30 and more than 100 AU from the star. In 2012, ESA reported that it holds at least ten times as many comets as the Solar System’s Kuiper belt.

sections.title: An older Sun
sections.text: With 93% of the Sun’s mass and nearly the same chemical makeup, it is about 7.7 billion years old. Early parallax measurements in 1950 placed it about 550 light-years away; Gaia shows it is twenty times closer. From 61 Virginis, our Sun would be a 4.5-magnitude star near Hamal.

hip-6193.name: Upsilon Piscium
hip-6193.introduction: is a white star in Pisces, about 321 light-years away, also known as 90 Piscium.

sections.title: Near the end of its prime
sections.text: About 461 million years old, it is roughly 98% of the way through its hydrogen-burning life. With 2.2 times the Sun’s mass, it shines 107 times as brightly.

msc-02321-1515.name: Sigma Ceti
msc-02321-1515.introduction: is a triple star system in Cetus, about 75 light-years away, led by a yellow-white star.

sections.title: Close partner, distant partner
sections.text: A faint companion, Ab, orbits the primary every 21 years and has been resolved with the SOAR telescope; it was last closest in 2015. Far out, the orange dwarf HD 15767 shares their motion about 9,300 AU away, taking an estimated 500,000 years per orbit.

sections.title: The whale’s breast
sections.text: With Pi, Epsilon and Rho Ceti, it formed Al Sufi’s Al Sadr al Ḳaiṭos, “the Whale’s Breast”.

msc-02398-4254.name: s Eridani
msc-02398-4254.introduction: is HD 16754, a multiple star system in Eridanus about 144 light-years away. In 2026, interferometers revealed that its white primary is circled by a tight pair of Sun-like stars.

sections.title: A triple found in 2026
sections.text: The two smaller stars are only about 0.22 AU apart and probably orbit each other in about a month, while the pair circles the primary roughly every five years. The arrangement should make their orbits change noticeably within a decade. These young stars explain the X-rays from the system.

sections.title: Six stars in all
sections.text: A pair of red dwarfs, B, lies 25 arcseconds away, and another red dwarf, D, lies 10.9 arcminutes away. The system is about 160 million years old.

orb6-17370+6845-a-b.name: Omega Draconis
orb6-17370+6845-a-b.introduction: is a pair of yellow-white stars in Draco, about 77 light-years away, that orbit each other every 5.28 days on an almost perfectly circular path.

sections.title: The hyena’s claws
sections.text: With 27 Draconis, it formed the Arabic “hyena’s claws” in the asterism of the Mother Camels. In Chinese astronomy, it is the first star of the Royal Secretary. The primary has about 1.5 times the Sun’s mass, the secondary about 1.2.

cns5-4368.name: Lambda Arae
cns5-4368.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Ara, about 68 light-years away, with 40% more mass than the Sun.

sections.title: Dust and a possible twin
sections.text: Spitzer detected excess infrared light suggesting a dust disk more than 15 AU from the star. There is some evidence that it is actually a pair of stars with identical masses.

msc-12349+2238.name: Phyllon Kissinou
msc-12349+2238.introduction: is 23 Comae Berenices, a binary star in Coma Berenices about 356 light-years away, a few degrees from the north galactic pole. Its name comes from Ptolemy’s Almagest, which described it as “shaped like an ivy leaf”.

sections.title: An ivy leaf
sections.text: Ptolemy’s description probably referred to the shape of the Coma Star Cluster. The IAU approved the name in May 2024 and noted that Phyllon and Kissinou can be applied to the primary and secondary.

sections.title: A stretched 33-year orbit
sections.text: The white subgiant primary and its companion orbit every 33 years on an extremely elongated path. The primary, about 210 million years old, shines about 100 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-52502.name: HD 93194
hip-52502.introduction: is a blue-white star in Carina, about 479 light-years away, and a member of the open cluster IC 2602.

sections.title: A hot cluster star
sections.text: Its spectral type, B3/5Vn, marks a hot main-sequence star whose broadened “nebulous” lines indicate rapid rotation.

hip-82671.name: Zeta¹ Scorpii
hip-82671.introduction: is a blue hypergiant in Scorpius, about 5,600 light-years away and one of the most luminous stars known in the Milky Way, shining between one and 1.6 million times as brightly as the Sun.

sections.title: A sleeping giant
sections.text: Its brightness and spectrum mark it as a luminous blue variable, but it has not shown their typical outbursts, so it is classed as a dormant one. With about 36 times the Sun’s mass and 160 times its radius, it sheds a Sun’s worth of mass every 640,000 years.

sections.title: A misleading pair
sections.text: To the naked eye it forms a pair with orange Zeta² Scorpii, but Zeta² is only 135 light-years away and much less luminous. Zeta¹ belongs to the Scorpius OB1 association and possibly the cluster NGC 6231. A faint companion was found by interferometry in 2021.

cns5-0262.name: HD 5015
cns5-0262.introduction: is HR 244, a yellow-white star in Cassiopeia about 62 light-years away. It passed within about 38 light-years of the Sun some 546,000 years ago.

sections.title: An older subgiant
sections.text: About 5.3 billion years old and 1.2 times the Sun’s mass, it has left the main sequence and become a subgiant almost twice the Sun’s radius.

hip-15197.name: Zibal
hip-15197.introduction: is Zeta Eridani, a white star in Eridanus about 119 light-years away with an unseen companion that circles it every 17.9 days. Its name is an old misreading of the Arabic riʼal, “ostrich chicks”.

sections.title: Ostrich chicks and dust
sections.text: The Arabic name originally belonged to several stars near Beid and Keid. Zibal itself is about 800 million years old and is circled by a debris disk about 31 AU from the star. The star 14 Eridani is listed as a wide companion of the system.

hip-55687.name: Epsilon Crateris
hip-55687.introduction: is an orange giant in Crater, about 396 light-years away.

sections.title: A Sun-mass giant
sections.text: With about the same mass as the Sun, it has expanded to almost 45 times the Sun’s radius and shines about 390 times as brightly.

hip-85755.name: c Ophiuchi
hip-85755.introduction: is 51 Ophiuchi, a blue-white star in Ophiuchus about 409 light-years away, surrounded by a disk of gas and dust that may be a planetary system in the last stage of formation.

sections.title: A distant Beta Pictoris
sections.text: Like Beta Pictoris, it has an edge-on disk of gas and dust, and changing absorption lines suggest comets falling toward the star. The Keck Interferometer Nuller found a dense inner dust cloud about 4 AU across surrounded by fine silicate dust out to about 1,000 AU.

sections.title: Young or evolved?
sections.text: It spins at least 267 km/s, close to its breakup speed. It is uncertain whether it is a very young star, perhaps only 300,000 years old, or an older Be star. Spectra show that its disk is strangely depleted of carbon.

hip-111123.name: Sigma Aquarii
hip-111123.introduction: is a white star in Aquarius, about 206 light-years away, 1.3 degrees south of the ecliptic, where the Moon can hide it.

sections.title: Unusual abundances
sections.text: Its spectrum shows at least double the normal amounts of magnesium, aluminum and silicon. Hipparcos data suggest an unseen companion with an orbit of 654 days.

msc-12225+2551.name: 12 Comae Berenices
msc-12225+2551.introduction: is the brightest member of the Coma Star Cluster, about 284 light-years away: a yellow giant and a hotter white star that orbit each other every 396.5 days.

sections.title: A giant and a white partner
sections.text: W. W. Campbell announced its changing velocity in 1910, and Vinter Hansen published the first orbit in the 1940s. The giant has 2.6 times the Sun’s mass, the white star about twice the Sun’s mass.

cns5-gj-335.name: Sigma² Ursae Majoris
cns5-gj-335.introduction: is a double star in Ursa Major, about 67 light-years away, made of a yellow-white subgiant and a faint orange dwarf 4 arcseconds apart.

sections.title: A slow orbit
sections.text: The two stars move so slowly that their orbit is poorly known, with estimates from 970 to more than 1,500 years. With nearby stars, it formed the Arabic asterism of the Gazelles.

msc-08424-5307.name: HY Velorum
msc-08424-5307.introduction: is HD 74560, a blue-white star in Vela about 490 light-years away and a member of the open cluster IC 2391.

sections.title: Pulsing in a pair of pairs
sections.text: Shyam Jakate discovered in 1979 that it varies; it slowly pulsates with a dominant period of 1.55 days. An unseen companion orbits it every 8.4 days, and the binary KT Velorum, 76 arcseconds away, is most likely bound to it.

hip-52370.name: V518 Carinae
hip-52370.introduction: is HD 92938, a blue-white star in Carina about 483 light-years away, in the open cluster IC 2602 just 5 arcminutes from its brightest member, Theta Carinae.

sections.title: Outbursts from a disk
sections.text: Hipparcos data showed that it varies by about 0.2 magnitudes. It is a Be star with a disk of material, which produces outbursts lasting several hundred days. It is also rich in helium and possibly a blue straggler.

hip-52736.name: HD 93607
hip-52736.introduction: is a blue-white star in Carina, about 491 light-years away, in the core of the open cluster IC 2602.

sections.title: One of the steadiest stars
sections.text: It is on the list of the least variable stars measured by Hipparcos, changing by less than a hundredth of a magnitude. Its age is uncertain but around 17 million years.

hip-7007.name: Mu Piscium
hip-7007.introduction: is an orange giant in Pisces, about 350 light-years away.

sections.title: Older than the Sun
sections.text: About 5.6 billion years old and 1.25 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to about 37 times the Sun’s radius. In Chinese astronomy, it is the fourth star of the Outer Fence.

hip-93174.name: Epsilon Coronae Australis
hip-93174.introduction: is the brightest W Ursae Majoris variable in the night sky, about 102 light-years away in Corona Australis: two stars so close that they touch and share their outer layers.

sections.title: Stars in contact
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 14.19 hours, only 3.8 solar radii apart, and their combined light varies between magnitudes 4.74 and 5.0. Mass transfer has reversed their roles: the present primary started with about 1.1 solar masses and now has 1.7, while its partner has shrunk from about 2.2 to 0.2. The two stars will eventually merge.

cns5-3248.name: HD 114613
cns5-3248.introduction: is a yellow subgiant in Centaurus, about 67 light-years away, slightly older than the Sun. It is easily seen with the naked eye but has no Bayer letter, because Centaurus has so many brighter stars.

sections.title: A planet that faded
sections.text: In 2014, a 10.5-year velocity cycle was attributed to a planet about half Jupiter’s mass. A 2023 study instead found an 18-year signal that looks like a magnetic activity cycle, suggesting that the earlier signal was not a planet.

sections.title: A fast magnetic cycle
sections.text: It has a magnetic cycle of about 897 days, roughly four and a half times shorter than the Sun’s and one of the shortest known. It was among the 37 targets of the first southern-sky planet search, the ESO-CES survey of 1992–1998.

cns5-0840.name: Kappa¹ Ceti
cns5-0840.introduction: is a young Sun-like star in Cetus, about 30 light-years away, that offers a look at the Sun as it may have been when life began on Earth.

sections.title: The young Sun
sections.text: Only 300–400 million years old, it rotates about once every nine days, and starspots at latitudes from 10° to 75° make it vary slightly. Its magnetic properties make it “an excellent match for the Sun at a key point in the Earth’s past”.

sections.title: A strong wind
sections.text: Magnetic measurements from 2016 show an average field of 24 gauss. Models suggest that the star loses mass through its wind 50 to 100 times faster than the Sun does today. Since 1943, its spectrum has also served as a reference for classifying other stars.

msc-17323+5510.name: Nu² Draconis
msc-17323+5510.introduction: is the brighter star of Nu Draconis, a wide naked-eye pair in Draco about 97 light-years away. In May 2026, it received the name Alawaidh, from the Arabic “Mother Camels”, an asterism it shares with Rastaban, Eltanin, Alrakis and Grumium.

sections.title: Kuma rejected
sections.text: The pair was long called Kuma, a name of obscure origin from Antonín Bečvář’s 1948 atlas, but the IAU rejected it because an asteroid already carries it.

sections.title: Metallic stars
sections.text: Both Nu¹ and Nu² Draconis are Am stars with unusually strong metal lines. Nu² has a small unseen companion that orbits every 38 days at about 0.27 AU.

hip-59847.name: 7 Comae Berenices
hip-59847.introduction: is a yellow giant near the Coma Star Cluster, about 249 light-years away. It is approaching and will come within about 83 light-years in 2.4 million years.

sections.title: A young helium burner
sections.text: About 730 million years old and 2.4 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 10 times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium in its core.

cns5-4385.name: 58 Ophiuchi
cns5-4385.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Ophiuchus, about 56 light-years away.

sections.title: A slightly bigger Sun
sections.text: About 2.7 billion years old, it has 1.2 times the Sun’s mass, 1.4 times its radius and three times its light.

hip-11345.name: Rho Ceti
hip-11345.introduction: is a white star in Cetus, about 559 light-years away. In October 2026, it received the name Chugao, from the Chinese asterism of Hay, of which it is the first star.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: It spins at least 219 km/s, bulging 10% at the equator, and shines about 330 times as brightly as the Sun. With Pi, Epsilon and Sigma Ceti, it formed Al Sufi’s “Whale’s Breast”.

orb6-02396-1152-a-b.name: Epsilon Ceti
orb6-02396-1152-a-b.introduction: is a pair of yellow-white stars in Cetus, about 77 light-years away, that orbit each other every 2.65 years.

sections.title: A close pair
sections.text: The two stars are on average only 0.11 AU apart, a ninth of Earth’s distance from the Sun. The system is about 1.8 billion years old; the primary has 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, the secondary about the Sun’s mass.

msc-02359+0536.name: Nu Ceti
msc-02359+0536.introduction: is a triple star system in Cetus, about 404 light-years away, believed to belong to the Ursa Major stream of stars moving together.

sections.title: A giant with two partners
sections.text: A yellow giant fusing helium has an unseen companion that orbits every 1.96 years. A 9th-magnitude yellow-white star 8 arcseconds away, discovered by Struve, shares their motion.

hip-94820.name: d Sagittarii
hip-94820.introduction: is 43 Sagittarii, a yellow giant in Sagittarius about 480 light-years away. Lying near the ecliptic, it is sometimes hidden by the Moon.

sections.title: A young helium burner
sections.text: About 350 million years old and 3.3 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 24 times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium in its core.

cns5-4139.name: h Draconis
cns5-4139.introduction: is 19 Draconis, a yellow-white star in Draco about 50 light-years away, with an unseen companion that circles it every 52.1 days.

sections.title: A faint partner
sections.text: The primary is 4% more massive than the Sun. Its companion, revealed by the primary’s motion, has only 37% of the Sun’s mass and 2% of its light. The system is about 4.7 billion years old, much like the Sun.

gj-442.name: HD 102365
gj-442.introduction: is 66 G. Centauri, a Sun-like star in Centaurus about 30 light-years away, with a red dwarf companion. At 11–13 billion years, it is more than twice the age of the Sun.

sections.title: A planet demoted
sections.text: A Neptune-like planet with a 122-day orbit was reported in 2012, not confirmed in 2013, detected again in 2023 and missed in 2025 observations, which instead linked the signal to the star’s magnetic field. In April 2026, the NASA Exoplanet Archive listed it as a false positive.

sections.title: An old interloper
sections.text: W. J. Luyten discovered the red dwarf companion in 1960; it lies about 211 AU from the primary. The system moves within the Epsilon Indi Moving Group, but its age and composition show that it is only passing through.

cns5-gj-9332.name: Y Velorum
cns5-gj-9332.introduction: is HD 91324, a yellow-white star in Vela about 72 light-years away, poor in iron.

sections.title: A distant red dwarf
sections.text: A faint red dwarf found by combining 2MASS and WISE data shares its motion 309 arcseconds away, at least 6,700 AU from the primary. The main star is about 3.5 billion years old and shines 4.6 times as brightly as the Sun.

cns5-0049.name: 6 Ceti
cns5-0049.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Cetus, about 62 light-years away, and one of the IAU’s standard stars for measuring radial velocity.

sections.title: A steady reference
sections.text: It moves away from us at a constant 16.7 km/s, which makes it a reliable yardstick for other velocity measurements. About 4.2 billion years old, it is poor in iron and shines three times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-102831.name: Alpha Microscopii
hip-102831.introduction: is a yellow giant in Microscopium, about 394 light-years away.

sections.title: A young giant
sections.text: About 400 million years old and 3.2 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to 18 times the Sun’s radius. It was found to be a probable spectroscopic binary in 2014; a 10th-magnitude star 20 arcseconds away is unrelated.

hip-109422.name: Tau Piscis Austrini
hip-109422.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Piscis Austrinus, about 60 light-years away and about 1.3 billion years old.

sections.title: Celestial money
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it is the fifth star of Celestial Money. A near-infrared excess once suggested a debris disk, but it diminished in later observations.

orb6-02422+4012-a-b.name: 12 Persei
orb6-02422+4012-a-b.introduction: is a pair of yellow-white stars in Perseus, about 78 light-years away, that orbit each other every 331 days on a stretched path.

sections.title: Two stars bigger than the Sun
sections.text: Both stars are larger than the Sun, with 1.38 and 1.24 solar masses, and orbit at an average distance of 1.27 AU. A planet circling both would need to orbit beyond 4.35 AU to be stable, outside the system’s habitable zone.

cns5-3736.name: c Boötis
cns5-3736.introduction: is 45 Boötis, a yellow-white star in Boötes about 64 light-years away and a member of the Ursa Major Moving Group.

sections.title: A bigger Sun
sections.text: About 1.6 billion years old, it has 1.2 times the Sun’s mass, spins at least 40 km/s and gives off X-rays.

cns5-gj-503.name: HD 114837
cns5-gj-503.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Centaurus, about 59 light-years away and approaching at 64 km/s. In about 240,000 years it will pass within about 22 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: A possible companion
sections.text: A 10th-magnitude star 4.2 arcseconds away may share its motion. The primary is about 3.4 billion years old and slightly poor in iron.

hip-64166.name: Psi Hydrae
hip-64166.introduction: is an orange giant in Hydra, about 232 light-years away, probably with an unseen companion.

sections.title: Kafanifani
sections.text: The Kalapalo people of Mato Grosso, Brazil, called it and Beta Hydrae Kafanifani. Interferometers show that the giant is about 10.6 times the Sun’s radius, and it now fuses helium in its core.

hip-79509.name: Kappa Normae
hip-79509.introduction: is a yellow giant in Norma, about 469 light-years away.

sections.title: A swollen giant
sections.text: Having cooled and expanded after leaving the main sequence, it is now 18 times the Sun’s radius and shines about 190 times as brightly.

hip-115738.name: Kappa Piscium
hip-115738.introduction: is a white star in Pisces, about 160 light-years away, at the southeastern corner of the Circlet. Binoculars show it with two faint companions.

sections.title: A star with uranium
sections.text: Kappa Piscium is a chemically peculiar star with unusual amounts of silicon, strontium and chromium. Its spectrum shows many lines of uranium and possibly the rare element holmium; its uranium and osmium may have come from a nearby supernova. Its magnetic field makes it vary slightly as it rotates.

hip-62763.name: 31 Comae Berenices
hip-62763.introduction: is a yellow giant in Coma Berenices, about 275 light-years away, that lies near the north galactic pole. Jim Kaler has informally called it Polaris Galacticum Borealis, the north galactic pole star.

sections.title: A rare spotted spinner
sections.text: It is one of the rare FK Comae Berenices variables, giants that spin fast and carry large starspots; its variability was announced in 1997. It is crossing the brief stage between the main sequence and the red giants, and its outer layers have only just begun to churn.

cns5-2396.name: HD 84117
cns5-2396.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Hydra, about 49 light-years away, nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life.

sections.title: Dust and a possible planet
sections.text: A cold debris disk circles it at about 27 AU. A difference between Hipparcos and Gaia measurements of its motion suggests a giant planet. The star is about 2.6 billion years old.

hip-79822.name: Eta Ursae Minoris
hip-79822.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Ursa Minor, about 98 light-years away.

sections.title: The brighter calf
sections.text: Some Arabic star charts label it “the brighter of the two calves”, paired with Zeta Ursae Minoris. The names may originally have described ibexes and belonged to Beta and Gamma Ursae Minoris. The star itself is about 1.7 billion years old and may have a faint, distant companion.

cns5-gj-55.3.name: Kappa Tucanae
cns5-gj-55.3.introduction: is a system of five stars in Tucana, about 76 light-years away, arranged in two groups some 6,700 AU apart.

sections.title: Five stars, nested orbits
sections.text: The yellow-white primary has a red dwarf partner that orbits every 8.14 years, and a yellow star, B, circles that pair every 1,122 years. Far away, two orange dwarfs, C and D, orbit each other every 85 years, and the two groups take about 300,000 years to circle each other.

sections.title: Flickering hot dust
sections.text: Near-infrared light reveals hot dust, perhaps carbon, in a narrow ring 0.1–0.3 AU from the primary at temperatures above 900 K. The emission fades and reappears within a year, and the red dwarf’s closest approach coincides with the dust ring.

hip-60697.name: 14 Comae Berenices
hip-60697.introduction: is the second-brightest member of the Coma Star Cluster, a white star about 288 light-years away.

sections.title: A shell star
sections.text: It spins at least 226 km/s and is a well-known shell star, surrounded by gas thrown off by its rotation. Its peculiar spectrum has received at least eight different classifications.

orb6-01418+4237-a-b.name: HD 10307
orb6-01418+4237-a-b.introduction: is HR 483, a Sun-like star in Andromeda about 48 light-years away, with a red dwarf companion. In 2003, astrobiologist Margaret Turnbull named it one of the most promising nearby candidates for hosting life.

sections.title: A message on its way
sections.text: On 6 July 2003, the 70-meter Eupatoria Planetary Radar sent the Cosmic Call 2 message toward HD 10307. It will arrive in September 2044.

sections.title: A close companion
sections.text: The red dwarf, with as little as 38% of the Sun’s mass, orbits every twenty years, coming within 4.2 AU and receding to 10.5 AU. Its pull could disturb planets in the primary’s habitable zone. The system also has a debris disk.

cns5-0346.name: Nu Phoenicis
cns5-0346.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Phoenix, about 50 light-years away, somewhat more massive than the Sun and 45% richer in iron.

sections.title: A cold dust ring
sections.text: Excess infrared light reveals cold dust, at about 96 K, starting about 10 AU from the star. HARPS shows its velocity constant to within 2.7 m/s. The star is probably a few billion years old, perhaps about 4.2.

cns5-3319.name: 70 Virginis
cns5-3319.introduction: is a yellow star in Virgo, about 59 light-years away, near the border with Coma Berenices. Its giant planet was announced on 17 January 1996.

sections.title: An early exoplanet
