sections.text: Measurements with the Shane telescope at Lick Observatory revealed a planet at least 7.4 times Jupiter’s mass on a 117-day, elongated orbit. A dusty disk orbits the star at about 3.4 AU.

sections.title: An old star with faint companions
sections.text: About 7.9 billion years old, the star may be beginning to evolve into a subgiant. A very faint star with about 8% of the Sun’s mass, found in 2011, is probably a companion, and an L-type brown dwarf 43 arcseconds away may also be bound.

hip-78493.name: Iota Coronae Borealis
hip-78493.introduction: is a white star in the Northern Crown, about 370 light-years away, with a companion that circles it every 35.5 days. In May 2026, it received the name Aurwandilsta, from an old Norse constellation.

sections.title: Aurvandill’s toe
sections.text: Aurwandils tá, “Aurvandill’s Toe”, is an old Norse constellation identified with Corona Borealis. The star itself is a chemically peculiar mercury-manganese star about 273 million years old.

cns5-gj-584.name: Eta Coronae Borealis
cns5-gj-584.introduction: is a pair of Sun-like stars in the Northern Crown, about 58 light-years away, with a distant brown dwarf companion.

sections.title: Twin suns
sections.text: Known as a binary since the late 18th century, the two yellow dwarfs orbit each other every 42 years. Currently 0.5 arcseconds apart, they need a telescope of more than 25 cm to split. The system is about three billion years old.

sections.title: A brown dwarf far out
sections.text: In 2001, the 2MASS survey revealed a brown dwarf, Eta Coronae Borealis C, sharing the pair’s motion at least 3,600 AU away. It has about 63 times Jupiter’s mass.

cns5-4512.name: 36 Draconis
cns5-4512.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Draco, about 76 light-years away and about three billion years old.

sections.title: A red dwarf companion
sections.text: Observations in 2010 and 2012 found a faint companion 3.3 arcseconds away, probably a red dwarf. The primary has 1.2 times the Sun’s mass and shines 4.7 times as brightly.

msc-21477-3054.name: Theta Piscis Austrini
msc-21477-3054.introduction: is a pair of white stars in Piscis Austrinus, about 321 light-years away, that orbit each other every 20 years.

sections.title: Equal twins
sections.text: South African astronomer W. S. Finsen discovered in 1951 that it is double. Both stars have the same brightness and spectral type. The pair came closest to the Sun about 2.7 million years ago, at about 256 light-years.

gj-663.name: 36 Ophiuchi
gj-663.introduction: is a triple system of orange dwarfs in Ophiuchus, only about 19 light-years away. Its primary, 36 Ophiuchi A, is named Guniibuu, the robin red-breast of the Kamilaroi and Euahlayi peoples of New South Wales.

sections.title: A close pair and a distant third
sections.text: A and B are nearly identical orange dwarfs about 5 arcseconds apart. The third star, C, lies about 12 arcminutes away and was once called 30 Scorpii. Its rotation suggests an age of about 600 million years, younger than the 1.4 billion years estimated for the pair, perhaps because A and B slowed each other’s spin.

sections.title: A sweet spot for life
sections.text: NASA’s Giada Arney counted 36 Ophiuchi C among five nearby orange dwarfs in a “sweet spot” for the possible development of life. Hipparcos and Gaia measurements hint that it has a giant planet. On 26 October 2021, Venus passed in front of the system as seen from the Indian Ocean.

hip-18505.name: HD 24479
hip-18505.introduction: is a blue-white star in Camelopardalis, about 384 light-years away, identified as a Be star by Olin Wilson in 1932.

sections.title: Late in its prime
sections.text: About 256 million years old, it has completed roughly 86% of its hydrogen-burning life. It has 3.1 times the Sun’s mass, spins at least 85 km/s and shines 156 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-21861.name: Beta Caeli
hip-21861.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Caelum, about 94 light-years away, with a small companion imaged in 2022.

sections.title: Star or brown dwarf?
sections.text: Detected in 2017, the companion orbits about 5 AU from the primary every seven years. Its mass lies somewhere between about 0.08 and 0.2 solar masses, near the boundary between stars and brown dwarfs. The Gemini Planet Imager very likely captured it in 2022.

hip-21060.name: Delta Caeli
hip-21060.introduction: is a hot blue-white star in Caelum, about 680 light-years away and only about nine million years old.

sections.title: Young and luminous
sections.text: With seven times the Sun’s mass and a surface temperature near 19,600 K, it shines about 2,000 times as brightly as the Sun.

gj-231.name: Alpha Mensae
gj-231.introduction: is the brightest star in Mensa, a Sun-like star about 33 light-years away. At magnitude 5.1, it is the faintest star to be the brightest in its constellation.

sections.title: Named for Table Mountain
sections.text: In December 2024, Alpha Mensae A received the name Hoerikwaggo, the Afrikaans form of the Khoekhoe name of Table Mountain in South Africa, which the constellation Mensa represents.

sections.title: A Sun-like neighbor
sections.text: With 96% of the Sun’s mass and 81% of its light, it is about 6.2 billion years old. It passed within about 10 light-years of the Sun some 250,000 years ago. A red dwarf companion orbits about 30 AU away, and a 2023 study found a planet candidate whose one-year period may be an instrumental artifact.

orb6-03128-0112-a-b.name: 94 Ceti
orb6-03128-0112-a-b.introduction: is a triple star system in Cetus, about 75 light-years away, whose yellow-white primary hosts a giant planet.

sections.title: A planet and two red dwarfs
sections.text: On 7 August 2000, the Geneva planet-search team announced a planet found with the Swiss Euler telescope at La Silla. A pair of red dwarfs, which orbit each other yearly, circles the primary every 2,000 years. A cold dust disk lies about 95 AU from the primary.

hip-25110.name: HD 33564
hip-25110.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Camelopardalis, about 68 light-years away, and a candidate member of the Ursa Major Moving Group.

sections.title: A doubtful planet
sections.text: In September 2005, a massive planet on an eccentric orbit was reported from a small set of ELODIE measurements. No later study confirmed it, and a 2025 study considered it dubious. An apparent dust disk turned out to be a background galaxy.

msc-03492+2408.name: Pleione
msc-03492+2408.introduction: is a star of the Pleiades cluster in Taurus, about 448 light-years away, named after the mother of the seven Pleiades sisters. Otto Struve called it “the most interesting member of the Pleiades cluster”.

sections.title: Spinning almost to pieces
sections.text: Pleione rotates once every 11.8 hours, with its equator moving at 329 km/s, faster than Achernar and close to its breakup speed. It throws off gas that forms disks around its equator.

sections.title: A star that changes its look
sections.text: Over a cycle of about 35 years, Pleione switches between a normal B star, a Be star and a shell star as its disk appears, vanishes and reforms. In 2005–2007, a new disk formed tilted relative to the old one, a double-disk structure not seen around other Be stars.

sections.title: Hard to see beside Atlas
sections.text: Its neighbor Atlas, less than 5 arcminutes away, is 3.7 times brighter, which makes Pleione difficult to pick out by eye. A close companion orbits every 218 days and may cause the disk to wobble over about 81 years.

sections.title: Purple Pleione
sections.text: Pleione seems to have faded significantly between the 17th and 19th centuries and still varies between magnitudes 4.8 and 5.5. Chesley Bonestell painted it as “Purple Pleione”, flattened into a flying saucer, for the 1955 book The World We Live In.

hip-98920.name: Eta Sagittae
hip-98920.introduction: is an orange giant in Sagitta, about 156 light-years away.

sections.title: Helium in the core
sections.text: About 1.7 billion years old and 1.7 times the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to seven times the Sun’s radius and now fuses helium in its core. It is probably a member of the Hyades–Pleiades stream of stars moving together.

hip-51437.name: Beta Sextantis
hip-51437.introduction: is a blue-white star in Sextans, about 365 light-years away, and a primary standard star of the MK spectral classification system.

sections.title: A puzzling variation
sections.text: Although it has served as a standard for measuring brightness and colors, it is also listed as a variable with a suspected period of 15.4 days. That period is hard to reconcile with its fast rotation, at least 85 km/s, so the cause remains unresolved.

cns5-2425.name: 15 Leonis Minoris
cns5-2425.introduction: is a yellow star in Ursa Major, about 61 light-years away, despite its Leo Minor name. At about 9.3 billion years, it is twice the Sun’s age.

sections.title: A hint of a giant planet
sections.text: Having 15% more mass than the Sun, it may be starting to become a subgiant. Hipparcos and Gaia measured slightly different motions for it, suggesting an orbiting giant planet.

hip-91875.name: Lambda Coronae Australis
hip-91875.introduction: is a white star in Corona Australis, about 204 light-years away, with a 10th-magnitude orange companion 29.5 arcseconds away.

sections.title: A flattened spinner
sections.text: About 273 million years old, the primary spins at least 149 km/s, bulging 7% at the equator, and shines 31 times as brightly as the Sun.

hip-14240.name: Mu Horologii
hip-14240.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Horologium, about 141 light-years away, evolving beyond its hydrogen-burning stage.

sections.title: Between subgiant and giant
sections.text: About two billion years old and 1.5 times the Sun’s mass, it shines 13 times as brightly as the Sun and spins at least 79 km/s.

orb6-18070+3034-a-b.name: b Herculis
orb6-18070+3034-a-b.introduction: is 99 Herculis, a binary star in Hercules about 51 light-years away, surrounded by a debris disk that circles the pair over its poles.

sections.title: A polar disk
sections.text: Herschel images show a narrow ring of icy debris about 120 AU out, tilted to orbit over the poles of the binary rather than in its orbital plane. Simulations suggest that two planets on polar orbits may be sculpting it.

sections.title: A 56-year orbit
sections.text: W. R. Dawes discovered the companion in 1859. A yellow-white star poor in metals and an orange dwarf orbit each other every 56.3 years on a stretched path averaging about 16.5 AU.

orb6-05353-0523-ca-cb.name: Theta¹ Orionis C
orb6-05353-0523-ca-cb.introduction: is the most massive star of the Trapezium, the tight cluster at the heart of the Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away. Its ultraviolet light makes the whole nebula glow.

sections.title: Lighting the Orion Nebula
sections.text: Theta¹ Orionis C1 produces most of the ultraviolet light that ionizes and slowly evaporates the Orion Nebula. Its wind is a hundred thousand times stronger than the Sun’s and streams out at 1,000 km/s.

sections.title: The first magnetic O star
sections.text: In 2002, it became the first O-type star found to have a magnetic field, probably a fossil left from its formation. The field confines its wind and should cut its mass loss by 80%. A massive companion, C2, orbits it every 11.4 years.

hip-40843.name: Chi Cancri
hip-40843.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Cancer, about 59 light-years away. It passed within about 42 light-years of the Sun some 274,000 years ago.

sections.title: Older than the Sun
sections.text: About 5.8 billion years old and about the Sun’s mass, it is 1.4 times as wide and 2.4 times as bright. Infrared light hints at a dusty debris disk, and its motion suggests an unseen companion.

hip-105570.name: Beta Equulei
hip-105570.introduction: is a white star in Equuleus, about 319 light-years away, with a dusty debris disk about 104 AU out.

sections.title: Late in its prime
sections.text: About 600 million years old, it is 93% of the way through its hydrogen-burning life. Four stars that appear nearby are unrelated.

cns5-4390.name: Cervantes
cns5-4390.introduction: is Mu Arae, a Sun-like star in Ara about 51 light-years away with four known planets, named after Don Quixote and the people around him. Its innermost planet was the first hot Neptune discovered.

sections.title: Don Quixote in the sky
sections.text: In the 2015 NameExoWorlds vote, the Planetario de Pamplona named the star after Miguel de Cervantes and its planets Quijote, Dulcinea, Rocinante and Sancho: the hero, his love, his horse and his squire.

sections.title: Four planets
sections.text: Quijote was announced in 2001, and the hot Neptune Dulcinea, in a 9-day orbit, followed in 2004. In 2006, two teams found a fourth planet, making it the second known four-planet system after 55 Cancri. Quijote lies in the habitable zone, where large moons could in principle hold water.

sections.title: An older, richer Sun
sections.text: Its oscillations show that it is about 10% more massive than the Sun and about 6.3 billion years old. It has twice the Sun’s share of iron and may be starting to become a subgiant.

hip-90887.name: HD 170642
hip-90887.introduction: is a white star in Corona Australis, about 223 light-years away, rich in iron.

sections.title: A fast young spinner
sections.text: About 480 million years old, it has 2.25 times the Sun’s mass, 74% more iron than the Sun and spins at least 177 km/s.

hip-58188.name: Eta Crateris
hip-58188.introduction: is a white star at the lip of Crater, the Cup, about 251 light-years away. With Zeta and 31 Crateris, it forms an almost perfect right triangle in the sky.

sections.title: An ordinary hot star
sections.text: About 350 million years old, it has 2.6 times the Sun’s mass and shines 57 times as brightly at nearly 9,900 K.

cns5-2294.name: c Ursae Majoris
cns5-2294.introduction: is a pair of stars in Ursa Major, about 66 light-years away, that orbit each other every 16.2 days. In about 1.3 million years, the system will pass within about 10 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: An early spectroscopic binary
sections.text: In 1919, it was among the first 75 spectroscopic binaries discovered at the Dominion Astrophysical Observatory. The primary is a Sun-like yellow star; the much fainter companion is most likely an orange dwarf.

cns5-0247.name: Phi² Ceti
cns5-0247.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Cetus, about 52 light-years away, also known as 19 Ceti.

sections.title: A slightly bigger Sun
sections.text: About 1.9 billion years old, it has 1.2 times the Sun’s mass and 1.85 times its light. It may vary slightly, between magnitudes 5.15 and 5.24.

orb6-02225-2349-a-b.name: Kappa Fornacis
orb6-02225-2349-a-b.introduction: is a triple star system in Fornax, about 76 light-years away: a Sun-like star circled by a close pair of red dwarfs.

sections.title: A companion too faint for its mass
sections.text: Hipparcos and older data showed the star wobbling every 26 years around a companion nearly as massive as itself, yet too faint to see; it was first thought to be a white dwarf. After the companion was imaged in 2007–2008, a 2013 study showed that it is actually two red dwarfs orbiting each other every 3.7 days.

sections.title: An older Sun
sections.text: The primary, about a fifth more massive than the Sun, is 5–6 billion years old and starting to evolve toward a subgiant. The tight red-dwarf pair is kept active by its rapid, synchronized spin and is the source of the system’s X-rays.

hip-92202.name: R Scuti
hip-92202.introduction: is a pulsating yellow supergiant in Scutum, about 1,300 light-years away, and the brightest RV Tauri variable in the sky. It lies about a degree northwest of the Wild Duck Cluster, Messier 11.

sections.title: A chaotic light curve
sections.text: Edward Pigott discovered its variability in 1795, when few variable stars were known. At its brightest it is visible to the naked eye, and at its faintest it needs good binoculars. Its light curve is extreme even for its class, with deep minima, standstills that can last years and spells of chaotic change.

sections.title: A giant in disguise
sections.text: Its spectrum makes it look like a supergiant, but it is thought to be a highly evolved low-mass star, swollen near the end of its life, shining up to about 10,000 times as brightly as the Sun. The AAVSO holds more than 110,000 observations of it.

hip-25918.name: Gamma Mensae
hip-25918.introduction: is an orange giant in Mensa, about 107 light-years away, moving like the old stars of the Galaxy’s halo.

sections.title: An old traveler
sections.text: About 10.6 billion years old, it has nearly the Sun’s mass and has expanded to five times the Sun’s radius. Its high velocity marks it as a Population II star, though its composition is Sun-like. It probably has an unseen companion.

cns5-gj-863.2.name: Upsilon Aquarii
cns5-gj-863.2.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Aquarius, about 75 light-years away. In 2024, NASA named it one of the stars most accessible for the Habitable Worlds Observatory to survey for potentially habitable planets.

sections.title: A disk near the edge
sections.text: Excess infrared light points to a dusty debris disk about 84 AU from the star. A faint companion, found at the Gemini Observatory in 2007, lies at least 139 AU away, so the disk orbits close to the region its pull makes unstable.

mu-cassiopeiae.name: Mu Cassiopeiae
mu-cassiopeiae.introduction: is a pair of old stars in Cassiopeia, only 25 light-years away and approaching at 97 km/s. At about 12.7 billion years, Mu Cassiopeiae A may be the oldest star visible to the naked eye.

sections.title: From before the Galactic disk
sections.text: It was one of the first high-velocity stars identified and moves through the Galaxy at 167 km/s relative to the Sun. With only a sixth of the Sun’s heavy elements, the pair is thought to have formed before the Milky Way’s disk. Around 5200 AD it will cross into Perseus.

sections.title: A faint partner
sections.text: Nicholas Wagman found its unseen companion from its wobble in 1961, and Peter Wehinger resolved it in 1966 at Kitt Peak. The companion, more than 330 times fainter, is probably a red dwarf orbiting between 3.3 and 11.9 AU away. It shares the name Marfak, “the elbow”, with Theta Cassiopeiae.

cns5-gj-684.name: 26 Draconis
cns5-gj-684.introduction: is a triple star system in Draco, about 47 light-years away, whose two brightest stars orbit each other every 76 years.

sections.title: A red dwarf with a planet
sections.text: About 12 arcminutes from the yellow-white and orange pair, the red dwarf GJ 685 shares their motion and has a known planet detected from its wobble. The system may belong to the Ursa Major moving group.

hip-12484.name: Zeta Horologii
hip-12484.introduction: is a pair of yellow-white stars in Horologium, about 161 light-years away, that orbit each other every 12.9 days.

sections.title: Warm dust around two stars
sections.text: J. H. Moore found in 1911–1912 that it is double. Infrared light reveals warm dust, at about 260 K, probably in a disk circling both stars within 4.8 AU.

spectroscopic-cns5-0170.name: 13 Ceti
spectroscopic-cns5-0170.introduction: is a triple star system in Cetus, about 69 light-years away, that shares the motion of the Hyades moving group although it is too old to belong to it.

sections.title: Two orbits
sections.text: G. W. Hough found the visual pair in 1844; the two stars orbit every 6.9 years. In 1907, E. B. Frost discovered that the primary has its own orange dwarf partner, orbiting every 2.1 days. The primary is an active star, the variable BU Ceti, and gives off X-rays.

hip-48926.name: Eta Antliae
hip-48926.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Antlia, about 108 light-years away, with a faint 11th-magnitude companion 31 arcseconds away that probably orbits it.

sections.title: A bigger, hotter Sun
sections.text: It has 55% more mass than the Sun, a 72% larger radius and shines 6.6 times as brightly at about 7,100 K.

zeta-reticuli.name: Zeta Reticuli
zeta-reticuli.introduction: is a wide pair of Sun-like stars in Reticulum, about 39 light-years away, that can be seen as a double with the naked eye from dark southern skies. It is famous in UFO folklore as the supposed home of alien visitors.

sections.title: The Zeta Reticuli incident
sections.text: The 1966 book The Interrupted Journey reproduced a “star map” Betty Hill said she saw aboard an alien craft. A fan, Marjorie Fish, linked it to Zeta Reticuli, and by 1974 the story was called the Zeta Reticuli incident. In Cosmos in 1980, Carl Sagan showed that the map did not match the real sky.

sections.title: Two suns, far apart
sections.text: Zeta¹ and Zeta² Reticuli are 5.2 arcminutes apart, at least 3,750 AU, and take 170,000 years or more to orbit each other. Both are slightly poorer in metals than the Sun and belong to the Zeta Herculis Moving Group.

sections.title: A disk that wasn’t
sections.text: Spitzer and Herschel seemed to show a debris disk around Zeta² Reticuli. ALMA observations in 2017 revealed that the structure does not move with the star: it was background confusion, not a disk.

cns5-0052.name: Theta Sculptoris
cns5-0052.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Sculptor, about 71 light-years away, with an unseen companion revealed by its wobble. It may come within about 49 light-years of the Sun in half a million years.

sections.title: A bigger Sun
sections.text: About 1.6 billion years old, it has 1.25 times the Sun’s mass and three times its light.

cns5-0438.name: 107 Piscium
cns5-0438.introduction: is an orange dwarf in Pisces, only 25 light-years away, approaching the Sun. In about 136,000 years it will pass within about 15 light-years.

sections.title: Numbered twice
sections.text: John Flamsteed accidentally gave this star two numbers: 107 Piscium and 2 Arietis. In early Chinese astronomy, it was the leading star of the Official in Charge of Pasturing.

sections.title: A calm neighbor
sections.text: About 6 billion years old, it has 86% of the Sun’s mass and 44% of its light, turns once every 35 days and shows a Sun-like activity cycle. Its habitable zone lies between about 0.5 and 1.1 AU.

cns5-gj-392.1.name: HD 90089
cns5-gj-392.1.introduction: is a triple star system in Camelopardalis, about 75 light-years away, whose yellow-white primary was confirmed as a close pair in 2026.

sections.title: A hidden twin
sections.text: Gaia measurements hinted at a companion, and in 2026 it was detected directly, only 0.024 arcseconds from the primary and nearly as bright in infrared light. A red dwarf 14 arcseconds away, confirmed in 2018, completes the system, and a cold dust disk lies about 145 AU out.

orb6-18570+3254-a-b.name: HD 176051
orb6-18570+3254-a-b.introduction: is a binary star in Lyra, about 49 light-years away, with a giant planet discovered by astrometry. In about 269,000 years, it will pass within about 17 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: Whose planet?
sections.text: The planet was found from the tiny wobble of the system’s position, but it is not known which of the two stars it orbits. The stars, of about 1.07 and 0.71 solar masses, circle each other every 61.4 years.

cns5-gj-264.1.name: HD 53705
cns5-gj-264.1.introduction: is part of a quadruple system in Puppis, about 56 light-years away and one of the nearest of its kind: a Sun-like star, two orange dwarfs and a small red dwarf.

sections.title: Four stars, two pairs
sections.text: James Dunlop first measured the HD 53705/HD 53706 pair in 1826; it has barely changed since, with an orbit lasting millennia. HD 53680, about 4,400 AU away, has its own small companion of about 0.22 solar masses, revealed by its wobble.

sections.title: Twice the Sun’s age
sections.text: HD 53705 is about 9 billion years old and poor in metals. The system’s motion marks it as a member of the Galaxy’s thick disk, home to many of its older stars.

hip-24873.name: Nu Leporis
hip-24873.introduction: is a blue-white star in Lepus, about 352 light-years away, probably with an unseen companion.

sections.title: A fast spinner
sections.text: With 3.3 times the Sun’s mass, it spins at least 285 km/s and shines 138 times as brightly as the Sun.

cns5-2009.name: Mu² Cancri
cns5-2009.introduction: is a yellow subgiant in Cancer, about 78 light-years away and approaching. In about 611,000 years, it will pass within about 17 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: An older Sun
sections.text: About 5.6 billion years old, it has 1.2 times the Sun’s mass and is beginning to expand into a subgiant. It is richer in heavy elements than the Sun.

cns5-2859.name: 61 Ursae Majoris
cns5-2859.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Ursa Major, about 31 light-years away and about two billion years old. In Larry Niven’s Known Space stories, its third planet is the homeworld of the Kzinti.

sections.title: A spotted, active star
sections.text: Its surface shows strong, persistent starspots, and its rotation period, 16–18 days, differs between latitudes more than on most stars. A flare was caught in 2013. Since 1943, its spectrum has served as a reference for classifying other stars.

gj-356.name: 11 Leonis Minoris
gj-356.introduction: is a yellow star in Leo Minor, about 37 light-years away, with more than twice the Sun’s share of heavy elements.

sections.title: A stretched 201-year orbit
sections.text: A faint 14th-magnitude red dwarf circles the primary every 201 years on a highly elongated orbit. The primary is an active star whose brightness varies slightly over 18 days.

hip-92953.name: HD 175219
hip-92953.introduction: is an orange giant in Corona Australis, about 313 light-years away.

sections.title: Poor in metals
sections.text: With nearly twice the Sun’s mass, it has expanded to about 12 times the Sun’s radius. It has less than half the Sun’s share of heavy elements.

cns5-gj-288.name: 171 Puppis
cns5-gj-288.introduction: is 171 G. Puppis, a triple star system in Puppis about 50 light-years away and among the oldest star systems near the Sun.

sections.title: One of the coolest white dwarfs
sections.text: Far from the inner pair, the white dwarf Van Biesbroeck 3 shares the system’s motion. At about 4,600 K, it is one of the coolest white dwarfs known.

sections.title: An ancient pair
sections.text: The primary, with only 16% of the Sun’s metals, has probably left the main sequence. An unseen companion of at least 0.42 solar masses orbits it every 23 years.

cns5-gj-376.name: 20 Leonis Minoris
cns5-gj-376.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Leo Minor, about 49 light-years away, with a hot Neptune and a red dwarf companion.

sections.title: The first NEID planet
sections.text: A planet candidate found in 2020 was confirmed in 2024 as the first discovery of the NEID Earth Twin Survey. It has at least 9.2 Earth masses and orbits every 31 days.

sections.title: An older Sun
sections.text: About seven billion years old, the primary has 12% more mass than the Sun. An active red dwarf lies 14.5 arcseconds away, at least 2,000 AU from it.

gj-620-1.name: HD 147513
gj-620-1.introduction: is a young Sun-like star in Scorpius, about 42 light-years away, with a white dwarf companion far away. Giuseppe Piazzi first cataloged it.

sections.title: Polluted by its partner
sections.text: Only about 400 million years old, it is a barium star, enriched in heavy elements. The white dwarf, now about 5,360 AU away, may once have been closer and dumped material onto it late in its life.

sections.title: A planet in doubt
sections.text: In 2002, the Geneva team announced a giant planet orbiting mostly within the habitable zone. It was never independently confirmed, and a 2025 study did not detect it.

hip-92989.name: V686 Coronae Australis
hip-92989.introduction: is HD 175362, a hot blue-white star in Corona Australis about 476 light-years away, with an unusually strong magnetic field.

sections.title: A magnetic, spotted star
sections.text: Its magnetic field swings between about −5,000 and 7,000 gauss. Its surface chemistry is uneven, and it varies between magnitudes 5.25 and 5.41 as it rotates, perhaps every 7.34 days. It belongs to the Scorpius–Centaurus association.

cns5-4262.name: w Herculis
cns5-4262.introduction: is 72 Herculis, a Sun-like star in Hercules about 48 light-years away and approaching at 79 km/s.

sections.title: A very old Sun
sections.text: About 13 billion years old by one estimate, it has the Sun’s mass and is poor in metals. In about 98,000 years, it will come within about 32 light-years of the Sun.

cns5-5514.name: HD 211415
cns5-5514.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Grus, about 46 light-years away. In 2003, astrobiologist Margaret Turnbull named it one of the most promising nearby candidates for hosting life.

sections.title: A stretched orbit
sections.text: About 6.5 billion years old, it has a companion that circles it every 220 years on a highly elongated orbit averaging about 42 AU.

spectroscopic-hip-108661.name: Eta Piscis Austrini
spectroscopic-hip-108661.introduction: is a double star in Piscis Austrinus, about 817 light-years away, whose two blue-white stars appear 1.8 arcseconds apart.

sections.title: A spinning Be star
sections.text: The primary is a Be star about 115 million years old that spins at least 265 km/s and is surrounded by a shell of gas. Its brightness is widely reported to vary between magnitudes 5.33 and 5.44.

cns5-5664.name: Helvetios
cns5-5664.introduction: is 51 Pegasi, a Sun-like star in Pegasus about 51 light-years away. In 1995, it became the first ordinary main-sequence star known to have a planet, a discovery that won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.title: The planet that changed astronomy
sections.text: On 6 October 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced 51 Pegasi b, found at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence. The planet has at least half Jupiter’s mass but orbits so close that it reaches about 1,200 °C. Such a hot Jupiter did not fit theories of planet formation and led to ideas of planetary migration.

sections.title: Helvetios and Dimidium
sections.text: In 2015, a Swiss astronomy society named the star Helvetios, after the Celtic Helvetians of ancient Switzerland, and the planet Dimidium, Latin for “half”, for its mass of at least half a Jupiter.

sections.title: A quiet, older Sun
sections.text: About 4.8 billion years old, slightly larger and more massive than the Sun, it has been magnetically quiet for decades and may be in a phase like the Sun’s Maunder minimum. A possible second companion reported in 2026 is probably an instrumental artifact.

hip-17489.name: Celaeno
hip-17489.introduction: is 16 Tauri, one of the stars of the Pleiades cluster in Taurus, about 438 light-years away. It is named after one of the Pleiades sisters of Greek mythology.

sections.title: The lost Pleiad
sections.text: Theon the Younger called it the “Lost Pleiad”. It is a blue-white star about 3.4 times the Sun’s radius that spins at least 185 km/s. The US Navy cargo ship USS Celeno was named after it.

gj-666.name: 41 Arae
gj-666.introduction: is 41 G. Arae, a triple star system in Ara about 29 light-years away: a Sun-like star and a pair of red dwarfs.

sections.title: A millennium-long orbit
sections.text: The yellow primary and the red-dwarf pair orbit each other in about a thousand years on a highly elongated path; they were last closest in 1908. The two red dwarfs circle each other every 88 days. The system crosses the sky by more than an arcsecond per year.

cns5-4501.name: Iota Pavonis
cns5-4501.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Pavo, about 58 light-years away, with a small stellar companion found by its wobble.

sections.title: A hidden red dwarf
sections.text: About 7 billion years old, the primary is older than the Sun. Its companion has about 0.13 times the Sun’s mass and orbits about 9 AU away. Because no double-star catalog lists it, the star was included on NASA’s target list for future searches for Earth-like planets.

msc-01028+3148.name: Sigma Piscium
msc-01028+3148.introduction: is a pair of blue-white stars in Pisces, about 383 light-years away, that orbit each other every 81 days on an extremely elongated path. It was once known as 40 Andromedae.

sections.title: Legs of the sky
sections.text: In Chinese astronomy, it belongs to the Legs mansion. Its galactic orbit carries it between about 24,000 and 29,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way.

cns5-1198.name: 58 Eridani
cns5-1198.introduction: is a young Sun-like star in Eridanus, about 43 light-years away and probably less than a billion years old.

sections.title: Spots and dust
sections.text: Starspots make it vary slightly every 11.3 days, as the variable IX Eridani, and its X-rays reveal its youth. A disk of dust circles the star. It probably belongs to the IC 2391 moving group.

hip-92814.name: HD 175156
hip-92814.introduction: is a hot blue-white bright giant in Scutum, about 1,850 light-years away. To appear as a fifth-magnitude star from so far, it must be far more luminous than the Sun.

sections.title: A hot surface
sections.text: A fit to its hydrogen lines gives a surface temperature of about 14,000 K, more than twice the Sun’s.

cns5-gj-292.name: 212 Puppis
cns5-gj-292.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Puppis, about 60 light-years away, with an orange dwarf companion, 212 Puppis B.

sections.title: A nearby pair
sections.text: Listed as Gliese 292 A and B in the catalog of nearby stars, the two stars form a recorded double: a yellow-white F-type dwarf and a cooler orange K-type dwarf.

msc-06035+1941.name: 64 Orionis
msc-06035+1941.introduction: is a blue-white star in northern Orion, about 870 light-years away, that is a spectroscopic binary with a further close companion.

sections.title: A multiple hot star
sections.text: Its shifting spectral lines reveal a close partner, and double-star catalogs record another companion resolved nearby. The bright primary is a hot B-type dwarf.

msc-08400-5303.name: HD 74146
msc-08400-5303.introduction: is a blue-white star in Vela, about 496 light-years away, and one of the brightest members of the young open cluster IC 2391, the Omicron Velorum Cluster.

sections.title: A variable double
sections.text: It is a spectroscopic binary with a further visual companion, and it varies slightly in brightness, carrying the variable-star name NZ Velorum.

msc-10465-6416.name: HD 93549
msc-10465-6416.introduction: is a blue-white star in Carina, about 487 light-years away, and one of the brightest members of IC 2602, the cluster known as the Southern Pleiades.

sections.title: Several stars in one point
sections.text: Its spectrum reveals a close partner, and high-resolution observations resolve further companions, so the light of this cluster star comes from a small multiple system. Its combined light points to a surface temperature of about 13,300 K.

cns5-gj-857.name: HD 212330
cns5-gj-857.introduction: is a Sun-like star in Tucana, about 66 light-years away, slightly cooler than the Sun and beginning to evolve beyond its hydrogen-burning stage.

sections.title: A spectroscopic binary with a partner
sections.text: Listed as Gliese 857, it is a spectroscopic binary, and a fainter companion, HD 212330 B, is recorded nearby in double-star catalogs.

orb6-07490-2455-a-b.name: 188 Puppis
orb6-07490-2455-a-b.introduction: is a yellow giant in Puppis, about 201 light-years away, with a close companion on a measured orbit.

sections.title: A slightly metal-poor giant
sections.text: Its spectrum classifies it as a yellow giant slightly poor in iron. Andrei Tokovinin resolved its companion, listed as TOK 194.

hip-22730.name: 5 Orionis
hip-22730.introduction: is a red giant in Orion, about 615 light-years away, near the end of its life.

sections.title: A cool, swollen star
sections.text: With a surface temperature of only about 3,800 K, an early M-type giant like this has expanded to dozens of times the Sun’s radius.

cns5-1853.name: 22 Lyncis
cns5-1853.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Lynx, about 67 light-years away and approaching at about 27 km/s.

sections.title: A slightly bigger Sun
sections.text: It is an F-type dwarf, a little hotter and brighter than the Sun, listed in the Gliese catalog of nearby stars as GJ 9234. Double-star catalogs record a faint visual companion.

hip-1645.name: d Piscium
hip-1645.introduction: is 41 Piscium, an orange giant in Pisces about 460 light-years away.

sections.title: An evolved giant
sections.text: Its K-type spectrum marks a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen into a giant, with a surface temperature near 4,400 K.

cns5-1004.name: HD 25457
cns5-1004.introduction: is a yellow-white star in Eridanus, about 61 light-years away, that SIMBAD classifies as a young star.

sections.title: A young nearby Sun
sections.text: Listed as Gliese 159, it is an F-type dwarf a little hotter than the Sun, at about 6,200 K.

hip-42459.name: HW Velorum
hip-42459.introduction: is HD 74071, a blue-white star in Vela about 518 light-years away and a member of the young open cluster IC 2391, the Omicron Velorum Cluster.

sections.title: A pulsating cluster star
sections.text: HW Velorum is classified as a Beta Cephei variable, a hot star whose brightness changes slightly as it pulsates.
